provenance.notes: The pre-flag is right to hedge. Angelou did use versions of this in interviews and talks from the 1990s onward, so the attribution is not fabricated — but the aphorism predates her. The earliest known instance credits Carl W. Buehner: 'They may forget what you said, but they will never forget how you made them feel,' printed in Richard L. Evans's Quote Book (1971). Angelou's characteristic triad ('what you said / what you did / how you made them feel') is her expansion of an existing saying, and I cannot fix a first Angelou utterance or its exact wording. Safest handling: treat the wording as unverified and do not present it as an original Angelou line.

text: The best way to predict the future is to create it.
text_raw: The best way to predict the future is to create it.
author: Peter Drucker (attributed with no evidence to Abraham Lincoln)
author_raw: Peter Drucker (attributed with no evidence to Abraham Lincoln)

flags.suspect_reason: Not Lincoln. Often attributed to Peter Drucker or Alan Kay.

provenance.notes: Definitely not Lincoln — nothing like it appears in the Collected Works, and the managerial idiom is anachronistic for the 1860s; it is a standard Lincoln graft. The Drucker attribution in the author field is the common replacement but is itself weakly evidenced: I cannot point to the book or article where Drucker wrote it. The best-documented neighbor is Alan Kay's 'The best way to predict the future is to invent it' (Xerox PARC, early 1970s), and Dennis Gabor's Inventing the Future (1963) argues that the future cannot be predicted but can be invented. The 'create it' variant floats between Drucker, Kay, Gabor, and Forrest Shaklee. Since I cannot say which is right, no reattribution.

text: It is not easy to find happiness in ourselves, and it is not possible to find it elsewhere.
text_raw: It is not easy to find happiness in ourselves, and it is not possible to find it elsewhere.
author: Agnes Repplier

provenance.notes: Consistently and, as far as I know, uncontestedly attributed to the American essayist Agnes Repplier (1855-1950), and the epigrammatic balance is characteristic of her prose. It is usually cited to one of her essay collections — Compromises (1904) is the volume most often named — but I cannot confirm the volume or essay from memory, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing. Attribution is stable; the citation is not established.

text: Keeping your commitment to your purpose does not depend on other people keeping theirs.
text_raw: Keeping your commitment to your purpose does not depend on other people keeping theirs.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: Same situation as q_0166. Attributed to Alan Cohen wherever it appears and consistent with his register, but recirculated without citation and not placeable in a specific book or column from training knowledge. Uncontested but unsourced.

text: Happy people do not demand a lot from the world because their happiness proceeds from a place deeper than the world can touch.
text_raw: Happy people do not demand a lot from the world because their happiness proceeds from a place deeper than the world can touch.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: As with the other two Alan Cohen entries in this batch: plausible, uncontested, and unsourced. I cannot place it in a titled work, and Cohen's material circulates chiefly through daily-inspiration excerpts that drop citations.

text: The individual is an aperture through which the whole energy of the universe is aware of itself.
text_raw: The individual is an aperture through which the whole energy of the universe is aware of itself.
author: Alan Watts

provenance.notes: Strongly Wattsian in both idea and vocabulary — 'aperture' is a word he genuinely used for the individual as the universe's point of self-awareness, and the thought parallels the documented passages in The Book: On the Taboo Against Knowing Who You Are (1966) about the universe peopling and looking at itself through our eyes. I cannot confirm this exact sentence in a printed Watts text, and much of the Watts material online comes from loosely transcribed lectures. Likely genuine in substance, wording unverified.

text: The only way to make sense out of change is to plunge into it, move with it, and join the dance.
text_raw: The only way to make sense out of change is to plunge into it, move with it, and join the dance.
author: Alan Watts

provenance.notes: One of the most widely reproduced Watts lines, attributed to him with unusual consistency and squarely on the theme of The Wisdom of Insecurity (1951), which is the book most often cited for it. I cannot confirm the page or even the volume from memory, so I am not recording a print source. The stability of the attribution earns 'attributed,' but without a located passage it stays below the promotion bar.

text: It’s not that I’m so smart, it’s just that I stay with problems longer.
text_raw: It’s not that I’m so smart, it’s just that I stay with problems longer.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: No primary source. This is one of the modest-genius lines that accrete to Einstein, and I cannot trace it to a paper, letter, or documented interview. The genuine, well-sourced neighbor is his letter to Carl Seelig of 11 March 1952: 'I have no special talents. I am only passionately curious.' The 'stay with problems longer' phrasing looks like a later restatement of that sentiment rather than something Einstein wrote. Uncertain, and Einstein's misattribution record argues for caution.

text: The measure of intelligence is the ability to change.
text_raw: The measure of intelligence is the ability to change.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: No Einstein source exists for this; it is routinely listed among his misattributed quotations. The phrasing is late-20th/21st-century motivational English and has the shape of a slogan retrofitted with a famous name — it may owe something to popularized readings of adaptability in intelligence research, but I know of no real originator and will not guess one. Recommend it not be promoted under Einstein's name in any form.

text: The ego is the mind's belief that it is completely on its own.
text_raw: The ego is the mind's belief that it is completely on its own.
author: A Course in Miracles

provenance.notes: The sentence matches ACIM's definition of the ego as the mind's belief in its own separation and autonomy, and it is quoted as ACIM in the secondary literature around the Course (Wapnick and others). I cannot pin the chapter and section, and ACIM circulates in multiple editions with different numbering, so I am not recording a citation I cannot place. Very likely genuine to the work; location unconfirmed.

text: You are free to believe what you choose and what you do attests to what you believe.
text_raw: You are free to believe what you choose and what you do attests to what you believe.
author: A Course in Miracles

provenance.notes: Reads as authentic ACIM in cadence and doctrine (freedom of belief, and behavior as the witness to belief), and it is quoted as such, but I cannot locate the passage in the Text, Workbook, or Manual for Teachers from memory. Slightly lower confidence than q_0191 because I have less independent recall of this specific line. Genuine-looking but unlocated.

text: Alone we can do so little; together we can do so much.
text_raw: Alone we can do so little; together we can do so much.
author: Helen Keller

provenance.notes: Extremely widely attributed to Helen Keller and not, to my knowledge, contested or reassigned to anyone else — but I cannot trace it to a book, essay, letter, or speech of hers. It is a staple of teamwork posters and fundraising copy, which is exactly the environment in which citations disappear. Plausible; unsourced.

text: Nearly all men can stand adversity, but if you want to test a man's character, give him power.
text_raw: Nearly all men can stand adversity, but if you want to test a man's character, give him power.
author: Abraham Lincoln

provenance.earliest_print_source: Robert G. Ingersoll, lecture 'Abraham Lincoln,' 1883
provenance.notes: Not Lincoln. Nothing of the kind appears in the Collected Works, and the attribution is 20th-century. The near-certain origin is Robert G. Ingersoll's celebrated lecture on Lincoln (1883), which argues: 'Nothing discloses real character like the use of power... Most people can bear adversity; but if you wish to know what a man really is, give him power.' A statement made *about* Lincoln was over time converted into a statement *by* Lincoln — a common mechanism for this particular magnet. Confidence value reflects the weakness of the Lincoln attribution; my confidence in the Ingersoll origin is considerably higher. | Suggested reattribution: Robert G. Ingersoll, from his 1883 lecture on Abraham Lincoln

text: You will either step forward in growth or you will step back into safety.
text_raw: You will either step forward in growth or you will step back into safety.
author: Abraham Maslow

provenance.earliest_print_source: Toward a Psychology of Being, Abraham H. Maslow, 1962
provenance.notes: The thought is documented Maslow: Toward a Psychology of Being (1962) frames growth as a repeated choice, in the form 'one can choose to go back toward safety or forward toward growth,' with growth chosen over and over and fear overcome again and again. The wording quoted here ('You will either step forward in growth or you will step back into safety') is the popular circulating variant rather than the printed sentence I can attest to, and it is often given in the second person as if from a lecture. Substance verified in the 1962 book; exact wording is a variant, so it should be presented as Maslow's idea, ideally with the printed phrasing substituted.

text: The abundance flows in many more avenues than dollars. And so, if you could focus upon the gifts that the Universe gives you: When you say "abundance", think about it in the abundance of health, the abundance of vitality, the abundance of clarity, the abundance of enthusiasm, the abundance of delicious people in your life, the abundance of loving letters in your life. The abundance of free-flowing traffic in your life. The abundance of wonderful experiences in your life... As you start thinking in terms of this abundance that doesn't have anything to do with dollars - the abundance relative to the dollars starts flowing too.
text_raw: The abundance flows in many more avenues than dollars. And so, if you could focus upon the gifts that the Universe gives you: When you say "abundance", think about it in the abundance of health, the abundance of vitality, the abundance of clarity, the abundance of enthusiasm, the abundance of delicious people in your life, the abundance of loving letters in your life. The abundance of free-flowing traffic in your life. The abundance of wonderful experiences in your life... As you start thinking in terms of this abundance that doesn't have anything to do with dollars - the abundance relative to the dollars starts flowing too.
author: Abraham-Hicks

provenance.notes: Abraham-Hicks material is channeled workshop transcript published by Esther and Jerry Hicks; individual passages circulate with a workshop city and date on the official site and in the Daily Quote mailings. The vocabulary and cadence here (the abundance 'flowing in many more avenues than dollars', 'delicious people', the recursive stacking of 'the abundance of...') is highly characteristic of the Abraham corpus, so authorship is plausible. But I cannot place this passage in a specific workshop, recording, or book, and transcript excerpts are routinely re-cut and paraphrased by quote sites. Attribution to the source is plausible; the exact wording is unverified.

text: You do not need to import greatness from another; you just need to act on your own.
text_raw: You do not need to import greatness from another; you just need to act on your own.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: Alan Cohen is a real and prolific inspirational author (The Dragon Doesn't Live Here Anymore, A Deep Breath of Life, Wisdom of the Heart, Enough Already), and this line is consistent with his aphoristic voice and his recurring 'the treasure is within you' theme. However, I cannot place it in a specific book, chapter, or newsletter. His one-liners circulate almost entirely through quote aggregators and his own daily-inspiration mailings, which leaves no verifiable print chain. Honest verdict: plausible author, no evidence.

text: We believe we are hurt when we don't receive love. But that is not what hurts us. Our pain comes when we do not give love. We were born to love. You might say that we are divinely created love machines. We function most powerfully when we are giving love. The world has led us to believe that our well-being is dependent on other people loving us. But this is the kind of upside down thinking that has caused so many of our problems. The truth is our well-being is dependent on our giving love. It is not about what comes back; it is about what goes out.
text_raw: We believe we are hurt when we don't receive love. But that is not what hurts us. Our pain comes when we do not give love. We were born to love. You might say that we are divinely created love machines. We function most powerfully when we are giving love. The world has led us to believe that our well-being is dependent on other people loving us. But this is the kind of upside down thinking that has caused so many of our problems. The truth is our well-being is dependent on our giving love. It is not about what comes back; it is about what goes out.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: This longer passage ('we are divinely created love machines', well-being depends on giving rather than receiving love) reads as genuine Alan Cohen prose rather than a quote-site fragment — the paragraph structure and the gentle contrarian turn are his. I have a weak recollection of this theme in his book-length work but cannot name the title or year with any confidence, and I will not guess one. Attribution plausible, source unlocated.

text: You can be helping many people, but if you are not helping yourself, you have missed the one person you were born to heal.
text_raw: You can be helping many people, but if you are not helping yourself, you have missed the one person you were born to heal.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: Consistent with Alan Cohen's writing on self-care and the helper's blind spot, and widely reproduced under his name. No specific book, article, or dated newsletter can be identified from my training knowledge, and no primary text is available to confirm the wording. Plausible but unevidenced.

text: To seek greatness outside yourself is turn your back on the treasure within.
text_raw: To seek greatness outside yourself is turn your back on the treasure within.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: Attributed to Alan Cohen across quote sites and thematically of a piece with q_0198 (greatness is internal, not imported). Note the transmitted text is ungrammatical — 'is turn your back' is missing 'to', which is a signature of quote-aggregator copying rather than a book text, and suggests the wording here has drifted from whatever the original was. No source located; no independent evidence for the attribution.

text: Take care what words you speak that follow "I am." In so speaking you create your life.
text_raw: Take care what words you speak that follow "I am." In so speaking you create your life.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: The 'watch what follows I AM' teaching is a shared commonplace of New Thought and metaphysical writing (Emmet Fox, Florence Scovel Shinn, Wayne Dyer, Joel Goldsmith and many others all state versions of it), so this particular phrasing is not distinctive enough for me to assign it to Alan Cohen on internal evidence. He may well have written it; the idea is not original to him. No source located.

text: Today's thoughts are previews of coming attractions.
text_raw: Today's thoughts are previews of coming attractions.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: This is a variant of the widely circulated 'Imagination is everything. It is the preview of life's coming attractions,' which is popularly attributed to Albert Einstein and has no basis in his writings — it is a well-known apocryphal Einstein line. The 'coming attractions' movie-trailer metaphor therefore has muddled provenance predating any Cohen usage, and the same sentence also floats attributed to Louise Hay and others. Alan Cohen may have used this phrasing, but the attribution chain is contaminated. Low confidence in the recorded author; I cannot identify who coined the movie-trailer formulation.

text: The quality of your life equals the ratio of appreciation to complaint.
text_raw: The quality of your life equals the ratio of appreciation to complaint.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: Gratitude-versus-complaint framing stated as a ratio; consistent with Alan Cohen's aphoristic style and widely reproduced under his name. No book, article, or dated source identifiable from training knowledge.

text: Why wait for your ship to come in when you are already on it?
text_raw: Why wait for your ship to come in when you are already on it?
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: A reworking of the older idiom 'waiting for my ship to come in' (which is a proverbial commonplace, not anyone's coinage) and close in shape to several circulating variants such as 'Don't wait for your ship to come in — swim out to it' and 'your ship has already come in.' The specific inversion here is attributed to Alan Cohen on quote sites, but the idiom's ubiquity makes independent coinage likely in multiple mouths. No source located.

text: Observe the direct connection between practicing trust and serendipitous events that follow.
text_raw: Observe the direct connection between practicing trust and serendipitous events that follow.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: Reads like an instruction from a practice-oriented passage or daily-inspiration entry, which matches how most Alan Cohen quotations enter circulation. Plausibly his; no specific book, chapter, or dated mailing identifiable, and no independent corroboration of the attribution.

text: People who do not need to please are irresistible because they radiate wholeness, a rare delicacy in a world of hungry hearts.
text_raw: People who do not need to please are irresistible because they radiate wholeness, a rare delicacy in a world of hungry hearts.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: The construction ('radiate wholeness, a rare delicacy in a world of hungry hearts') is more crafted than the average aggregator one-liner and is idiomatic of Alan Cohen's prose, which raises my confidence that it is genuinely his and not a floating anonymous line. I still cannot place it in a specific title — his books on people-pleasing and contentment are the likeliest home but I will not name one as a citation without being able to confirm it.

text: If you are going to retire from anything, retire from fear and illusion.
text_raw: If you are going to retire from anything, retire from fear and illusion.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: Attributed to Alan Cohen and consistent with his voice and his frequent play on conventional life-stage language. No primary source identifiable; the only visible provenance is quote-aggregator repetition, which is not evidence.

text: Trying to define yourself is like trying to bite your own teeth.
text_raw: Trying to define yourself is like trying to bite your own teeth.
author: Alan Watts

provenance.notes: Authentically Watts in both idea and image. The self-referential-impossibility metaphor is one he used repeatedly in variant forms — biting your own teeth, seeing your own eyes, lifting yourself by your own bootstraps, the knife that cannot cut itself — deployed against the notion of a self that can stand outside itself and define itself. The attribution to Watts is strong on internal evidence and consistent citation. I cannot pin it to a particular book or lecture, however; many circulating Watts lines come from recorded talks that were later transcribed, so no print source is offered.

text: We cannot solve our problems with the same thinking we used when we created them.
text_raw: We cannot solve our problems with the same thinking we used when we created them.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: One of the most-repeated Einstein lines and not found in his writings in this form. What Einstein actually said is documented: in a May 1946 telegram from the Emergency Committee of Atomic Scientists, quoted in the New York Times, 'a new type of thinking is essential if mankind is to survive and move toward higher levels.' The popular 'we cannot solve our problems with the same thinking we used when we created them' is a much later compression, appearing in management and self-help literature decades afterward, and it is treated as unsourced in the Einstein quotation scholarship (Calaprice's collections place this family of sayings outside the verified material). Kept as attributed_unverified rather than apocryphal because a genuine Einstein statement sits at the root of the paraphrase — but the sentence as written should not be quoted as his words.

text: If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it well enough.
text_raw: If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it well enough.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: No evidence Einstein said or wrote this; it is a standard entry in the misattributed-Einstein lists and does not appear in his published papers, letters, or interviews. The nearest documented ancestor belongs to Ernest Rutherford, reported as saying that a physical theory is no good unless you can explain it to a barmaid — a remark recorded secondhand and itself imperfectly sourced. Similar sentiments are also attributed to Feynman. The Einstein version appears to be a late-twentieth-century construction with no traceable origin, so no true author can be named.

text: Out of clutter, find simplicity. From discord, find harmony. In the middle of difficulty lies opportunity.
text_raw: Out of clutter, find simplicity. From discord, find harmony. In the middle of difficulty lies opportunity.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: Circulated as Einstein's 'Three Rules of Work.' No primary source exists — it does not appear in his papers or correspondence, and the triad structure is characteristic of twentieth-century motivational compilation rather than of Einstein's prose. The third clause, 'in the middle of difficulty lies opportunity,' is the oldest and most widely repeated of the three and appears in Einstein quotation collections under attributed-but-unsourced headings; even that one has no located primary text. Treat the whole triad as unverified.

text: If you judge a fish by its ability to climb a tree, it will think it’s stupid.
text_raw: If you judge a fish by its ability to climb a tree, it will think it’s stupid.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: A well-documented misattribution, usually circulated in the longer form beginning 'Everybody is a genius. But if you judge a fish by its ability to climb a tree...'. It appears nowhere in Einstein's writings and is absent from the scholarly Einstein quotation collections; researchers tracing it have found no instance in his lifetime, with the saying surfacing in this shape only in recent decades. The same pedagogical point is made in George Reavis's fable 'The Animal School' (circulated from around 1940), which is a thematic analogue rather than a demonstrated source. No credible author can be identified.

text: A great relationship is not something that happens to you. It is something you choose.
text_raw: A great relationship is not something that happens to you. It is something you choose.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: Attributed to Alan Cohen and compatible with his relationship writing, but this is a generic self-help formulation ('X is not something that happens to you, it is something you choose') that recurs verbatim in many authors' work about love, happiness, and success. The template is too common for the wording alone to establish authorship, and no source can be located.

text: The mystery of life is not a problem to be solved but a reality to be experienced.
text_raw: The mystery of life is not a problem to be solved but a reality to be experienced.
author: Aart Van Der Leeuw

provenance.notes: The recorded author appears to be a confusion of two different Dutch writers. My recollection places this line with J.J. van der Leeuw (Jacobus Johannes van der Leeuw, 1893-1934), the Dutch theosophical writer, in his book The Conquest of Illusion (1928), whose opening pages frame life as a mystery to be lived rather than a problem to be solved. Aart van der Leeuw (1876-1931) was a separate Dutch poet and novelist, and the surname collision is the likely origin of the swap. The quote is also frequently and wrongly attributed to Frank Herbert via Dune, and to various others, which shows how loose its circulation is. I hold the J.J. van der Leeuw reattribution at moderate confidence only — the confidence value given reflects the weak standing of the recorded 'Aart' attribution. Do not promote without checking the 1928 text. | Suggested reattribution: J.J. van der Leeuw (Jacobus Johannes van der Leeuw), The Conquest of Illusion (1928) — moderate confidence, needs confirmation against the text

text: The world would have you agree with its dismal dream of limitation. But the light would have you soar like the eagle of your sacred visions.
text_raw: The world would have you agree with its dismal dream of limitation. But the light would have you soar like the eagle of your sacred visions.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: The imagery ('dismal dream of limitation', 'the eagle of your sacred visions') is distinctly Alan Cohen's devotional register and closely echoes the A Course in Miracles vocabulary he works within, which supports his authorship. Still no locatable book, chapter, or dated source; his aphorisms of this kind typically originate in daily-inspiration mailings that leave no citable print record.

text: Everybody is ‘you’. Everybody is ‘I’. That’s our name. We all share that.
text_raw: Everybody is ‘you’. Everybody is ‘I’. That’s our name. We all share that.
author: Alan Watts

provenance.notes: Sounds authentically like Alan Watts speaking rather than writing — the clipped fragments and the spoken-register repetition are typical of his recorded lectures, and the point (that 'you' and 'I' are shared pronouns naming the same universal subject) is one he made often. But precisely because it reads as transcript, I cannot tie it to a specific talk, recording, or published text, and lecture transcriptions of Watts circulate in many loosely edited versions. Plausibly genuine, wording unverified.

text: I was absent at the moment I took up the most space.
text_raw: I was absent at the moment I took up the most space.
author: Albert Camus

provenance.notes: The line reads like a translation of Camus ('j'etais absent au moment ou je prenais le plus de place') and is thematically consistent with the self-accusing narrator of La Chute (The Fall, 1956) or the Carnets. I cannot place it in a specific work or confirm the translation, and I will not name a book I am not sure of. Attribution to Camus is plausible and consistently made, but unverified.

text: When I do good, I feel good. When I do bad, I feel bad. That's my religion.
text_raw: When I do good, I feel good. When I do bad, I feel bad. That's my religion.
author: Abraham Lincoln

provenance.notes: A very widely repeated Lincoln line, but it rests on later recollection rather than a contemporaneous document. It circulates via post-assassination memoirs and religious biographies of Lincoln, and reference works generally file it under attributed rather than sourced. Lincoln is a known misattribution magnet, so I am holding this below the promotion bar; the sentiment fits his recorded remarks about religion, but no primary source is in my knowledge.

text: Body impermanent like spring mist; mind insubstantial like empty sky; thoughts unestablished like breezes in space. Think about these three points over and over.
text_raw: Body impermanent like spring mist; mind insubstantial like empty sky; thoughts unestablished like breezes in space. Think about these three points over and over.
author: Adept Godrakpa

provenance.notes: 'Adept Godrakpa' is the distinctive rendering used for Gotsangpa Gonpo Dorje (1189-1258), the Tibetan Kagyu yogi, in Cyrus Stearns' translation of his songs of realization published by Wisdom Publications around 2000. The imagery (body like spring mist, mind like empty sky, thoughts like breezes) and the three-point contemplative structure match that body of doggerel-song instruction closely, so the attribution is probably right. I am not certain enough of the exact page or the exact translated wording to record a print citation, so the source field stays null.

text: Being self-centered is healthy if you know who is the self you are centered in.
text_raw: Being self-centered is healthy if you know who is the self you are centered in.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: Alan Cohen is a prolific inspirational author (The Dragon Doesn't Live Here Anymore, Wisdom of the Heart) whose aphorisms circulate through books, newsletters, and daily-quote services with consistent attribution but almost never with a book-and-page citation. Attribution is plausible and uncontested; no primary source in my knowledge.

text: Because God is real, the more real you are, the more you are like God.
text_raw: Because God is real, the more real you are, the more you are like God.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: Same situation as the other Alan Cohen aphorisms in this batch: consistently attributed to him across quote collections, no traceable first appearance in my knowledge. Nothing suggests a different author; the uncertainty is about sourcing, not about who wrote it.

text: You can't get a right brain answer to a left brain question. Ask your heart, not your mind.
text_raw: You can't get a right brain answer to a left brain question. Ask your heart, not your mind.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: Widely circulated as Alan Cohen, typically without citation. The left-brain/right-brain framing places it in the late-twentieth-century self-help idiom he writes in, which is consistent with the attribution, but I cannot locate a specific book or column.

text: Love is natural. Cynicism is learned. Come home.
text_raw: Love is natural. Cynicism is learned. Come home.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: Attributed to Alan Cohen wherever I have seen it, with no source given. Short enough and aphoristic enough that provenance drift is easy; I have no evidence of an earlier or different author, but no evidence for the attribution beyond repetition either.

text: The first step to waking up is the discovery that you have been asleep.
text_raw: The first step to waking up is the discovery that you have been asleep.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: Attributed to Alan Cohen without citation. Worth flagging that the idea, and nearly the phrasing, is central to Anthony de Mello's Awareness ('spirituality means waking up... most people are asleep and don't know it'), so this may be a restatement of de Mello that acquired Cohen's name, or a genuine Cohen line in the same lineage. I cannot tell which, so I am not proposing a reattribution.

text: The inferior teacher tells you that something is wrong with you and offers to fix it. The superior teacher tells you that something is right with you and helps you bring it forth.
text_raw: The inferior teacher tells you that something is wrong with you and offers to fix it. The superior teacher tells you that something is right with you and helps you bring it forth.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Alan Cohen and one of his more frequently reproduced lines, which slightly strengthens the attribution, but I can point to no book, essay, or dated appearance. Sourcing unverified.

text: Enlightenment does not ask you to be perfect; it simply asks you to find perfection right where you stand.
text_raw: Enlightenment does not ask you to be perfect; it simply asks you to find perfection right where you stand.
author: Alan Cohen

provenance.notes: Attributed to Alan Cohen in quote collections with no citation. Voice and vocabulary are consistent with his other work; nothing more than that supports it.

text: Nothing is exactly as it seems, nor is it otherwise.
text_raw: Nothing is exactly as it seems, nor is it otherwise.
author: Alan Watts

provenance.notes: This is a Buddhist scriptural formula, not an Alan Watts original. The line 'Things are not what they seem, nor are they otherwise' is a well-known rendering from the Lankavatara Sutra, and Watts quoted this kind of formulation in his writing on Zen and Mahayana. Attributing it to Watts credits the popularizer rather than the source. My confidence is in the Lankavatara provenance of the formula; I cannot confirm which translation this exact English wording comes from, and it is possible Watts's own paraphrase is what circulates. | Suggested reattribution: Lankavatara Sutra (as quoted/paraphrased by Alan Watts)

text: The mind, when it is the proper state, is ready to respond in any direction.
text_raw: The mind, when it is the proper state, is ready to respond in any direction.
author: Alan Watts

provenance.notes: I cannot place this in Alan Watts's books or recorded talks. The idea (a mind in its natural state, unfixed and therefore able to respond in any direction) is standard mushin/wu-hsin material that Watts wrote about in The Way of Zen, and the phrasing also resembles English renderings of Takuan Soho's The Unfettered Mind, which Watts drew on. That makes the attribution plausible but unsupported. Possibly a paraphrase of Watts rather than his words.

text: If at first the idea is not absurd, then there is no hope for it.
text_raw: If at first the idea is not absurd, then there is no hope for it.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: No source in Einstein's writings, letters, or interviews that I know of; reference compilations of Einstein quotations treat it as attributed rather than sourced. The sentiment closely tracks a documented Niels Bohr remark to Wolfgang Pauli ('we are all agreed that your theory is crazy; the question is whether it is crazy enough to have a chance of being correct'), and this may be a compressed folk version of that exchange re-badged with Einstein's name. I cannot establish the true origin, so no reattribution.

text: At such moments one imagines that one stands on some spot of a small planet gazing in amazement at the cold and yet profoundly moving beauty of the eternal, the unfathomable. Life and death flow into one, and there is neither evolution nor eternity, only being.
text_raw: At such moments one imagines that one stands on some spot of a small planet gazing in amazement at the cold and yet profoundly moving beauty of the eternal, the unfathomable. Life and death flow into one, and there is neither evolution nor eternity, only being.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: This reads as authentic Einstein prose and I recall it from collections of his writings on the religious feeling of the scientist, associated with his early-1930s credo material ('Mein Glaubensbekenntnis' / The World As I See It). The distinctive cadence and the 'neither evolution nor eternity, only being' close are hard to fake and are consistent with his German essays in translation. I am confident enough in authorship to call it attributed, but I cannot pin the exact essay or year, so I am leaving the citation null and staying under the promotion bar.

text: It is better to believe than to disbelieve; in so doing you bring everything to the realm of possibility.
text_raw: It is better to believe than to disbelieve; in so doing you bring everything to the realm of possibility.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: I have no record of this in Einstein's writings, and it sits awkwardly against his documented positions, which consistently favour inquiry over belief and reject the 'better to believe' framing as such. It circulates mainly through quotation websites. Einstein is the single largest misattribution magnet in the corpus; absent any source, this should not be promoted.

text: Nothing truly valuable arises from ambition or from a mere sense of duty; it stems rather from love and devotion towards men and towards objective things.
text_raw: Nothing truly valuable arises from ambition or from a mere sense of duty; it stems rather from love and devotion towards men and towards objective things.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: I believe this is authentic Einstein, from his mid-1930s statements collected in The World As I See It / Mein Weltbild, and it is quoted with consistent wording in serious Einstein compilations rather than only on quote sites. The phrase 'love and devotion towards men and towards objective things' is a characteristic translation of his German. I cannot confirm the specific essay or letter, so the citation stays null and I am holding below 0.80.

text: We should take care not to make the intellect our god; it has, of course, powerful muscles, but no personality.
text_raw: We should take care not to make the intellect our god; it has, of course, powerful muscles, but no personality.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: Authentic Einstein as far as I know it. The fuller passage continues 'It cannot lead, it can only serve; and it is not fastidious in its choice of a leader', and it appears in the standard English collections of his essays (Ideas and Opinions / Out of My Later Years). The extended, coherent context is good evidence of genuineness. I am not certain enough which original essay or year it comes from to record an earliest print source, so it sits just under the promotion bar pending a human check against Ideas and Opinions.

text: The world we have created is a product of our thinking; it cannot be changed without changing our thinking.
text_raw: The world we have created is a product of our thinking; it cannot be changed without changing our thinking.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: Almost certainly a paraphrase rather than Einstein's words. What is documented is his 1946 campaign for atomic-age rethinking: 'The unleashed power of the atom has changed everything save our modes of thinking, and thus we drift toward unparalleled catastrophe', and 'a new type of thinking is essential if mankind is to survive'. This line compresses that into modern self-help phrasing. No source for this exact wording. Closely related to q_0243 below, which is the better-known version of the same drift.

text: The significant problems we face cannot be solved at the same level of thinking we were at when we created them.
text_raw: The significant problems we face cannot be solved at the same level of thinking we were at when we created them.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: One of the most-repeated Einstein misattributions and a documented case of quote drift. It has no source in Einstein's writings; the wording appears in late-twentieth-century management, therapy, and self-help literature and was retro-attributed to him, evolving out of his genuine 1946 remarks about needing a new mode of thinking in the atomic age. Quote-investigation work and the standard Einstein quotation reference both place it in the unsourced/misattributed category. No identifiable individual author, so apocryphal rather than a reattribution.

text: Whoever undertakes to set himself up as a judge of Truth and Knowledge is shipwrecked by the laughter of the Gods.
text_raw: Whoever undertakes to set himself up as a judge of Truth and Knowledge is shipwrecked by the laughter of the Gods.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: I am fairly confident this is authentic. The German original is known ('Wer sich als Richter auf dem Gebiete der Wahrheit und Erkenntnis aufzuwerfen unternimmt, wird vom Gelaechter der Goetter zerschmettert'), which is strong evidence against a modern English-language invention, and it is generally dated to an Einstein aphorism of the early 1950s. I cannot confirm the publication it first appeared in, so no citation and no promotion; a human check against the standard Einstein quotation reference should settle it.

text: It is every man’s obligation to put back into the world at least the equivalent of what he takes out of it.
text_raw: It is every man’s obligation to put back into the world at least the equivalent of what he takes out of it.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Einstein and compatible with his documented views on social obligation ('a hundred times every day I remind myself that my inner and outer life are based on the labors of other men'), but I cannot place this specific sentence in any of his writings or interviews. The plain, proverbial phrasing is the kind that attracts famous names. Attribution plausible, sourcing absent.

text: There are only two ways to live your life: One is as though nothing is a miracle, the other is as though everything is a miracle. I believe in the latter.
text_raw: There are only two ways to live your life: One is as though nothing is a miracle, the other is as though everything is a miracle. I believe in the latter.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: Correctly pre-flagged. There is no Einstein source for this; it does not appear in his published writings, letters, or interviews, and the standard Einstein quotation reference lists it among sayings attributed to him without support. Attributions to Einstein surface long after his death and appear to be a rebadging of an older inspirational commonplace. No identifiable original author, so apocryphal.

text: Peace cannot be kept by force. It can only be achieved by understanding.
text_raw: Peace cannot be kept by force. It can only be achieved by understanding.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Einstein and entirely consonant with his documented pacifist writings of the late 1920s and 1930s, where the force-versus-understanding contrast recurs. I cannot place the specific document from memory — candidates I associate with it (a c. 1930 pacifist statement, the material collected in Mein Weltbild / The World As I See It, or the Einstein on Peace compilation) are recollections I am not confident enough to print as a citation, so I have left the source field null rather than guess. Kept below the promotion bar for that reason.

text: Logic will get you from A to B. Imagination will take you everywhere.
text_raw: Logic will get you from A to B. Imagination will take you everywhere.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: No source in Einstein's writings, letters, or recorded conversations. This is a stock item in the unsourced/misattributed section of the Einstein Wikiquote page. It surfaces in motivational compilations decades after his death and reads as a modern aphorism rather than a translation from German. It is likely a compressed echo of his genuine 'Imagination is more important than knowledge' (Viereck interview, 1929), but the 'A to B' phrasing is not his. I cannot identify who actually coined it.

text: Nothing will benefit human health and increase the chances for survival of life on Earth as much as the evolution to a vegetarian diet.
text_raw: Nothing will benefit human health and increase the chances for survival of life on Earth as much as the evolution to a vegetarian diet.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: Heavily circulated in vegetarian advocacy literature but not found in Einstein's collected writings or correspondence; it appears in the misattributed material on the Einstein Wikiquote page. Einstein's authentic statements on the subject are different and much more qualified — the 1930 letter to Hermann Huth ('Although I have been prevented by outward circumstances from observing a strictly vegetarian diet, I have long been an adherent to the cause in principle') and a 1954 letter to Hans Muehsam written after he adopted the diet on medical advice. The sweeping 'survival of life on Earth' framing is not his idiom. True coiner unknown to me.

text: It is the supreme art of the teacher to awaken joy in creative expression and knowledge.
text_raw: It is the supreme art of the teacher to awaken joy in creative expression and knowledge.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: Very widely attributed, including in education scholarship, and a German original circulates ('Es ist die wichtigste Kunst des Lehrers, die Freude am Schaffen und Erkennen zu wecken'), which is mild evidence of genuine provenance rather than a back-translated invention. But I cannot place a primary document. It is plausibly connected to his writings and addresses on education (e.g. the 1936 Albany address 'On Education'), yet I do not actually recall it in that text, and some Einstein quote scholarship files lines of this kind as unsourced. Honest verdict: probably his, not demonstrable from what I know.

text: When you’re courting a nice girl an hour seems like a second. When you sit on a red-hot cinder a second seems like an hour. That’s relativity.
text_raw: When you’re courting a nice girl an hour seems like a second. When you sit on a red-hot cinder a second seems like an hour. That’s relativity.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: The joke is authentically Einstein's — it was his stock popular gloss on relativity, given to reporters (his secretary Helen Dukas handed out a version of it) and recorded in multiple accounts from the late 1920s onward. Two cautions. First, this specific wording ('courting a nice girl', 'red-hot cinder') is one of several circulating variants; the more commonly documented form is 'When you sit with a nice girl for two hours it seems like a minute; when you sit on a hot stove for a minute it seems like two hours.' Second, the citation often attached to it online — 'Journal of Exothermic Science and Technology (JEST), Vol. 1, No. 9, 1938' — is a spoof, not a real journal, so I have deliberately not printed it. Substance solid, exact wording and source not verifiable.

text: Any fool can make things bigger, more complex, and more violent. It takes a touch of genius - and a lot of courage – to move in the opposite direction.
text_raw: Any fool can make things bigger, more complex, and more violent. It takes a touch of genius - and a lot of courage – to move in the opposite direction.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.earliest_print_source: Small Is Beautiful: A Study of Economics as if People Mattered, E. F. Schumacher, 1973
provenance.notes: I do not believe this is Einstein's. I recall it from E. F. Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful (1973), where the wording runs 'Any intelligent fool can make things bigger, more complex, and more violent. It takes a touch of genius — and a lot of courage — to move in the opposite direction.' Note that the corpus version has dropped 'intelligent', which is the tell of a quote that has passed through attribution drift. Caveat on my own certainty: I am confident the line is Schumacher's in print and not Einstein's, but less certain whether Schumacher coined it or was himself echoing an earlier source, so treat the reattribution as probable rather than settled. | Suggested reattribution: E. F. Schumacher

text: I want to know the thoughts of God; the rest are details.
text_raw: "I want to know the thoughts of God; the rest are details."
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.earliest_print_source: Esther Salaman, 'A Talk With Einstein', The Listener, vol. 54 (1955)
provenance.notes: This is a compression of a longer remark Einstein made to the physicist Esther Salaman around 1925, which she published from memory in 1955: 'I want to know how God created this world. I am not interested in this or that phenomenon, in the spectrum of this or that element. I want to know His thoughts; the rest are details.' So the source is a recollection recorded roughly thirty years after the conversation, and the popular one-sentence form here is an editor's condensation rather than Einstein's own sentence. Genuine in substance; the exact wording is not.

text: When I examine myself and my methods of thought, I come to the conclusion that the gift of fantasy has meant more to me than my talent for absorbing positive knowledge.
text_raw: "When I examine myself and my methods of thought, I come to the conclusion that the gift of fantasy has meant more to me than my talent for absorbing positive knowledge."
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.earliest_print_source: George Sylvester Viereck, 'What Life Means to Einstein', The Saturday Evening Post, 26 October 1929 (republished in Glimpses of the Great, 1930)
provenance.notes: I recall this from the 1929 Viereck interview, the same conversation that produced 'Imagination is more important than knowledge.' The 'gift of fantasy' phrasing is characteristic of that interview's translation. Hedge: I am confident about the interview but not about the exact page, and I cannot rule out that the line comes from a neighbouring Viereck piece rather than the Saturday Evening Post printing itself — hence attributed rather than verified, and held below the promotion bar pending a human check against the printed interview.

text: I never came upon any of my discoveries through the process of rational thinking.
text_raw: I never came upon any of my discoveries through the process of rational thinking.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: Widely quoted and thoroughly consistent with Einstein's documented statements about intuition preceding reasoning (the Viereck interview, the Wertheimer conversations, the Hadamard survey on mathematical invention). But I cannot place a primary source for this exact sentence, and lines of this shape are exactly the kind that get retrofitted onto Einstein by inspirational compilers. I have a faint association with a mid-century popular biography, but it is too faint to print as a citation. Plausible but unverified.

text: I feel myself so much a part of all life that I am not in the least concerned with the beginning or the end of the concrete existence of any particular person in this unending stream.
text_raw: I feel myself so much a part of all life that I am not in the least concerned with the beginning or the end of the concrete existence of any particular person in this unending stream.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: I am fairly confident this is genuine Einstein on death and the individual life. I associate it with his spoken credo of autumn 1932 ('Mein Glaubensbekenntnis', recorded for the German League of Human Rights) and with the material collected in Dukas and Hoffmann's Albert Einstein: The Human Side. The variant wording I recall is closer to 'so much a part of everything living ... the concrete existence of any one person in this eternal flow', which suggests the corpus text is a different translation of the same German. Because I cannot settle which of those two sources carries it, I have left the print source null rather than guess between them.

text: A person experiences life as something separated from the rest - a kind of optical delusion of consciousness. Our task must be to free ourselves from this self-imposed prison, and through compassion, to find the reality of oneness.
text_raw: A person experiences life as something separated from the rest - a kind of optical delusion of consciousness. Our task must be to free ourselves from this self-imposed prison, and through compassion, to find the reality of oneness.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: This is a degraded paraphrase of the authentic 1950 letter to Robert S. Marcus, which the corpus already holds correctly as q_0260. The giveaways are 'self-imposed prison' and 'to find the reality of oneness' — neither phrase is in Einstein's letter; the original says the delusion 'is a kind of prison for us' and that our task is 'widening our circles of compassion to embrace all living creatures and the whole of nature in its beauty.' The oneness formulation entered circulation through later spiritual literature. Recommendation for the human reviewer: this is a duplicate of q_0260 in corrupted form and should be dropped in favour of the archival wording, not promoted alongside it.

text: All I want to do is learn to think like God thinks. All the other things are just details.
text_raw: All I want to do is learn to think like God thinks. All the other things are just details.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: A loose popular restatement of the same Salaman-reported remark behind q_0257 ('I want to know how God created this world ... I want to know His thoughts; the rest are details', The Listener, 1955). The 'All I want to do is learn to think like God thinks' wording is not attested in Einstein's own words or in Salaman's account; it reads as a paraphrase of a paraphrase. Duplicative of q_0257, which is the better-supported form of the same line.

text: My religion consists of a humble admiration of the illimitable superior spirit who reveals himself in the slight details we are able to perceive with our frail and feeble mind.
text_raw: My religion consists of a humble admiration of the illimitable superior spirit who reveals himself in the slight details we are able to perceive with our frail and feeble mind.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: Long-standing and consistent attribution, and the vocabulary ('illimitable superior spirit', 'frail and feeble mind') matches Einstein's cosmic-religion register closely enough that I think it is genuine — compare the verified 1936 Phyllis Wright letter at q_0265, which says something very similar. I cannot place the primary document, however. It circulates in the standard Einstein compilations with varying and sometimes absent citations, and I do not want to pick one from memory. Probably genuine, source unplaced.

text: The intuitive mind is a sacred gift and the rational mind is a faithful servant. We have created a society that honors the servant and has forgotten the gift.
text_raw: The intuitive mind is a sacred gift and the rational mind is a faithful servant. We have created a society that honors the servant and has forgotten the gift.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Metaphoric Mind: A Celebration of Creative Consciousness, Bob Samples, 1976
provenance.notes: A well-known misattribution and one I am confident about. Bob Samples wrote a loose gloss on Einstein — approximately 'Albert Einstein called the intuitive or metaphoric mind a sacred gift. He added that the rational mind was a faithful servant. It is paradoxical that in the context of modern life we have begun to worship the servant and defile the divine' — and that commentary was subsequently quoted back as if it were Einstein's own sentence. The 'sacred gift / faithful servant / honors the servant and has forgotten the gift' formulation is Samples' prose, not Einstein's, and no such passage exists in Einstein's writings. Recommend reattribution or removal. | Suggested reattribution: Bob Samples (paraphrasing Einstein)

text: When the solution is simple, God is answering.
text_raw: When the solution is simple, God is answering.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: No source in Einstein's writings, letters, or reported conversations that I know of. It appears in late-twentieth-century quotation compilations attached to his name, which is the standard signature of an Einstein-magnet aphorism. I cannot identify a true origin either, so I am not offering a reattribution. Honest answer: unknown, and almost certainly not his.

text: The human mind is not capable of grasping the Universe. We are like a little child entering a huge library. The walls are covered to the ceilings with books in many different tongues. The child knows that someone must have written these books. It does not know who or how. It does not understand the languages in which they are written. But the child notes a definite plan in the arrangement of the books—-a mysterious order which it does not comprehend, but only dimly suspects.
text_raw: The human mind is not capable of grasping the Universe. We are like a little child entering a huge library. The walls are covered to the ceilings with books in many different tongues. The child knows that someone must have written these books. It does not know who or how. It does not understand the languages in which they are written. But the child notes a definite plan in the arrangement of the books—-a mysterious order which it does not comprehend, but only dimly suspects.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.earliest_print_source: George Sylvester Viereck interview with Einstein, 1929–1930 (published as 'What Life Means to Einstein', The Saturday Evening Post, 26 October 1929, and in Glimpses of the Great, 1930)
provenance.notes: The child-in-the-library metaphor is genuinely Einstein's and is documented from his conversations with Viereck; the version I recall runs 'We are in the position of a little child entering a huge library whose walls are covered to the ceiling with books in many different tongues ... The child notes a definite plan in the arrangement of the books, a mysterious order which it does not comprehend, but only dimly suspects. That, it seems to me, is the attitude of the human mind, even the greatest and most cultured, toward God.' Caveats: the corpus text is a reported conversation, not something Einstein wrote, and its opening sentence ('The human mind is not capable of grasping the Universe') plus the truncated ending differ from the rendering I know. Attributed rather than verified because I cannot confirm which printing carries this exact wording.

text: What I see in Nature is a magnificent structure that we can comprehend only very imperfectly, and that must fill a thinking person with a feeling of humility. This is a genuinely religious feeling…
text_raw: What I see in Nature is a magnificent structure that we can comprehend only very imperfectly, and that must fill a thinking person with a feeling of humility. This is a genuinely religious feeling…
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.earliest_print_source: Albert Einstein: The Human Side, ed. Helen Dukas and Banesh Hoffmann (1979)
provenance.notes: I recall this from the Dukas and Hoffmann collection of Einstein's personal correspondence, drawn from a letter or reply written in his last years (mid-1950s), and continuing past the ellipsis to say that this feeling has nothing to do with mysticism. Dukas was his secretary and the collection works from the archive, so the chain is good. Hedge: I am confident about the collection but not about the exact letter, recipient, or date, so I have named only the book and left the specifics out rather than invent them. Held below the promotion bar pending a page-level check.

text: True religion is real living; living with all one’s soul, with all one’s goodness and righteousness.
text_raw: True religion is real living; living with all one’s soul, with all one’s goodness and righteousness.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: Widely attributed to Einstein in quotation collections and compatible with his 'true religiosity' language, but I cannot place a primary source. The phrasing is noticeably plainer than his usual translated register, which makes me slightly wary that it is a paraphrase of a longer passage rather than a sentence he wrote. Not enough for me to call it misattributed, not nearly enough to promote. Uncertain.

text: The high destiny of the individual is to serve rather than to rule.
text_raw: The high destiny of the individual is to serve rather than to rule.
author: Albert Einstein

provenance.notes: Consistent with Einstein's 1930s social essays and commonly cited to him; I recall the line in the orbit of The World As I See It (1934) but cannot place the specific essay or page from memory, so I am not supplying a citation. Not one of the classic Einstein fakes (no self-help cadence, no science-vs-religion punchline), and the sentiment matches his repeated writing on the individual's obligation to community. Plausible but unconfirmed at the primary-source level.

text: The greatest discovery of any generation is that human beings can alter their lives by altering the attitudes of their minds.
text_raw: The greatest discovery of any generation is that human beings can alter their lives by altering the attitudes of their minds.
author: Albert Schweitzer

provenance.notes: This is a floating self-help aphorism with two competing attributions and no primary source under either. It is far more commonly attributed to William James ('The greatest discovery of my generation is that a human being can alter his life by altering his attitudes of mind'), and that James version is a known unverified attribution - it does not appear in James's published works and surfaces in mid-20th-century inspirational literature. The Schweitzer variant ('of any generation') looks like downstream drift from the James version. Neither attribution is supportable; I cannot identify the true originator, so I am not proposing a reattribution.

text: I do not know what path in life you will take, but I do know this: If on that path you do not find a way to serve, you will never be happy.
text_raw: I do not know what path in life you will take, but I do know this: If on that path you do not find a way to serve, you will never be happy.
author: Albert Schweitzer

provenance.notes: This is a loose paraphrase of a line widely attributed to Schweitzer in the form 'I don't know what your destiny will be, but one thing I know: the only ones among you who will be really happy are those who will have sought and found how to serve.' Even that canonical form has no confirmed primary source - it is usually reported secondhand as advice to students, without a traceable speech or text. The wording given here ('what path in life you will take... you will never be happy') is a further-degraded retelling. The sentiment is authentically Schweitzerian, but neither the wording nor the source can be verified.

text: In everyone's life, at some time, our inner fire goes out. It is then burst into flame by an encounter with another human being. We should all be thankful for those people who rekindle the inner spirit.
text_raw: In everyone's life, at some time, our inner fire goes out. It is then burst into flame by an encounter with another human being. We should all be thankful for those people who rekindle the inner spirit.
author: Albert Schweitzer

provenance.notes: Genuinely Schweitzer's, to the best of my knowledge; the standard translation runs 'Sometimes our light goes out but is blown into flame again by an encounter with another human being. Each of us owes deepest thanks to those who have rekindled this inner light.' I recall it being sourced to Memoirs of Childhood and Youth (1924), but I am not confident enough in that placement to record it as a citation. The version in the corpus is a rephrasing ('our inner fire goes out', 'burst into flame'). Attribution good, exact source and wording unconfirmed.

text: People don't grow old. When they stop growing, they become old.
text_raw: People don't grow old. When they stop growing, they become old.
author: Aldous Huxley

provenance.notes: I cannot place this in Huxley's work, and the aphoristic snap of it is unlike his prose, which is discursive even when epigrammatic. It sits in a family of interchangeable aging aphorisms whose attributions rotate freely - compare 'Nobody grows old merely by living a number of years; we grow old by deserting our ideals' (Samuel Ullman) and 'We do not stop playing because we grow old; we grow old because we stop playing' (attributed variously to Oliver Wendell Holmes and George Bernard Shaw, unverified in both). No traceable source; honest answer is that I do not know who said it.

text: It is a bit embarrassing to have been concerned with the human problem all one's life and find at the end that one has no more to offer by way of advice than 'try to be a little kinder.'
text_raw: It is a bit embarrassing to have been concerned with the human problem all one's life and find at the end that one has no more to offer by way of advice than 'try to be a little kinder.'
author: Aldous Huxley

provenance.notes: Authentic Huxley, from the last years of his life (c. 1961-62) - the self-deprecating cadence and the phrase 'the human problem' are characteristic, and the remark is well documented in the Huxley literature as a summing-up he offered near the end. It is usually reported from a late lecture or interview rather than from something he wrote, and I cannot fix the specific occasion or the secondary source that first printed it, so I am leaving the citation null. Attribution strong, provenance of the report unconfirmed.

text: The nature of the universe is such that ends can never justify the means. On the contrary, the means always determine the end.
text_raw: The nature of the universe is such that ends can never justify the means. On the contrary, the means always determine the end.
author: Aldous Huxley

provenance.notes: This is Huxley's central thesis about means and ends and reads as authentically his - the argument that means determine ends is the spine of his 1937 book Ends and Means, written under Gerald Heard's and the pacifist movement's influence. The standard attribution points to Ends and Means (1937), but I cannot confirm this exact sentence pair appears there rather than in a related essay or in his Gandhi commentary, so I am not recording a citation. Attribution to Huxley is sound; the specific work is unconfirmed.

text: Art is an echo of the creative force that birthed Galaxies. Creativity is the way that the cosmos evolves and communicates with itself. The great uplifting of humanity beyond its self destruction is the redemptive mission of art.
text_raw: Art is an echo of the creative force that birthed Galaxies. Creativity is the way that the cosmos evolves and communicates with itself. The great uplifting of humanity beyond its self destruction is the redemptive mission of art.
author: Alex Grey

provenance.notes: Alex Grey is a living visionary artist and the passage is squarely in his register - the cosmic-evolutionary framing of creativity and the phrase 'the redemptive mission of art' echo his book The Mission of Art (1998) and his lecture material. But I cannot place this specific wording in a published text or talk, and contemporary artist statements circulate heavily paraphrased on social media. Plausibly authentic, unconfirmed.

text: All generalizations are dangerous, even this one.
text_raw: All generalizations are dangerous, even this one.
author: Alexander Dumas

provenance.notes: Standardly attributed to Alexandre Dumas fils in 20th-century quotation dictionaries ('Toutes les generalisations sont dangereuses, y compris celle-ci'), but I know of no primary source in his plays or novels, and quotation dictionaries of that era propagated attributions without sourcing. A close cousin, 'No generalization is wholly true, not even this one', is attributed to Oliver Wendell Holmes - the two may share an origin or may be independent formulations of an old joke. NOTE: if this attribution is kept, the corpus name should be 'Alexandre Dumas' (fils), not the anglicized 'Alexander Dumas'.

text: A person who doubts himself is like a man who would enlist in the ranks of his enemies and bear arms against himself. He makes his failure certain by himself being the first person to be convinced of it.
text_raw: A person who doubts himself is like a man who would enlist in the ranks of his enemies and bear arms against himself. He makes his failure certain by himself being the first person to be convinced of it.
author: Alexander Dumas

provenance.notes: I cannot place this in either Dumas pere or Dumas fils. It circulates on aggregator sites credited to a bare 'Alexandre Dumas', which is a common pattern for orphaned motivational lines - the enlist-against-yourself conceit reads more like 19th-century moralist or later self-help prose than like Dumas's narrative voice, though I would not call it a misattribution without evidence of a different author. No traceable source. NOTE: the corpus name is anglicized ('Alexander'); the French author is Alexandre Dumas, and which Dumas is intended is itself unclear.

text: What this power is I cannot say; all I know is that it exists and it becomes available only when a man is in that state of mind in which he knows exactly what he wants and is fully determined not to quit until he finds it.
text_raw: What this power is I cannot say; all I know is that it exists and it becomes available only when a man is in that state of mind in which he knows exactly what he wants and is fully determined not to quit until he finds it.
author: Alexander Graham Bell

provenance.notes: This reaches modern readers through Napoleon Hill, who quotes it as Alexander Graham Bell in Think and Grow Rich (1937) - I am fairly but not fully confident of that placement, so I have not recorded it as a citation. The material point is that Hill is an unreliable transmitter: his claimed interviews with and quotations from Carnegie, Edison, Bell and others have been repeatedly challenged, and several are undocumented outside his own books. I know of no Bell letter, lecture, or notebook containing this sentence. Treat the attribution as weak pending a primary source.

text: Get in over your head as often and as joyfully as possible.
text_raw: Get in over your head as often and as joyfully as possible.
author: Alexander Isley

provenance.notes: Alexander Isley is a real and identifiable graphic designer (founding art director of Spy magazine, later Alexander Isley Inc.), and the line has the flavor of design-school advice given in an AIGA talk or a published list of maxims for young designers - the kind of source that rarely makes it into quotation records. I cannot confirm the wording or the occasion. Attribution plausible and specific enough not to look invented, but unverified.

text: Some people will never learn anything… because they understand everything too soon.
text_raw: Some people will never learn anything… because they understand everything too soon.
author: Alexander Pope

provenance.notes: Very likely genuine Pope, from the aphorism collection Thoughts on Various Subjects (first published 1727 in the Pope-Swift Miscellanies), where the sentence runs closer to 'Some people will never learn anything, for this reason, because they understand everything too soon.' Two caveats keep this below verified: the Miscellanies were a joint Pope-Swift production and individual maxims are sometimes disputed between them, and the corpus text is a compressed modernization with an ellipsis rather than the original wording.

text: Art flourishes when there is a sense of adventure.
text_raw: Art flourishes when there is a sense of adventure.
author: Alfred North Whitehead

provenance.earliest_print_source: Adventures of Ideas, Alfred North Whitehead, 1933
provenance.notes: Consistent with Whitehead's treatment of Adventure as a civilizing force in the final part of Adventures of Ideas, where he argues that art and civilization decay without the sense of adventure. I am confident in the author and reasonably confident in the book; the exact wording circulates in two forms ('when there is' / 'where there is'), which suggests some paraphrase drift, so I am holding this just under the verified bar rather than claiming chapter and page.

text: I used to be an atheist until I realized I am god.
text_raw: I used to be an atheist until I realized I am god.
author: Alfred North Whitehead

provenance.notes: Almost certainly not Whitehead. The flippant one-liner register is entirely foreign to his prose, and the theological claim contradicts his actual position: Whitehead's process theology in Process and Reality (1929) and Religion in the Making (1926) develops a dipolar God distinct from, though internally related to, the world - he had no interest in the human-as-deity conceit, and he was not an atheist earlier in life in the sense the joke requires. This reads as a modern quip or bumper-sticker line that acquired a philosopher's name for weight. I cannot identify the actual originator, so no reattribution is offered. Recommend removal rather than reassignment.

text: Being happy is not the only happiness.
text_raw: Being happy is not the only happiness.
author: Alice Walker

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Alice Walker in quote collections and I have a weak recollection of it appearing in her fiction (possibly The Temple of My Familiar, 1989), but I cannot place the sentence in a specific work with confidence. No competing claimant, so the attribution is plausible; the sourcing is not established.

text: Anybody can observe the Sabbath, but making it holy surely takes the rest of the week.
text_raw: Anybody can observe the Sabbath, but making it holy surely takes the rest of the week.
author: Alice Walker

provenance.notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Alice Walker, and the aphoristic-theological turn is characteristic of her essays. I cannot identify the book, essay, or interview it comes from, so I will not name one. Plausible but unsourced.

text: The most common way people give up their power is by thinking they don't have any.
text_raw: The most common way people give up their power is by thinking they don't have any.
author: Alice Walker

provenance.notes: One of the most-circulated Alice Walker lines, attributed to her with unusual consistency and no rival claimant, which is mild evidence in its favor. But it circulates without a source citation everywhere I have seen it; I cannot place it in a specific book, essay, or speech. Attribution likely correct, provenance unestablished.

text: Design is intelligence made visible.
text_raw: Design is intelligence made visible.
author: Alina Wheeler

provenance.notes: Attributed to Alina Wheeler (author of Designing Brand Identity) in most design-quote contexts, but the same line is also circulated as Le Corbusier's, and I cannot confirm either. If it is Wheeler's it would most plausibly come from Designing Brand Identity, but I cannot confirm that it originates with her rather than being quoted by her. Competing attribution keeps confidence low.

text: If I could wish for my life to be perfect, it would be tempting, but I would have to decline, for life would no longer teach me anything.
text_raw: If I could wish for my life to be perfect, it would be tempting, but I would have to decline, for life would no longer teach me anything.
author: Allyson Jones

provenance.notes: I have no knowledge of an author named Allyson Jones associated with this or any quotation, and no recollection of the line itself. No traceable source; honest answer is that I do not know where this came from or whether the attributed person exists as a public author.

text: The illiterate of the 21st century will not be those who cannot read and write, but those who cannot learn, unlearn, and relearn.
text_raw: The illiterate of the 21st century will not be those who cannot read and write, but those who cannot learn, unlearn, and relearn.
author: Alvin Toffler

provenance.earliest_print_source: Future Shock, Alvin Toffler, 1970 (quoting psychologist Herbert Gerjuoy)
provenance.notes: Toffler did not originate this. In Future Shock (1970) he quotes psychologist Herbert Gerjuoy: 'The illiterate of the future will not be the person who cannot read. It will be the person who does not know how to learn.' The widely circulated '21st century / learn, unlearn, and relearn' wording is a later popular reshaping of that sentence, not a verbatim Toffler line. Toffler is the transmitter, Gerjuoy the source of the thought; the exact modern wording is of uncertain authorship. | Suggested reattribution: Herbert Gerjuoy, as quoted by Alvin Toffler in Future Shock (1970)

text: The most difficult thing is the decision to act, the rest is merely tenacity. The fears are paper tigers. You can do anything you decide to do. You can act to change and control your life; and the procedure, the process is its own reward.
text_raw: The most difficult thing is the decision to act, the rest is merely tenacity. The fears are paper tigers. You can do anything you decide to do. You can act to change and control your life; and the procedure, the process is its own reward.
author: Amelia Earhart

provenance.notes: Very widely attributed to Earhart and consistent with her documented voice on risk and resolve; I believe it derives from her own writing or correspondence, but I cannot place it in a specific book (The Fun of It, Last Flight) or letter, so I will not cite one. Plausible and uncontested, but unsourced in what I know.

text: No kind action ever stops with itself. One kind action leads to another. Good example is followed. A single act of kindness throws out roots in all directions, and the roots spring up and make new trees. The greatest work that kindness does to others is that it makes them kind themselves.
text_raw: No kind action ever stops with itself. One kind action leads to another. Good example is followed. A single act of kindness throws out roots in all directions, and the roots spring up and make new trees. The greatest work that kindness does to others is that it makes them kind themselves.
author: Amelia Earhart

provenance.notes: Attributed to Earhart in quote collections, but the diction ('Good example is followed', 'throws out roots in all directions, and the roots spring up and make new trees') reads as nineteenth-century moral-essay prose rather than Earhart's plain twentieth-century style, and I cannot place it in any of her writings. I suspect an older, uncredited source that has been re-labelled with a famous name, but I cannot identify that source, so I am not proposing a reattribution. Treat the Earhart attribution as doubtful.

text: Of course I realized there was a measure of danger. Obviously I faced the possibility of not returning when first I considered going. Once faced and settled there really wasn't any good reason to refer to it.
text_raw: Of course I realized there was a measure of danger. Obviously I faced the possibility of not returning when first I considered going. Once faced and settled there really wasn't any good reason to refer to it.
author: Amelia Earhart

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Earhart and strongly consistent with her documented statements about accepting the hazards of her flights (compare the pre-1937 'popping-off' letter to G.P. Putnam). I believe it is genuine and comes from her own writing or an interview, most likely around the 1932 Atlantic solo or the 1937 world flight, but I cannot pin the specific text, so no print source is named.

text: Never interrupt someone doing what you said couldn't be done.
text_raw: Never interrupt someone doing what you said couldn't be done.
author: Amelia Earhart

provenance.notes: This is a modern internet aphorism with a snappy cadence unlike Earhart's prose, and I know of no source for it in her writings, letters, or contemporary press.
