Sagan and Ann Druyan wrote the original story on which the film was based, and Sagan died in December 1996 before its release, but I do not believe this speech appears in Sagan's 1985 novel. Attributing it to Sagan as an author is not supportable; it belongs to the screenwriters. | Suggested reattribution: Contact (1997 film), screenplay by James V. Hart and Michael Goldenberg

text: You have to know the past to understand the present.
text_raw: You have to know the past to understand the present.
author: Carl Sagan

provenance.notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Sagan, commonly to Cosmos (1980) and to the television series. It is short and aphoristic, which is exactly the shape of quotation that drifts, and I cannot place it at a specific page from memory. Nothing suggests another author — this is uncertainty about sourcing, not about attribution. Below the promotion bar on locus alone.

text: We inhabit a universe where atoms are made in the centers of stars; where each second a thousand suns are born; where life is sparked by sunlight and lightning in the airs and waters of youthful planets; where the raw material for biological evolution is sometimes made by the explosion of a star halfway across the Milky Way; where a thing as beautiful as a galaxy is formed a hundred billion times - a Cosmos of quasars and quarks, snowflakes and fireflies, where there may be black holes and other universe and extraterrestrial civilizations whose radio messages are at this moment reaching the Earth. How pallid by comparison are the pretensions of superstition and pseudoscience; how important it is for us to pursue and understand science, that characteristically human endeavor.
text_raw: We inhabit a universe where atoms are made in the centers of stars; where each second a thousand suns are born; where life is sparked by sunlight and lightning in the airs and waters of youthful planets; where the raw material for biological evolution is sometimes made by the explosion of a star halfway across the Milky Way; where a thing as beautiful as a galaxy is formed a hundred billion times - a Cosmos of quasars and quarks, snowflakes and fireflies, where there may be black holes and other universe and extraterrestrial civilizations whose radio messages are at this moment reaching the Earth. How pallid by comparison are the pretensions of superstition and pseudoscience; how important it is for us to pursue and understand science, that characteristically human endeavor.
author: Carl Sagan

provenance.earliest_print_source: Broca's Brain: Reflections on the Romance of Science, Carl Sagan, 1979 (chapter unconfirmed)
provenance.notes: Unmistakably Sagan's prose — the catalogue structure ('quasars and quarks, snowflakes and fireflies') and the closing turn on 'the pretensions of superstition and pseudoscience' are his. My recollection places it in Broca's Brain, most likely the pseudoscience essay 'Night Walkers and Mystery Mongers,' but I hold that loosely; it could belong to Cosmos or The Demon-Haunted World, which cover the same terrain. Author confident, locus uncertain.

text: It is the tension between creativity and skepticism that has produced the stunning and unexpected findings of science.
text_raw: It is the tension between creativity and skepticism that has produced the stunning and unexpected findings of science.
author: Carl Sagan

provenance.notes: The creativity/skepticism tension is one of Sagan's signature arguments — most fully developed in 'The Burden of Skepticism' (Skeptical Inquirer, 1987) and in the introduction to Broca's Brain (1979), where he writes of an 'exquisite balance' between the two. This particular sentence is consistently attributed to him and fits, but I cannot confidently assign it to either source, so I am leaving the print citation null rather than picking one.

text: The universe is a pretty big place. If it's just us, seems like an awful waste of space.
text_raw: The universe is a pretty big place. If it's just us, seems like an awful waste of space.
author: Carl Sagan

provenance.notes: To my knowledge this is dialogue from the 1997 film Contact — spoken by Ted Arroway to young Ellie and echoed by her later — and not text Sagan wrote. I recall it being listed among misattributions on Sagan's Wikiquote page for exactly this reason. Sagan wrote the novel and co-wrote the story, so the association is understandable, but the screenplay is by James V. Hart and Michael Goldenberg. I am not certain the line is absent from the 1985 novel, which is why this is 'likely' rather than settled; a text search of the novel would resolve it. | Suggested reattribution: Contact (1997 film), screenplay by James V. Hart and Michael Goldenberg

text: The visions we offer our children shape the future.
text_raw: The visions we offer our children shape the future.
author: Carl Sagan

provenance.earliest_print_source: Pale Blue Dot: A Vision of the Human Future in Space, Carl Sagan, 1994 (chapter unconfirmed)
provenance.notes: This is the opening of a longer Sagan passage that continues 'It matters what those visions are. Often they become self-fulfilling prophecies. Dreams are maps.' My recollection places it in Pale Blue Dot, but I cannot confirm the chapter and cannot rule out one of his Parade essays from the same period. Author attribution is solid; the citation is offered with an explicit caveat. Note also that the single-sentence excerpt is weaker than the full passage.

text: Time is the coin of your life. It is the only coin you have, and only you can determine how it will be spent. Be careful lest you let other people spend it for you.
text_raw: Time is the coin of your life. It is the only coin you have, and only you can determine how it will be spent. Be careful lest you let other people spend it for you.
author: Carl Sandburg

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Carl Sandburg across quotation collections and never, to my knowledge, to anyone else, which is mild evidence for authenticity. I cannot place it in a specific poem, essay, or interview, and I have no recollection of a primary citation. Attribution is stable but unverified at the source level.

text: You say you have no faith? Love - and faith will come. You say you are sad? Love - and joy will come. You say you are alone? Love - and you will break out of your solitude. You say you are in hell? Love - and you will find yourself in heaven.
text_raw: You say you have no faith? Love - and faith will come. You say you are sad? Love - and joy will come. You say you are alone? Love - and you will break out of your solitude. You say you are in hell? Love - and you will find yourself in heaven.
author: Carlo Carretto

provenance.notes: Carlo Carretto (1910-1988), Little Brother of Jesus, is the consistent attribution and the passage matches his devotional style and his repeated 'Love, and...' constructions. Most likely from Letters from the Desert (Lettere dal deserto, 1964) or The God Who Comes, but I cannot confirm which book or verify the English translation wording, so no print source is asserted.

text: The basic difference between an ordinary man and a warrior is that a warrior takes everything as a challenge while an ordinary man takes everything either as a blessing or a curse.
text_raw: The basic difference between an ordinary man and a warrior is that a warrior takes everything as a challenge while an ordinary man takes everything either as a blessing or a curse.
author: Carlos Castaneda

provenance.notes: Reads as a don Juan teaching from the Castaneda corpus and the vocabulary ('warrior', 'ordinary man', 'challenge') is characteristic of Tales of Power (1974) and the aphorism compilation The Wheel of Time (1998). I cannot pin the volume or page. Separate caveat for the corpus: Castaneda's don Juan material is widely held by scholars to be fiction, so 'Castaneda wrote it' is a different claim from 'a Yaqui teacher said it'.

text: Cruelty is a lack of imagination.
text_raw: Cruelty is a lack of imagination.
author: Carlos Fuentes

provenance.notes: The Fuentes attribution circulates in quotation aggregators but I cannot locate it in any of his novels, essays, or interviews from memory. The underlying idea ('cruelty is a failure of imagination') is a commonplace that has been voiced by several writers, which makes single-author attribution weak. Honest answer: unplaced.

text: When you hold resentment toward another, you are bound to that person or condition by an emotional link that is stronger than steel. Forgiveness is the only way to dissolve that link and get free.
text_raw: When you hold resentment toward another, you are bound to that person or condition by an emotional link that is stronger than steel. Forgiveness is the only way to dissolve that link and get free.
author: Catherine Ponder

provenance.notes: Catherine Ponder, New Thought minister, is the uniform attribution and the phrasing ('bound to that person by an emotional link stronger than steel') matches her prosperity-and-forgiveness teaching. Probably from The Dynamic Laws of Prosperity (1962) or a companion Dynamic Laws title, but I cannot confirm the book or edition, so no citation is asserted.

text: The more a man knows, the more he forgives.
text_raw: The more a man knows, the more he forgives.
author: Catherine the Great

provenance.notes: Attributed to Catherine the Great in English quotation dictionaries, but I know of no primary Russian or French source in her correspondence or memoirs. The sentiment closely tracks the older French maxim 'tout comprendre, c'est tout pardonner' (associated with Mme de Stael, Corinne, 1807), and the line is also floated under Confucius, which is a classic sign of a free-floating aphorism. Attribution is plausible but unsupported.

text: If we study the lives of great men and women carefully and unemotionally we find that, invariably, greatness was developed, tested and revealed through the darker periods of their lives. One of the largest tributaries of the river of greatness is always the stream of adversity.
text_raw: If we study the lives of great men and women carefully and unemotionally we find that, invariably, greatness was developed, tested and revealed through the darker periods of their lives. One of the largest tributaries of the river of greatness is always the stream of adversity.
author: Cavett Robert

provenance.notes: Cavett Robert (1907-1997), founder of the National Speakers Association, is the consistent attribution and the passage is idiomatic of mid-century American motivational speaking, so authorship is plausible. His material circulated largely through recorded talks rather than books, and I cannot cite a published source or a datable first appearance.

text: It is not the strongest of the species that survive, nor the most intelligent, but the one most responsive to change.
text_raw: It is not the strongest of the species that survive, nor the most intelligent, but the one most responsive to change.
author: Charles Darwin

provenance.earliest_print_source: 'Lessons from Europe for American Business', Leon C. Megginson, Southwestern Social Science Quarterly, vol. 44, 1963
provenance.notes: Not Darwin. This is one of the best-documented misattributions in the corpus: it originates as Leon C. Megginson's 1963 paraphrase of ideas in On the Origin of Species ('...it is not the most intellectual of the species that survives; it is not the strongest that survives; but the species that survives is the one that is able best to adapt and adjust to the changing environment...'). Later compression into a terse epigram, plus quotation marks, converted the paraphrase into a fake Darwin quote. Wikiquote lists it under Darwin's misattributed section. Darwin himself never wrote it; 'survival of the fittest' was Herbert Spencer's phrase, adopted by Darwin only in later editions. | Suggested reattribution: Leon C. Megginson (1963), paraphrasing Darwin

text: A man who dares to waste one hour of time has not discovered the value of life.
text_raw: A man who dares to waste one hour of time has not discovered the value of life.
author: Charles Darwin

provenance.notes: Unlike q_0458 this one is generally treated as genuine Darwin and is usually said to come from his correspondence, plausibly by way of The Life and Letters of Charles Darwin (ed. Francis Darwin, 1887). I cannot identify the specific letter, recipient, or date from memory, so I will not assert a citation. Given that Darwin is a misattribution magnet, moderate rather than high confidence is the honest reading.

text: The important thing is this: to be able at a moment's notice to sacrifice what we are for what we could become.
text_raw: The important thing is this: to be able at a moment's notice to sacrifice what we are for what we could become.
author: Charles du Bos

provenance.notes: Uniformly attributed to the French critic Charles du Bos (1882-1939), most likely from his Approximations essays or his Journal, and the aphoristic register fits him. I cannot confirm the French original or a volume, and the English wording varies ('at a moment's notice' / 'at any moment'), which suggests translation drift. No citation asserted.

text: The details are not the details. They make the design.
text_raw: The details are not the details. They make the design.
author: Charles Eames

provenance.notes: Well established as Charles Eames and quoted throughout design literature and Eames Office material; it is one of the lines the Eames Office itself repeats. Circulates in two variants ('They make the design' and '...they make the product'), which indicates it comes from spoken remarks or interviews rather than a fixed printed text. Strong attribution, no single primary source I can cite.

text: If you open your heart, love opens your mind.
text_raw: If you open your heart, love opens your mind.
author: Charles John Quarto

provenance.notes: Charles John Quarto is a real songwriter and poet, but I have no independent knowledge of this line in his published work. It appears to circulate only through quotation aggregators. No traceable source; 'I don't know' is the accurate verdict.

text: This may shock you, but I believe the single most significant decision I can make on a day-to-day basis is my choice of attitude. It is more important than my past, my education, my bankroll, my successes or failures, fame or pain, what other people think of me or say about me, my circumstances, or my position. Attitude is that "single string" that keeps me going or cripples my progress. It alone fuels my fire or assaults my hope. When my attitudes are right, there's no barrier too high, no valley too deep, no dream too extreme, no challenge too great for me.
text_raw: This may shock you, but I believe the single most significant decision I can make on a day-to-day basis is my choice of attitude. It is more important than my past, my education, my bankroll, my successes or failures, fame or pain, what other people think of me or say about me, my circumstances, or my position. Attitude is that "single string" that keeps me going or cripples my progress. It alone fuels my fire or assaults my hope. When my attitudes are right, there's no barrier too high, no valley too deep, no dream too extreme, no challenge too great for me.
author: Charles R. Swindoll

provenance.notes: Genuine Swindoll in substance: this is from his much-anthologized 'Attitude' material, the same body of writing as the far more famous 'The longer I live, the more I realize the impact of attitude on life' passage. My recollection places it in Strengthening Your Grip (1982), in the chapter on attitudes, but I am not confident enough in the book or year to assert it as a citation. Note that Swindoll's attitude texts are heavily paraphrased online, so the exact wording here may not be his published wording.

text: The person who does not work for the love of work but only for money is not likely to make money nor to find much fun in life.
text_raw: The person who does not work for the love of work but only for money is not likely to make money nor to find much fun in life.
author: Charles Schwab

provenance.notes: Attributed to 'Charles Schwab' without disambiguation. Period and diction point to Charles M. Schwab (1862-1939) of Bethlehem Steel, not Charles R. Schwab the modern broker; if genuine it most likely comes from his popular business writing of the 1910s-20s, possibly Succeeding With What You Have (1917). I cannot confirm the source, and the ambiguity of the bare name is itself a provenance defect worth fixing in the corpus. | Suggested reattribution: Charles M. Schwab (Bethlehem Steel, 1862-1939) - disambiguation, not reattribution

text: So live your life that the fear of death can never enter your heart. Trouble no one about their religion; respect others in their view, and demand that they respect yours. Love your life, perfect your life, beautify all things in your life. Seek to make your life long and its purpose in the service of your people. Prepare a noble death song for the day when you go over the great divide. Always give a word or a sign of salute when meeting or passing a friend, even a stranger, when in a lonely place. Show respect to all people and grovel to none. When you arise in the morning give thanks for the food and for the joy of living. If you see no reason for giving thanks, the fault lies only in yourself. Abuse no one and nothing, for abuse turns the wise ones to fools and robs the spirit of its vision. When it comes your time to die, be not like those whose hearts are filled with the fear of death, so that when their time comes they weep and pray for a little more time to live their lives over again in a different way. Sing your death song and die like a hero going home.
text_raw: So live your life that the fear of death can never enter your heart. Trouble no one about their religion; respect others in their view, and demand that they respect yours. Love your life, perfect your life, beautify all things in your life. Seek to make your life long and its purpose in the service of your people. Prepare a noble death song for the day when you go over the great divide. Always give a word or a sign of salute when meeting or passing a friend, even a stranger, when in a lonely place. Show respect to all people and grovel to none. When you arise in the morning give thanks for the food and for the joy of living. If you see no reason for giving thanks, the fault lies only in yourself. Abuse no one and nothing, for abuse turns the wise ones to fools and robs the spirit of its vision. When it comes your time to die, be not like those whose hearts are filled with the fear of death, so that when their time comes they weep and pray for a little more time to live their lives over again in a different way. Sing your death song and die like a hero going home.
author: Chief Tecumseh, Shawnee Nation

provenance.notes: Almost certainly not Tecumseh. Tecumseh died in 1813 and his authenticated speeches survive only through interpreters and hostile or secondhand transcription; this polished English passage is not among them and has no contemporaneous record. Its wide circulation is modern - it spread through 20th-century 'Native American wisdom' anthologies and then explosively through the 2012 film Act of Valor, which used it as a closing text. The style (aphoristic, individualist, self-help cadence) reads as 20th-century composition. I cannot identify the actual author, so apocryphal rather than likely_misattributed. Recommend not promoting it under a named historical figure.

text: Be not afraid of changing slowly; be afraid only of standing still.
text_raw: Be not afraid of changing slowly; be afraid only of standing still.
author: Chinese proverb

provenance.notes: This is a genuine Chinese proverb rather than a floating Western invention: it renders the common saying bu pa man, jiu pa zhan (不怕慢，就怕站), 'do not fear going slow, fear only standing still'. The corpus text says 'changing slowly' where the standard English rendering is 'growing slowly' - a variant, not a different proverb. Confidence reflects that the genre label 'Chinese proverb' is accurate; a proverb by nature has no single author or first printing.

text: If you are patient in one moment of anger, you will escape a hundred days of sorrow.
text_raw: If you are patient in one moment of anger, you will escape a hundred days of sorrow.
author: Chinese proverb

provenance.notes: Corresponds to the widely used Chinese saying ren yi shi zhi qi, mian bai ri zhi you (忍一时之气，免百日之忧), 'endure a moment's anger, avoid a hundred days of sorrow'. The label 'Chinese proverb' is therefore accurate as a genre attribution. As with all proverbs there is no author and no first-print source to verify.

text: The miracle is not to fly in the air, or to walk on the water; but to walk on the earth.
text_raw: The miracle is not to fly in the air, or to walk on the water; but to walk on the earth.
author: Chinese proverb

provenance.notes: The 'Chinese proverb' label is doubtful. The thought is Chan/Zen rather than proverbial - closest classical antecedent is Layman Pang's 'my miraculous power and spiritual activity: drawing water and carrying firewood'. The specific modern English phrasing most resembles Thich Nhat Hanh's line 'The miracle is not to walk on water; the miracle is to walk on the green earth', which is Vietnamese Zen, not a Chinese proverb. I am not confident enough to name a true source, so no reattribution is suggested, but the current label should be treated as unreliable.

text: Tell me, I'll forget. Show me, I may remember. But involve me and I'll understand.
text_raw: Tell me, I'll forget. Show me, I may remember. But involve me and I'll understand.
author: Chinese proverb

provenance.notes: A much-laundered saying: variously credited to Confucius, Xunzi, Benjamin Franklin, Native American sources, and 'Chinese proverb', which is the signature of an aphorism with no real home. There is a genuine classical antecedent in the Xunzi (ch. 8): hearing is not as good as seeing, seeing is not as good as knowing, knowing is not as good as putting into practice - but the modern tell/show/involve triad appears to be a 20th-century Western educational formulation rather than a translation. Label is unreliable; true origin unidentified.

text: A bit of fragrance always clings to the hand that gives roses.
text_raw: "A bit of fragrance always clings to the hand that gives roses."
author: Chinese proverb

provenance.notes: Circulates as both a Chinese proverb and as a line by Hada Bejar, and neither attribution has support I can verify. I know of no Chinese original for it, which weakens the proverb label. Untraceable from training knowledge.

text: Spirituality is the sacred center out of which all life comes, including Mondays and Tuesdays and rainy Saturday afternoons in all their mundane and glorious detail. ... The spiritual journey is the soul's life commingling with ordinary life.
text_raw: "Spirituality is the sacred center out of which all life comes, including Mondays and Tuesdays and rainy Saturday afternoons in all their mundane and glorious detail. ... The spiritual journey is the soul's life commingling with ordinary life."
author: Christina Baldwin

provenance.notes: Christina Baldwin is the consistent attribution and the passage matches her journal-writing and spiritual-practice books, most likely Life's Companion: Journal Writing as a Spiritual Quest (1990). I cannot confirm the book or page. Note also that the corpus text is elided with an ellipsis, so it splices two non-adjacent sentences - worth flagging independent of authorship.

text: Everybody builds a dream in their lifetime. You’re either going to build your dream, or somebody else's. So build your own!
text_raw: Everybody builds a dream in their lifetime. You’re either going to build your dream, or somebody else's. So build your own!
author: Christopher LaBrec

provenance.notes: I have no knowledge of Christopher LaBrec as a published author or public figure, and no recollection of this line outside quotation aggregators. It has the shape of a motivational-poster attribution of unknown origin. Honest verdict: unverifiable.

text: You can buy a person's time; you can buy their physical presence at a given place. You can even buy a measured number of their skilled muscular motions per hour, but you cannot buy enthusiasm... you can not buy loyalty. You cannot buy the devotion of hearts, minds, or souls. You must earn these.
text_raw: You can buy a person's time; you can buy their physical presence at a given place. You can even buy a measured number of their skilled muscular motions per hour, but you cannot buy enthusiasm... you can not buy loyalty. You cannot buy the devotion of hearts, minds, or souls. You must earn these.
author: Clarence Francis

provenance.notes: Clarence Francis, chairman of General Foods (1935-1954), is the standard and stable attribution in management literature, typically credited to a speech or company address in the 1940s-50s. I cannot name the speech or date. The corpus text is gender-neutralized ('a person's time... their physical presence'); the circulating original reads 'a man's time... his physical presence', which should be noted if the quote is promoted.

text: Anything you do from the soulful self will help lighten the burdens of the world. Anything. You have no idea what the smallest word, the tiniest generosity can cause to be set in motion. Be outrageous in forgiving. Be dramatic in reconciling. Mistakes? Back up and make them as right as you can, then move on. Be off the charts in kindness. In whatever you are called to, strive to be devoted to it in all aspects large and small. Fall short? Try again. Mastery is made in increments, not in leaps. Be brave, be fierce, be visionary. Mend the parts of the world that are within your reach. To strive to live this way is the most dramatic gift you can ever give to the world.
text_raw: "Anything you do from the soulful self will help lighten the burdens of the world. Anything. You have no idea what the smallest word, the tiniest generosity can cause to be set in motion. Be outrageous in forgiving. Be dramatic in reconciling. Mistakes? Back up and make them as right as you can, then move on. Be off the charts in kindness. In whatever you are called to, strive to be devoted to it in all aspects large and small. Fall short? Try again. Mastery is made in increments, not in leaps. Be brave, be fierce, be visionary. Mend the parts of the world that are within your reach. To strive to live this way is the most dramatic gift you can ever give to the world."
author: Clarissa Pinkola Estes

provenance.notes: Genuine Clarissa Pinkola Estes. This passage is from her widely circulated essay known as 'We Were Made for These Times' / 'Letter to a Young Activist During Troubled Times', which spread online in the early 2000s and was later collected in her published work. I am confident about the essay but not about its first print appearance or exact date, so no citation is asserted. Caveat: the online versions of this essay vary in wording and are sometimes reordered, so the exact text here may be a circulated variant.

text: You must speak straight so that your words may go as sunlight to our hearts.
text_raw: You must speak straight so that your words may go as sunlight to our hearts.
author: Cochise

provenance.notes: A staple of Native American oratory anthologies, consistently attributed to Cochise and plausibly drawn from accounts of his 1871-72 negotiations with U.S. officers (the Howard/Jeffords parleys). I cannot confirm an original transcript or the anthology that first printed it. All surviving Cochise speech is mediated through interpreters and later journalistic reconstruction, so even a genuine source would be a secondhand rendering. Honest answer: plausible, unconfirmed.

text: By three methods we may learn wisdom: First, by reflection, which is noblest; second, by imitation, which is easiest; and third, by experience, which is the bitterest.
text_raw: By three methods we may learn wisdom: First, by reflection, which is noblest; second, by imitation, which is easiest; and third, by experience, which is the bitterest.
author: Confucius

provenance.notes: Does not appear in the Analects or any Confucian classic that I know of. This is a modern English-language aphorism that spread through 20th-century quotation books and later quote sites; the tidy 'noblest / easiest / bitterest' rhetorical triad is characteristic of Western epigram construction, not of the Analects' terse recorded exchanges. I do not know who actually composed it, so I offer no reattribution. Confucius is a magnet for invented maxims of exactly this shape.

text: Will you allow yourself to be hostage to the ego or host to God?
text_raw: Will you allow yourself to be hostage to the ego or host to God?
author: Course in Miracles

provenance.earliest_print_source: A Course in Miracles, Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976 (Text)
provenance.notes: The antithesis 'host to God or hostage to the ego' is genuine ACIM language and recurs in the Text; I am confident of the source work but not of the exact chapter/section, so I have not cited one. The line as given here is phrased as a question and reads as a rewording of the canonical declarative sentence rather than a verbatim quotation, which is why this is 'attributed' rather than 'verified'. Anyone promoting this should check the wording against the FIP Text.

text: There are two kinds of people who never amount to much: those who cannot do what they are told, and those who can do nothing else.
text_raw: There are two kinds of people who never amount to much: those who cannot do what they are told, and those who can do nothing else.
author: Cyrus Curtis

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Cyrus H. K. Curtis, the Curtis Publishing / Saturday Evening Post publisher, in mid-20th-century business-epigram collections of the B. C. Forbes type. I cannot place a primary source — no speech, letter, or interview I can name — and business aphorisms of this vintage migrate freely between Curtis, Carnegie, and other publisher-industrialist figures. Plausible but unconfirmed.

text: To see directly into one’s original nature, this is Zen... This Nature is the Mind, and the Mind is Buddha, and the Buddha is the Way, and the Way is Zen.
text_raw: To see directly into one’s original nature, this is Zen... This Nature is the Mind, and the Mind is Buddha, and the Buddha is the Way, and the Way is Zen.
author: D. T. Suzuki

provenance.notes: The content and idiom are consistent with D. T. Suzuki's expository writing on Zen (An Introduction to Zen Buddhism, Essays in Zen Buddhism, and the Barrett-edited Selected Writings), and the closing chain 'Nature is Mind, Mind is Buddha, Buddha is the Way, the Way is Zen' echoes the Chan formulations he liked to render in English. But I cannot place the volume or page, and the ellipsis suggests the line has been stitched from a longer passage. Note also that quote sites routinely confuse D. T. Suzuki with Shunryu Suzuki, so the attribution deserves a source check.

text: If you understand real practice, then archery or other activities can be Zen. If you don't understand how to practice archery in its true sense, then even though you practice very hard, what you acquire is just technique. It won't help you through and through. Perhaps you can hit the mark without trying, but without a bow and arrow you cannot do anything. If you understand the point of practice, then even without a bow and arrow the archery will help you. How you get that kind of power or ability is only through right practice.
text_raw: If you understand real practice, then archery or other activities can be Zen. If you don't understand how to practice archery in its true sense, then even though you practice very hard, what you acquire is just technique. It won't help you through and through. Perhaps you can hit the mark without trying, but without a bow and arrow you cannot do anything. If you understand the point of practice, then even without a bow and arrow the archery will help you. How you get that kind of power or ability is only through right practice.
author: D. T. Suzuki

provenance.earliest_print_source: Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, Shunryu Suzuki, Weatherhill, 1970
provenance.notes: This is Shunryu Suzuki, not D. T. Suzuki. The passage is from Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind — the plainspoken lecture voice ('it won't help you through and through', 'without a bow and arrow you cannot do anything') is Shunryu Suzuki's transcribed dharma-talk register, not D. T. Suzuki's scholarly prose. My confidence in the reattribution to Shunryu Suzuki is high (~0.85); the 0.2 above reflects confidence in the stated author, D. T. Suzuki, which is low. I am confident of the book but not of the chapter, so none is cited. This is the single most common Suzuki/Suzuki mix-up in quote corpora. | Suggested reattribution: Shunryu Suzuki

text: People who cease to grow can't inspire others. Leadership begins with challenging oneself.
text_raw: People who cease to grow can't inspire others. Leadership begins with challenging oneself.
author: Daisaku Ikeda

provenance.notes: Consistent with Ikeda's enormous published output of guidance essays, editorials, and daily-encouragement columns circulated through SGI publications, and I have no reason to doubt it. But that same output is the problem: his aphorisms circulate detached from the essay or speech they came from, and I cannot name the source. Plausible, unplaced.

text: The period of greatest gain in knowledge and experience is the most difficult period in one’s life.
text_raw: The period of greatest gain in knowledge and experience is the most difficult period in one’s life.
author: Dalai Lama

provenance.notes: Ubiquitous on quote sites under the Dalai Lama's name, but I can identify no book, talk, or interview behind it. The generic phrasing is typical of lines that accrete to him rather than originate with him. The 14th Dalai Lama is a strong misattribution magnet — the volume of translated, transcribed, and paraphrased teaching makes him easy to attach anything to.

text: We can let the circumstances of our lives harden us so that we become increasingly resentful and afraid, or we can let them soften us, and make us kinder. We always have the choice.
text_raw: We can let the circumstances of our lives harden us so that we become increasingly resentful and afraid, or we can let them soften us, and make us kinder. We always have the choice.
author: Dalai Lama

provenance.notes: This is Pema Chodron, not the Dalai Lama. The harden/soften antithesis closing on 'We always have the choice' is one of her signature passages, from her late-1990s/early-2000s books (When Things Fall Apart, 1997, and The Places That Scare You, 2001 are the two candidates I would check first) — I am confident of the author but not of which book, so I cite neither rather than guess. Confidence in the reattribution to Chodron is roughly 0.75; the 0.2 above reflects the stated attribution to the Dalai Lama. | Suggested reattribution: Pema Chodron

text: This is my simple religion. There is no need for temples; no need for complicated philosophy. Our own brain, our own heart is our temple; the philosophy is kindness.
text_raw: This is my simple religion. There is no need for temples; no need for complicated philosophy. Our own brain, our own heart is our temple; the philosophy is kindness.
author: Dalai Lama

provenance.notes: One of the better-supported Dalai Lama attributions: it appears in edited collections of his teachings from around 1990 onward and is quoted with unusually stable wording, which usually indicates a real printed origin rather than internet drift. It also matches his repeated public formulation 'my religion is kindness.' I cannot name the specific volume or talk, so I leave the source null rather than guess at one. Strong secondary evidence, no primary source in hand.

text: The problem isn't materialism as such. Rather it is the underlying assumption that full satisfaction can arise from gratifying the senses alone. Unlike animals whose quest for happiness is restricted to survival and to the immediate gratification of sensory desires, we human beings have the capacity to experience happiness at a deeper level which, when achieved, can overwhelm unhappy experiences.
text_raw: The problem isn't materialism as such. Rather it is the underlying assumption that full satisfaction can arise from gratifying the senses alone. Unlike animals whose quest for happiness is restricted to survival and to the immediate gratification of sensory desires, we human beings have the capacity to experience happiness at a deeper level which, when achieved, can overwhelm unhappy experiences.
author: Dalai Lama

provenance.notes: The length, the qualified argument, and the human/animal contrast are characteristic of the Dalai Lama's book-length ethical writing of the late 1990s (Ethics for the New Millennium, The Art of Happiness with Howard Cutler) rather than of a fabricated aphorism — invented quotes are rarely this long or this hedged. That raises my confidence that it is genuine, but I cannot place the book or article, and passages of this kind are often lightly edited by whoever excerpts them.

text: The deep root of failure in our lives is to think, ‘Oh how useless and powerless I am.’ It is essential to think strongly and forcefully, ‘I can do it,’ without boasting or fretting.
text_raw: The deep root of failure in our lives is to think, ‘Oh how useless and powerless I am.’ It is essential to think strongly and forcefully, ‘I can do it,’ without boasting or fretting.
author: Dalai Lama

provenance.notes: Widely circulated under the Dalai Lama's name, often via daily-wisdom compilations of the Path to Tranquility type edited by Renuka Singh. The content matches his standard teaching against self-disparagement, which he treats as a distinctively Western affliction. No primary source I can name, and compilation books rarely cite their own origins, so the chain of custody is weak.

text: The essence of all religions is love, compassion, and tolerance. Kindness is my true religion. The clear proof of a person's love of God is if that person genuinely shows love to fellow human beings.
text_raw: The essence of all religions is love, compassion, and tolerance. Kindness is my true religion. The clear proof of a person's love of God is if that person genuinely shows love to fellow human beings.
author: Dalai Lama

provenance.notes: Reads as a composite: three separate Dalai Lama themes welded into one paragraph. 'Kindness is my true religion' is a real and characteristic formulation of his; the sentences on either side circulate independently elsewhere. Composite quotes are common on aggregator sites and are individually genuine but collectively unsourceable. I would not promote this as a single utterance without finding a source that carries all three sentences together.

text: Be kind whenever possible. It is always possible.
text_raw: Be kind whenever possible. It is always possible.
author: Dalai Lama

provenance.notes: Extremely famous and almost universally attributed to the Dalai Lama, but to my knowledge it sits in the unsourced/attributed section on Wikiquote rather than the sourced section — no book, speech, or interview has been pinned to it. Fame is not evidence: this is a case where near-universal attribution coexists with zero documented provenance. Honest verdict is low confidence despite how well known the line is.

text: If you want others to be happy, practice compassion. If you want to be happy, practice compassion.
text_raw: If you want others to be happy, practice compassion. If you want to be happy, practice compassion.
author: Dalai Lama

provenance.notes: A near-ubiquitous Dalai Lama attribution with very stable wording, and it faithfully renders a real and repeated theme in his teaching on compassion as self-interested as well as altruistic. But I cannot locate a primary source, and like several of his most-shared lines it may be a compressed paraphrase of a longer spoken passage rather than a verbatim quotation.

text: If you were to spend a few minutes every day thinking about and trying to develop compassion, eventually compassion, the essence of spiritual practice, will become part of your life. When that happens I am convinced that not only will your life be happier but you will also make a direct contribution of peace and happiness in the world as a whole.
text_raw: If you were to spend a few minutes every day thinking about and trying to develop compassion, eventually compassion, the essence of spiritual practice, will become part of your life. When that happens I am convinced that not only will your life be happier but you will also make a direct contribution of peace and happiness in the world as a whole.
author: Dalai Lama

provenance.notes: Length and the first-person 'I am convinced' make a genuine spoken or written origin likely — this reads like transcript, not aggregator invention. Consistent with his talks and writings on compassion practice (The Compassionate Life and similar collections would be where I would look). No source I can name, so the attribution stays unverified.

text: We need not only a trained intelligence, but also a warm heart. Then a sense of community and a sense of responsibility will arise naturally.
text_raw: We need not only a trained intelligence, but also a warm heart. Then a sense of community and a sense of responsibility will arise naturally.
author: Dalai Lama

provenance.notes: 'Warm heart' and 'warm-heartedness' are genuine signature terms of the Dalai Lama's public teaching, which supports the attribution at a thematic level. But the intelligence-plus-heart construction is also a widely shared moral commonplace — compare King's 'intelligence plus character' — and I cannot place this specific sentence in any of his talks or books. Thematically plausible, textually unplaced.

text: Success is getting what you want; happiness is wanting what you get.
text_raw: Success is getting what you want; happiness is wanting what you get.
author: Dale Carnegie

provenance.notes: Contested and probably not Carnegie. This chiasmus circulates under several names — Dale Carnegie, Ingrid Bergman, and others — which is the classic signature of a floating aphorism that predates all of its claimed authors. I do not recall encountering it in How to Win Friends and Influence People or How to Stop Worrying and Start Living. Because I cannot identify a probable true origin, I am recording this as unverified rather than as a misattribution, but the Carnegie credit should be treated as weak.

text: Dreams are renewable. No matter what our age or condition, there are still untapped possibilities within us and new beauty waiting to be born.
text_raw: Dreams are renewable. No matter what our age or condition, there are still untapped possibilities within us and new beauty waiting to be born.
author: Dale Turner

provenance.notes: Attributed to Dale E. Turner, the Seattle-area minister and long-running Seattle Times columnist, and the sentiment and cadence fit his inspirational column work. His columns are the likely origin, but individual columns are rarely cited by the quote collections that reprint him, and I cannot name a date or title. Plausible, unconfirmed.

text: Conscious evolution begins as we take responsibility for clearing our own obstructions.
text_raw: Conscious evolution begins as we take responsibility for clearing our own obstructions.
author: Dan Millman

provenance.notes: Consistent with Dan Millman's vocabulary — 'conscious evolution', 'obstructions' — and with his post-Peaceful Warrior instructional books (No Ordinary Moments, The Life You Were Born to Live, The Laws of Spirit). Millman is a living author who circulates his own lines, so the attribution itself is low-risk, but I cannot name the book or page.

text: When we feel stuck, going nowhere - even starting to slip backward - we may actually be backing up to get a running start.
text_raw: When we feel stuck, going nowhere - even starting to slip backward - we may actually be backing up to get a running start.
author: Dan Millman

provenance.notes: A recognizable Millman line with a distinctive image (backing up to get a running start) that argues against generic invention, and consistent with his 1990s books. Attribution to Millman is low-risk; the specific source is unplaced in my knowledge, so it stays unverified.

text: Energy follows thought. We move toward, but not beyond, what we can imagine. By expanding our deepest beliefs about what is possible, we change our experience of it.
text_raw: Energy follows thought. We move toward, but not beyond, what we can imagine. By expanding our deepest beliefs about what is possible, we change our experience of it.
author: Dan Millman

provenance.notes: 'Energy follows thought' is a New Thought commonplace that long predates Millman, but the surrounding sentences ('we move toward, but not beyond, what we can imagine') are his phrasing and consistent with his instructional writing. So the passage as a whole is plausibly his composition even though its opening maxim is inherited. No source located.

text: Death is not sad. The sad thing is that most people don't ever really live at all.
text_raw: Death is not sad. The sad thing is that most people don't ever really live at all.
author: Dan Millman

provenance.earliest_print_source: Way of the Peaceful Warrior, Dan Millman, 1980 (widely cited to this book; page/edition unverified)
provenance.notes: I recall this line as spoken by the 'Socrates' character in Millman's Way of the Peaceful Warrior (1980), usually quoted as 'Death is not sad. The sad thing is that most people don't really live at all.' The attribution to Millman is consistent everywhere I have seen it and the voice matches the book. I cannot confirm the exact page or edition from memory, so I am holding this below the primary-source band.

text: The secret of happiness is not found in seeking more, but in developing the capacity to enjoy less.
text_raw: The secret of happiness is not found in seeking more, but in developing the capacity to enjoy less.
author: Dan Millman

provenance.notes: Circulates widely and consistently under Dan Millman's name, but I cannot place it in any specific book of his. The sentiment is close to his 'peaceful warrior' material, which makes the attribution plausible rather than evidenced. No primary source known to me.

text: Managing your money does not depend upon becoming wealthy or declaring vows of poverty. Rather, it is about creating stability and sufficiency – a balanced flow of monetary energy through your life.
text_raw: Managing your money does not depend upon becoming wealthy or declaring vows of poverty. Rather, it is about creating stability and sufficiency – a balanced flow of monetary energy through your life.
author: Dan Millman

provenance.notes: Reads like Millman's prose and likely comes from Everyday Enlightenment: The Twelve Gateways to Personal Growth (1998), which contains a gateway on managing finances framed around sufficiency rather than wealth or poverty. I cannot confirm the passage, so I am not asserting that book as the source.

text: How you handle or mishandle your money tells us who you are and, more important, it tells YOU who you are. Your priorities, passions, goals, and fears are shown clearly in the flow of your money. Your value system, or lack of one causes money to flow around you, past you, or to you. When money is in your possession, what you do with it screams loudly who you are.
text_raw: How you handle or mishandle your money tells us who you are and, more important, it tells YOU who you are. Your priorities, passions, goals, and fears are shown clearly in the flow of your money. Your value system, or lack of one causes money to flow around you, past you, or to you. When money is in your possession, what you do with it screams loudly who you are.
author: Dave Ramsey

provenance.notes: This passage is consistently attributed to Dave Ramsey and matches his voice and his standard theme that money behavior reveals character. It most likely comes from The Total Money Makeover or the Financial Peace material, but I cannot pin the book or page, so no print source is asserted. Attribution is strong; the citation is not.

text: A successful person is one who can lay a firm foundation with the bricks that others throw at him or her.
text_raw: A successful person is one who can lay a firm foundation with the bricks that others throw at him or her.
author: David Brinkley

provenance.notes: Standardly attributed to broadcaster David Brinkley (usually as 'A successful man is one who can lay a firm foundation with the bricks others have thrown at him'), but I know of no speech, broadcast, or book of his where it originates. Variants of the 'foundation from thrown bricks' aphorism circulated in American inspirational writing before Brinkley's prominence, which makes him a plausible popularizer rather than a confirmed author. The text here has also been gender-neutralized from the common form.

text: The world turns aside to let any person pass who knows whither he or she is going.
text_raw: The world turns aside to let any person pass who knows whither he or she is going.
author: David S. Jordan

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Philosophy of Despair, David Starr Jordan, 1902 (widely cited; exact page unverified)
provenance.notes: Genuine David Starr Jordan, the Stanford naturalist and first president of the university. The original reads 'The world turns aside to let any man pass who knows whither he is going' and is commonly cited to his 1902 essay The Philosophy of Despair. The corpus records the author as 'David S. Jordan'; the standard form of the name is David Starr Jordan. The quote text here has been gender-neutralized from the original. | Suggested reattribution: David Starr Jordan (name normalization, same person)

text: Goals are as essential to success as air is to life.
text_raw: Goals are as essential to success as air is to life.
author: David Schwartz

provenance.notes: Attributed to David J. Schwartz and generally traced to The Magic of Thinking Big (1959), whose chapter on goals argues exactly this. The attribution is consistent and the source book is very likely correct, but I cannot verify the wording or page from memory, so I am leaving the print citation blank rather than asserting it. Note the corpus records the author as 'David Schwartz'; the usual byline is David J. Schwartz.

text: Dreams are the seeds of change. Nothing ever grows without a seed, and nothing ever changes without a dream.
text_raw: Dreams are the seeds of change. Nothing ever grows without a seed, and nothing ever changes without a dream.
author: Debby Boone

provenance.notes: Attributed to singer Debby Boone across quote compilations, with no primary source I can identify — no book, interview, or speech. The attribution is uniform but rests entirely on quote-site repetition, which is weak evidence.

text: The problem is never how to get new, innovative thoughts into your mind, but how to get old ones out.
text_raw: "The problem is never how to get new, innovative thoughts into your mind, but how to get old ones out."
author: Dee Hock

provenance.notes: A signature Dee Hock line, from the Visa founder's chaordic-organization material. It was widely circulated after the 1996 Fast Company profile of Hock and appears in the same vein as Birth of the Chaordic Age (1999). Attribution to Hock is strong and consistent; I cannot confirm which of the two is the earliest print appearance, so I am not asserting a citation.

text: By becoming a conscious choice-maker, you begin to generate actions that are evolutionary for you.
text_raw: By becoming a conscious choice-maker, you begin to generate actions that are evolutionary for you.
author: Deepak Chopra

provenance.notes: Chopra's vocabulary — 'conscious choice-maker' and actions that are 'evolutionary' are his terms from the Law of Karma chapter of The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success (1994). Attribution to Chopra is solid; I cannot confirm this exact sentence, so it may be a condensation of the passage rather than a verbatim line.

text: Happiness is a continuation of happenings which are not resisted.
text_raw: Happiness is a continuation of happenings which are not resisted.
author: Deepak Chopra

provenance.notes: Widely quoted as Chopra and consistent with his teaching on non-resistance, but I cannot place it in any of his books or talks. Short aphorisms like this one attach easily to famous teachers, so I am keeping this well below the promotion bar.

text: When you struggle against this moment, you're actually struggling against the entire universe. Instead, you can make the decision that today you will not struggle against the whole universe by struggling against this moment. This means that your acceptance of this moment is total and complete. You accept things as they are, not as you wish they were in this moment. This is important to understand. You can wish for things in the future to be different, but in this moment you have to accept things as they are.
text_raw: When you struggle against this moment, you're actually struggling against the entire universe. Instead, you can make the decision that today you will not struggle against the whole universe by struggling against this moment. This means that your acceptance of this moment is total and complete. You accept things as they are, not as you wish they were in this moment. This is important to understand. You can wish for things in the future to be different, but in this moment you have to accept things as they are.
author: Deepak Chopra

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success, Deepak Chopra, 1994 — Law of Least Effort chapter (locus from memory, page unverified)
provenance.notes: This is the acceptance component of the Law of Least Effort in The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success, where Chopra defines acceptance as agreeing to accept this moment as it is because struggling against it is struggling against the whole universe. I am confident in the book and chapter; I cannot verify the exact wording or page.

text: Unity consciousness is a state of enlightenment where we pierce the mask of illusion which creates separation and fragmentation. Behind the appearance of separation is one unified field of wholeness. Here the seer and the scenery are one.
text_raw: "Unity consciousness is a state of enlightenment where we pierce the mask of illusion which creates separation and fragmentation. Behind the appearance of separation is one unified field of wholeness. Here the seer and the scenery are one."
author: Deepak Chopra

provenance.notes: The language is unmistakably Chopra's Vedanta framing — unity consciousness, the unified field, 'the seer and the scenery are one' — and it is consistently credited to him. I cannot place which book it comes from (candidates include The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success and Ageless Body, Timeless Mind), so I am not asserting a source.

text: Happiness cannot be traveled to, owned, earned, worn or consumed. Happiness is the spiritual experience of living every minute with love, grace, and gratitude.
text_raw: Happiness cannot be traveled to, owned, earned, worn or consumed. Happiness is the spiritual experience of living every minute with love, grace, and gratitude.
author: Denis Waitley

provenance.notes: One of the most widely circulated Denis Waitley lines, attributed to him uniformly across compilations and consistent with his Seeds of Greatness material. No primary source known to me, so the attribution is strong by repetition rather than by citation.

text: Forgiving often seems more difficult in western cultures, simply because we are taught to compete, be better, win, and conquer. We aren't taught the intricacies of deep listening and understanding. Nor are we are taught to see, or readily accept, different perspectives. But truly, listening is the first step on the ladder to creating beautiful personal and business relationships. Too often we make assumptions about what others are thinking, feeling or doing, and this affects our ability to work successfully together. Forgiveness is the solution to these issues, opening the door to abundance and creativity.
text_raw: "Forgiving often seems more difficult in western cultures, simply because we are taught to compete, be better, win, and conquer. We aren't taught the intricacies of deep listening and understanding. Nor are we are taught to see, or readily accept, different perspectives. But truly, listening is the first step on the ladder to creating beautiful personal and business relationships. Too often we make assumptions about what others are thinking, feeling or doing, and this affects our ability to work successfully together. Forgiveness is the solution to these issues, opening the door to abundance and creativity."
author: Denise Trifiletti

provenance.notes: I have no knowledge of Denise Trifiletti or of this passage. The length and register suggest it was excerpted from a contributed essay in a multi-author inspirational anthology rather than being a circulating quotation. I cannot confirm or dispute the attribution — the honest answer here is that I do not know.

text: You can tell how high a society is by how much of its garbage is recycled.
text_raw: You can tell how high a society is by how much of its garbage is recycled.
author: Dhyani Ywahoo

provenance.notes: Attributed to Dhyani Ywahoo, the Cherokee teacher and author of Voices of Our Ancestors (1987), which would be the natural source. I recall the attribution but cannot confirm the passage in that book or any other, so the citation stays open.

text: When busyness is the measure of time, no matter how much time exists it is never enough.
text_raw: When busyness is the measure of time, no matter how much time exists it is never enough.
author: Diana Hunt

provenance.notes: Diana Hunt co-authored The Tao of Time (1990) with Pam Hait, and this line's theme of busyness as the measure of time fits that book, which is presumably why it is credited to her. I cannot verify the passage, and where a book has two authors an unattributed excerpt is doubly uncertain.

text: Nothing is easier than self-deceit. For what each man wishes, that he also believes to be true.
text_raw: Nothing is easier than self-deceit. For what each man wishes, that he also believes to be true.
author: Diane Arbus

provenance.earliest_print_source: Third Olynthiac, Demosthenes, 349 BCE
provenance.notes: This is Demosthenes, not Diane Arbus. The line is a standard English rendering from the Third Olynthiac: 'Nothing is easier than self-deceit. For what each man wishes, that he also believes to be true.' It has nothing to do with photography and predates Arbus by well over two millennia. Confidence here reflects my certainty in the Demosthenes attribution. Note that this is one of three quotes in this batch wrongly filed under Arbus (see also q_0520 and q_0522), which suggests a block-assignment error in the upstream source list rather than three independent slips. | Suggested reattribution: Demosthenes

text: The world can only be grasped by action, not by contemplation. The hand is the cutting edge of the mind.
text_raw: The world can only be grasped by action, not by contemplation. The hand is the cutting edge of the mind.
author: Diane Arbus

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Ascent of Man, Jacob Bronowski, 1973
provenance.notes: This is Jacob Bronowski from The Ascent of Man (1973), in the discussion of toolmaking and human evolution: 'The hand is the cutting edge of the mind.' Both sentences are his, not Diane Arbus's. Confidence reflects certainty in the Bronowski attribution; I have not verified the page. Second of three Arbus misfilings in this batch. | Suggested reattribution: Jacob Bronowski

text: If you have knowledge, let others light their candles in it.
text_raw: If you have knowledge, let others light their candles in it.
author: Diane Arbus

provenance.earliest_print_source: Gnomologia: Adagies and Proverbs, Thomas Fuller, 1732
provenance.notes: Not Diane Arbus. This is a proverb collected by Thomas Fuller in Gnomologia (1732), whose form is 'If you have knowledge, let others light their candles at it' (note 'at', not 'in'). It is also very commonly misattributed to Margaret Fuller, the 19th-century American writer, apparently through surname confusion. Confidence reflects my certainty that the line is the Fuller proverb rather than anything of Arbus's; between Thomas Fuller as collector and any earlier proverbial origin, Gnomologia is the earliest print appearance I know. Third of three Arbus misfilings in this batch. | Suggested reattribution: Thomas Fuller (Gnomologia, 1732); frequently misattributed to Margaret Fuller

text: We're afraid of feelings. We rush through our lives searching yet not living. For those who have the interest to look closely, life becomes art.
text_raw: We're afraid of feelings. We rush through our lives searching yet not living. For those who have the interest to look closely, life becomes art.
author: Diane Mariechild

provenance.notes: Diane Mariechild is a real author — Mother Wit (1981) and The Inner Dance — and this is credited to her in quote compilations, but I cannot locate it in her work or identify any earlier appearance. No traceable source; 'I don't know' is the honest verdict.

text: Realize that now, in this moment of time, you are creating. You are creating your next moment based on what you are feeling and thinking. That is what's real. We can let go of the unconscious belief that being anxious about the past or the future will somehow protect us and instead reprogram our cells with new ways of responding.
text_raw: "Realize that now, in this moment of time, you are creating. You are creating your next moment based on what you are feeling and thinking. That is what's real. We can let go of the unconscious belief that being anxious about the past or the future will somehow protect us and instead reprogram our cells with new ways of responding."
author: Doc Childre

provenance.notes: Consistently circulated as Doc Childre, founder of HeartMath, and the vocabulary (creating the next moment from what you feel and think, 'reprogram our cells') matches HeartMath's house language. I cannot place it in a specific title from memory — plausibly The HeartMath Solution (1999) or one of the Transforming... series, but I will not name a book I cannot confirm. Attribution to Childre is plausible; the source is unverified.

text: When emotions are managed by the heart, they heighten your awareness of the world around you and add sparkle to life. The result is new intelligence and a new view of life.
text_raw: When emotions are managed by the heart, they heighten your awareness of the world around you and add sparkle to life. The result is new intelligence and a new view of life.
author: Doc Childre & Howard Martin

provenance.notes: The Childre & Martin co-byline points to The HeartMath Solution (HarperSanFrancisco, 1999), effectively their only widely read joint book, and the content (heart-managed emotions producing 'new intelligence') is that book's central thesis. I can recall the thesis but not this sentence verbatim in place, so I am leaving the print source null rather than assigning a page-level citation I cannot support.

text: Generally, appreciation means some blend of thankfulness, admiration, approval, and gratitude. In the financial world, something that ‘appreciates’ grows in value. With the power tool of appreciation, you get the benefit of both perspectives: as you learn to be consistently thankful and approving, your life will grow in value.
text_raw: Generally, appreciation means some blend of thankfulness, admiration, approval, and gratitude. In the financial world, something that ‘appreciates’ grows in value. With the power tool of appreciation, you get the benefit of both perspectives: as you learn to be consistently thankful and approving, your life will grow in value.
author: Doc Childre & Howard Martin

provenance.notes: Same posture as q_0526. 'Appreciation' as a named HeartMath 'power tool' with the financial-appreciation wordplay is characteristic of The HeartMath Solution (1999), which devotes a chapter to appreciation. Consistent with the attributed authors but not verified against the text.

text: You can never get to peace and inner security without first acknowledging all of the good things in your life. If you're forever wanting and longing for more without first appreciating things the way they are, you'll stay in discord.
text_raw: You can never get to peace and inner security without first acknowledging all of the good things in your life. If you're forever wanting and longing for more without first appreciating things the way they are, you'll stay in discord.
author: Doc Childre & Howard Martin

provenance.notes: Circulates as Childre & Martin and reads like the appreciation material in The HeartMath Solution (1999). 'Discord' vs. 'coherence' is HeartMath vocabulary. No specific passage I can confirm; treated as plausible but unverified.

text: To be in harmony with the oneness of things is to be without anxiety about imperfection.
text_raw: To be in harmony with the oneness of things is to be without anxiety about imperfection.
author: Dogen Zenji

provenance.notes: This line does not read like any Dogen translation I know; it reads like Richard B. Clarke's English rendering of the Hsin Hsin Ming (Xinxin Ming, 'Verses on the Faith Mind') ascribed to Sengcan, the Third Chan Patriarch, which contains a closely parallel line about being in harmony with the Way and therefore without anxiety about imperfection. The Dogen ascription appears to be an internet-era drift. I am confident the Dogen attribution is weak; moderately (not fully) confident about the Sengcan source, so treat the reattribution as a lead to check rather than a settled fact. | Suggested reattribution: Sengcan (Seng-ts'an), Hsin Hsin Ming, as rendered by Richard B. Clarke — needs confirmation

text: There is nothing extraordinary about nirvana. The only thing extraordinary is our refusal to accept the true nature of reality. Nothing inherently exists outside of our minds. Neither does the mind exist as a separate entity apart from the world...
text_raw: There is nothing extraordinary about nirvana. The only thing extraordinary is our refusal to accept the true nature of reality. Nothing inherently exists outside of our minds. Neither does the mind exist as a separate entity apart from the world...
author: Dogen Zenji

provenance.notes: I cannot place this in the Shobogenzo or any Dogen text I know, and the diction is wrong for him: 'nothing inherently exists' is Madhyamaka/Yogacara textbook phrasing from modern Buddhist-studies English, not thirteenth-century Soto Zen as it comes into English. The trailing ellipsis suggests it was clipped from a secondary source — possibly a modern teacher's commentary that was later collapsed onto Dogen's name. No credible attribution available.

text: You can go through the motions of Zen, but it is the heart that finally counts.
text_raw: You can go through the motions of Zen, but it is the heart that finally counts.
author: Zen saying

provenance.notes: 'Zen saying' is a non-attribution — it names a genre, not a source. I do not recognize this as a classical Chan/Zen line from any koan collection, the Zenrin Kushu, or a standard anthology; the phrasing is modern English aphorism. Honest answer: origin unknown.

text: The more self-love we have, the less we will experience self-abuse. Self-abuse comes from self-rejection, and self-rejection comes from having an image of what it means to be perfect and never measuring up to that ideal. Our image of perfection is the reason we reject ourselves the way we are, and why we don't accept others the way they are.
text_raw: The more self-love we have, the less we will experience self-abuse. Self-abuse comes from self-rejection, and self-rejection comes from having an image of what it means to be perfect and never measuring up to that ideal. Our image of perfection is the reason we reject ourselves the way we are, and why we don't accept others the way they are.
author: Don Miguel Ruiz

provenance.notes: The vocabulary is unmistakably don Miguel Ruiz — self-abuse, self-rejection, the internalized image of perfection are the load-bearing terms of his Toltec framework — and the attribution circulates consistently. I believe it is from either The Four Agreements (1997) or The Mastery of Love (1999) and cannot resolve which from memory, so the print source stays null. Author attribution strong; source unverified.

text: When you are aware that you are the force that is life, anything is possible. Miracles happen all the time, because those miracles are performed by the heart. The heart is in direct communion with the human soul, and when the heart speaks, even with the resistance of the head, something inside you changes; your heart opens another heart, and true love is possible.
text_raw: "When you are aware that you are the force that is life, anything is possible. Miracles happen all the time, because those miracles are performed by the heart. The heart is in direct communion with the human soul, and when the heart speaks, even with the resistance of the head, something inside you changes; your heart opens another heart, and true love is possible."
author: Don Miguel Ruiz

provenance.notes: Consistent with Ruiz's idiom ('you are the force that is life', heart in communion with soul, head-versus-heart resistance) and consistently attributed to him; the content is closest to The Mastery of Love (1999). I cannot confirm the book or passage, so the citation is left null.

text: One of the great dangers of transformational work is that the ego attempts to sidestep deep psychological work by leaping into the transcendent too soon. This is because the ego always fancies itself much more ‘advanced’ than it actually is.
text_raw: One of the great dangers of transformational work is that the ego attempts to sidestep deep psychological work by leaping into the transcendent too soon. This is because the ego always fancies itself much more ‘advanced’ than it actually is.
author: Don Richard Riso & Russ Hudson

provenance.notes: Riso and Hudson co-wrote only Enneagram books, and this is a signature Riso/Hudson warning about spiritual bypassing and the ego's self-flattery about its own level of development. Most likely The Wisdom of the Enneagram (1999); I cannot confirm the volume or page, so the citation is left null. Author-pair attribution is solid.

text: Learn to pause... or nothing worthwhile will catch up to you.
text_raw: Learn to pause... or nothing worthwhile will catch up to you.
author: Doug King

provenance.notes: Circulates widely on quotation sites credited to 'Doug King' with no identifying detail — no dates, no work, no discipline. I cannot identify the person or any publication. This is the profile of an aphorism whose attribution is an artifact of quote-site copying. Honest answer: unknown.

text: Success is not the key to happiness. Happiness is the key to success. If you love what you are doing, you will be successful.
text_raw: Success is not the key to happiness. Happiness is the key to success. If you love what you are doing, you will be successful.
author: Dr. Albert Schweitzer

provenance.notes: This is a known Schweitzer magnet-quote and I do not believe it is his. It has no counterpart in his theological, medical, or ethical writing, its register is late-twentieth-century American motivational literature, and the Schweitzer ascription appears only in that literature — Wikiquote carries it in the misattributed/unsourced section and Quote Investigator has examined the saying without finding support in Schweitzer. I do not reliably know who originated it (it spread through business and self-help speaking in the 1980s-90s), so I am leaving the reattribution null rather than guessing.

text: There are two primary choices in life: to accept conditions as they exist, or accept the responsibility for changing them.
text_raw: There are two primary choices in life: to accept conditions as they exist, or accept the responsibility for changing them.
author: Dr. Denis Waitley

provenance.notes: Attributed to Denis Waitley with reasonable consistency and it fits his material in The Psychology of Winning (1979) and Seeds of Greatness (1983). I cannot pin the book, and this genre of two-choices aphorism circulates loosely enough that I would not rule out an earlier source. Plausible but unverified.

text: Failure should be our teacher, not our undertaker. Failure is delay, not defeat. It is a temporary detour, not a dead end. Failure is something we can avoid only by saying nothing, doing nothing, and being nothing.
text_raw: Failure should be our teacher, not our undertaker. Failure is delay, not defeat. It is a temporary detour, not a dead end. Failure is something we can avoid only by saying nothing, doing nothing, and being nothing.
author: Dr. Denis Waitley

provenance.notes: I know this paragraph as William Arthur Ward, whose widely reprinted aphorisms include 'Failure should be our teacher, not our undertaker' and 'Failure is delay, not defeat. It is a temporary detour, not a dead end.' The Waitley ascription likely arises because Waitley used a similar detour/dead-end line in his own speaking, letting the two authors' material blend on quote sites. Confident the Ward version predates and matches more exactly; not certain enough to name a specific Ward collection, so no citation given. | Suggested reattribution: William Arthur Ward

text: Success is not something that can be measured or worn on a watch of hung on the wall. It is not the esteem of colleagues, or the admiration of the community, or the appreciation of patients. Success is the certain knowledge that you have become yourself, the person you were meant to be from all time. That should be reward enough.
text_raw: Success is not something that can be measured or worn on a watch of hung on the wall. It is not the esteem of colleagues, or the admiration of the community, or the appreciation of patients. Success is the certain knowledge that you have become yourself, the person you were meant to be from all time. That should be reward enough.
author: Dr. George Sheehan

provenance.notes: The closing sentence — success as 'the certain knowledge that you have become yourself, the person you were meant to be from all time' — is a signature George Sheehan line, and the doctor's-eye details (esteem of colleagues, appreciation of patients) fit him as a cardiologist-writer. Most likely from Running & Being (1978) or Personal Best (1989); I cannot confirm which, so the source is null. Also note a transcription error in the stored text: 'worn on a watch of hung on the wall' should read 'or hung on the wall'.

text: Simplicity (kanso) means the achievement of maximum effect with minimum means.
text_raw: Simplicity (kanso) means the achievement of maximum effect with minimum means.
author: Dr. Koichi Kawana

provenance.notes: Koichi Kawana (1930-1990), the Japanese-American architect and designer of several major American Japanese gardens, is credited with this definition in Japanese-garden and design literature, and the attribution is consistent. Caution on one detail: the parenthetical '(kanso)' looks like a later editorial gloss added by design writers popularizing the seven principles of Zen aesthetics — Garr Reynolds' Presentation Zen material is the likely vector — rather than Kawana's own wording. I cannot name the original publication or lecture, so no citation is given.

text: Never be limited by other people's limited imaginations
text_raw: Never be limited by other people's limited imaginations
author: Dr. Mae Jemison

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Mae Jemison, the first African American woman in space, and consistent with her recorded speaking on STEM and imagination. The fuller form usually circulates as 'Never be limited by other people's limited imaginations... Never limit others because of your own limited imagination.' I cannot place a specific speech, interview, or print appearance from memory, so this rests on consistency of attribution rather than a located source.

text: If you expect the best, you will be the best. Learn to use one of the most powerful laws in this world; change your mental habits to belief instead of disbelief. Learn to expect, not to doubt. In so doing, you bring everything into the realm of possibility.
text_raw: If you expect the best, you will be the best. Learn to use one of the most powerful laws in this world; change your mental habits to belief instead of disbelief. Learn to expect, not to doubt. In so doing, you bring everything into the realm of possibility.
author: Dr. Norman Vincent Peale

provenance.notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Norman Vincent Peale, and squarely in the idiom of his positive-thinking writing (most often pointed at The Power of Positive Thinking, 1952, or a later title such as You Can If You Think You Can). I cannot confirm which book or page, so no print source is asserted.

text: At the heart of personality is the need to feel a sense of being lovable without having to qualify for that acceptance.
text_raw: At the heart of personality is the need to feel a sense of being lovable without having to qualify for that acceptance.
author: Dr. Paul Tournier

provenance.notes: Attributed to the Swiss physician-writer Paul Tournier and thematically consistent with his work on acceptance and grace (The Meaning of Persons, Guilt and Grace). It circulates almost entirely through quotation collections and counseling literature without a book or page cited. I cannot locate it in any Tournier title from memory.

text: Every achiever that I have ever met says, ‘My life turned around when I began to believe in me.’
text_raw: Every achiever that I have ever met says, ‘My life turned around when I began to believe in me.’
author: Dr. Robert H. Schuller

provenance.notes: Attributed to Robert H. Schuller and consistent with his possibility-thinking material and Hour of Power broadcasts, where much of his most-quoted phrasing originated as spoken rather than printed. No specific book, sermon, or date is known to me.

text: Be who you are and say what you feel, because those who mind don't matter and those who matter don't mind.
text_raw: Be who you are and say what you feel, because those who mind don't matter and those who matter don't mind.
author: Dr. Seuss

provenance.notes: Not found in any Dr. Seuss book; this is one of the best-documented Seuss misattributions and Wikiquote carries it in the misattributed section. The core aphorism — 'those who mind don't matter, and those who matter don't mind' — predates Geisel's popular fame and is traced by quotation researchers to Bernard Baruch in the late 1930s (also circulated earlier in similar wording about seating guests at dinner). The composite sentence beginning 'Be who you are and say what you feel' appears to be a modern welding of that aphorism onto a Seuss-flavored opening; the author of the composite is unknown. | Suggested reattribution: Bernard M.
