My recollection points to either the Amherst College address honoring Robert Frost (26 October 1963) or his remarks for the National Cultural Center (1962); both are real speeches with closely related language, and I cannot tell which contains this sentence. Attribution to JFK is solid; the specific occasion is not, so no source is printed.

text: The measure of success is not whether you have a tough problem to deal with, but whether it's the same problem you had last year.
text_raw: The measure of success is not whether you have a tough problem to deal with, but whether it's the same problem you had last year.
author: John Foster Dulles

provenance.notes: Attributed to Dulles with fair consistency in management and leadership literature, but I cannot tie it to any speech, dispatch, or writing of his. The formulation reads more like postwar business-book aphorism than diplomatic prose, which raises the possibility that a management author coined or reshaped it and the Dulles name attached later. No evidence of a specific alternate author, so no reattribution suggested.

text: When we experience the pain of another person, we instinctively want to take away that pain. But by taking away the other person’s pain, we also take away his or her opportunity to grow. To be truly compassionate, we must be able to share another person’s suffering and pain - knowing there is nothing we can do to relieve it and that we are not responsible for it, and yet knowing and understanding what that pain feels like.
text_raw: When we experience the pain of another person, we instinctively want to take away that pain. But by taking away the other person’s pain, we also take away his or her opportunity to grow. To be truly compassionate, we must be able to share another person’s suffering and pain - knowing there is nothing we can do to relieve it and that we are not responsible for it, and yet knowing and understanding what that pain feels like.
author: John Gray

provenance.notes: Cannot place this passage. 'John Gray' is ambiguous: the self-help author of Men Are from Mars, Women Are from Venus and What You Feel, You Can Heal; the political philosopher (Straw Dogs); and others. The therapeutic register suggests the self-help John Gray, but the specific argument (that removing another's pain removes their growth) is a commonplace of pastoral-care and codependency writing and could belong to several authors. Unverified on both source and which John Gray.

text: Don't be discouraged by a failure. It can be a positive experience. Failure is, in a sense, the highway to success, inasmuch as every discovery of what is false leads us to seek earnestly after what is true, and every fresh experience points out some form of error which we shall afterwards carefully avoid.
text_raw: "Don't be discouraged by a failure. It can be a positive experience. Failure is, in a sense, the highway to success, inasmuch as every discovery of what is false leads us to seek earnestly after what is true, and every fresh experience points out some form of error which we shall afterwards carefully avoid."
author: John Keats

provenance.notes: Two problems. (1) The core sentence, 'Failure is, in a sense, the highway to success...', appears in nineteenth-century quotation dictionaries credited to Keats, but I cannot locate it in his letters or poems, and the reasoning about 'discovery of what is false' is uncharacteristically didactic-empiricist for Keats. (2) The opening two sentences ('Don't be discouraged by a failure. It can be a positive experience.') read as a modern motivational preamble grafted onto the older sentence - flat, contemporary diction unlike the rest. Recommend not promoting; at minimum strip the prepended sentences.

text: When written in Chinese the word 'crisis' is composed of two characters. One represents danger, and the other represents opportunity.
text_raw: When written in Chinese the word 'crisis' is composed of two characters. One represents danger, and the other represents opportunity.
author: John Kennedy

provenance.notes: The attribution is broadly sound - Kennedy did use this line in campaign-era speeches (I associate it with his 1959-60 addresses, including a United Negro College Fund speech in Indianapolis, April 1959) - but two things should block promotion. (1) FACTUALLY FALSE: the etymology is wrong. Sinologist Victor Mair has repeatedly debunked it; the second character in weiji is ji, meaning incipient moment or crux, not 'opportunity'. (2) NOT ORIGINAL: the trope predates Kennedy in English-language missionary writing on China (Quote Investigator traces it to the late 1930s), so he popularized rather than coined it. Also note the author field reads 'John Kennedy'; should be 'John F. Kennedy'. Recommend rejection on accuracy grounds even though the speaker is real.

text: Truth is unique to each moment. You cannot step in the same stream twice. So wipe the slate clean. Wake up in this moment and truly be here. Let go of what you think happened. It is gone. It no longer exists. Tell your stories, but don't get stuck in them. This moment is like no other.
text_raw: Truth is unique to each moment. You cannot step in the same stream twice. So wipe the slate clean. Wake up in this moment and truly be here. Let go of what you think happened. It is gone. It no longer exists. Tell your stories, but don't get stuck in them. This moment is like no other.
author: John MacEnulty

provenance.notes: I have no reliable knowledge of John MacEnulty as a published author and cannot locate this passage in anything I know. The content is a restatement of the Heraclitean river commonplace ('You cannot step in the same stream twice') wrapped in contemporary mindfulness language, which makes independent verification harder rather than easier. No source, no date, no corroborating attribution. Honest answer is that I do not know.

text: Design is a solution to a problem. Art is a question to a problem.
text_raw: Design is a solution to a problem. Art is a question to a problem.
author: John Maeda

provenance.notes: Genuine Maeda - the design/art distinction is one of his recurring formulations, expressed in his talks, interviews, and writing (including his TED remarks on art, technology and design). Contemporary and well documented as his, but I cannot pin the first appearance to a specific book, post, or talk transcript, so no citation is printed. Attribution itself is not in question.

text: Keep close to Nature's heart, yourself; and break clear away, once in a while, and climb a mountain or spend a week in the woods. Wash your spirit clean.
text_raw: Keep close to Nature's heart, yourself; and break clear away, once in a while, and climb a mountain or spend a week in the woods. Wash your spirit clean.
author: John Muir

provenance.notes: Genuine Muir, from his correspondence rather than a published book; it is reproduced in the standard Muir biographical literature (Bade's The Life and Letters of John Muir, 1924, and Wolfe's John of the Mountains, 1938). I am confident it is his but cannot confirm which volume carries it or the letter's recipient and date, so no citation is printed. Attribution strong, locus unconfirmed.

text: If one pulls on a single thread in nature, you'll find it attached to everything else.
text_raw: If one pulls on a single thread in nature, you'll find it attached to everything else.
author: John Muir

provenance.notes: The thought is Muir's but this is not his wording. It is a loose modern paraphrase of the authentic sentence in My First Summer in the Sierra (1911): 'When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the universe' - which the corpus already holds correctly as q_0822. The 'pull a single thread' rewording has no basis in Muir's text and also breaks grammatical agreement ('If one pulls... you'll find'). Recommend dropping this in favor of q_0822 rather than promoting a corrupted variant.

text: The power of imagination makes us infinite.
text_raw: The power of imagination makes us infinite.
author: John Muir

provenance.earliest_print_source: John of the Mountains: The Unpublished Journals of John Muir, ed. Linnie Marsh Wolfe, 1938
provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Muir in the Sierra Club's John Muir quotation collection, which cites his unpublished journals as gathered in John of the Mountains (1938). I recall that pairing but cannot confirm the page or the journal date from memory, so this rests on strong secondary evidence rather than a primary check. No rival claimant known.

text: A forest is a cathedral where the priest is nature.
text_raw: A forest is a cathedral where the priest is nature.
author: Anon.

provenance.notes: Credited to 'Anon.', and I can place no source at all. The line reads as a modern aphorism working a very old trope — the forest-as-cathedral figure runs from Bryant's 'The groves were God's first temples' (1825) through Muir and countless nature writers — but this specific sentence has no traceable origin I know of. Honest answer: unknown, probably an internet-era composition.

text: Not what we have but what we enjoy, constitutes our abundance.
text_raw: Not what we have but what we enjoy, constitutes our abundance.
author: John Petit-Senn

provenance.notes: Attributed with unusual consistency to Jean-Antoine (John) Petit-Senn (1792-1870), the Swiss-French aphorist whose 'Bluettes et Boutades' was Englished in the 19th century and mined heavily by Victorian quotation dictionaries. The style matches his epigrams and no competing author is ever named. I cannot place the specific collection or year from memory, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing at a title.

text: Patience and perseverance have a magical effect before which difficulties disappear and obstacles vanish.
text_raw: Patience and perseverance have a magical effect before which difficulties disappear and obstacles vanish.
author: John Quincy Adams

provenance.notes: Ubiquitously attributed to John Quincy Adams in quotation compilations, and the sentiment and register are period-plausible, but I cannot locate it in his diaries, letters, or public papers from memory. Wide repetition in secondary collections is not evidence of origin. No contrary attribution known either, so this is honest uncertainty rather than suspicion of a specific misattribution.

text: If your actions inspire others to dream more, learn more, do more and become more, you are a leader.
text_raw: If your actions inspire others to dream more, learn more, do more and become more, you are a leader.
author: John Quincy Adams

provenance.notes: A known misattribution magnet. This is modern leadership-seminar prose — 'dream more, learn more, do more, become more' — and its diction is late-20th-century American management writing, not early-19th-century political English. Quote Investigator examined it and found no support in John Quincy Adams's writings, with the earliest sightings in the 1990s motivational literature. I do not know who actually wrote it, so I am not proposing a replacement author.

text: Patience and perseverance have a magical effect before which difficulties disappear and obstacles vanish.
text_raw: Patience and perseverance have a magical effect before which difficulties disappear and obstacles vanish.
author: John Quincy Adams

provenance.notes: Exact duplicate of q_0829 (same text, same author, different category tag) — flagging for dedupe. Same verdict: consistently attributed to John Quincy Adams across quotation compilations, but I cannot locate it in his diaries, letters, or public papers from training knowledge, and repetition in secondary collections is not provenance.

text: The time will come when you will satisfy a need for money by steadfastly depending on the Master Self within - and not on anything in the world of form. Until you do this, you will continue to experience the uncertainties of supply for the rest of your life. Every soul must learn this lesson, and until it does, it will be given opportunity after opportunity in the form of apparent lack and limitation. You may be experiencing such a challenge right at this moment. Realize that this is the opportunity you have been waiting for to demonstrate the truth of your birthright.
text_raw: The time will come when you will satisfy a need for money by steadfastly depending on the Master Self within - and not on anything in the world of form. Until you do this, you will continue to experience the uncertainties of supply for the rest of your life. Every soul must learn this lesson, and until it does, it will be given opportunity after opportunity in the form of apparent lack and limitation. You may be experiencing such a challenge right at this moment. Realize that this is the opportunity you have been waiting for to demonstrate the truth of your birthright.
author: John Randolph Price

provenance.notes: The vocabulary is distinctively John Randolph Price's — 'the Master Self within', 'the world of form', 'your birthright', 'demonstrate the truth' — all core New Thought terms he used throughout The Superbeings (1981) and The Abundance Book (1987), and the subject (money as a spiritual demonstration) is squarely his. Attribution is plausible on internal evidence, but I cannot say which book or page this passage comes from, so I will not name one.

text: The future is not some place we are going, but one we are creating. The paths are not to be found, but made. And the activity of making them changes both the maker and their destination.
text_raw: The future is not some place we are going, but one we are creating. The paths are not to be found, but made. And the activity of making them changes both the maker and their destination.
author: John Schaar

provenance.earliest_print_source: Legitimacy in the Modern State, John H. Schaar, 1981
provenance.notes: Genuinely Schaar, the political theorist at UC Santa Cruz, and usually cited to Legitimacy in the Modern State (1981). The canonical wording is longer and slightly different: 'The future is not a result of choices among alternative paths offered by the present, but a place that is created — created first in the mind and will, created next in activity. The future is not some place we are going to, but one we are creating. The paths are not to be found, but made, and the activity of making them changes both the maker and the destination.' The corpus text is an accurate condensation, but 'their destination' is a drift from 'the destination'.

text: Do all the good you can, in all the ways you can, to all the souls you can, in every place you can, at all the times you can, with all the zeal you can, as long as you can.
text_raw: Do all the good you can, in all the ways you can, to all the souls you can, in every place you can, at all the times you can, with all the zeal you can, as long as you can.
author: John Wesley

provenance.notes: Known as 'Wesley's Rule' and printed on a great deal of Methodist material, but Wesley scholars — including the editors of the Wesley Works project and the denomination's own historians — have searched his sermons, journals, and letters and cannot find it. The consensus is that it does not appear anywhere in his authenticated writings; sightings begin well after his death. The attribution is traditional rather than evidenced. I do not know who composed it, so no reattribution.

text: Things turn out the best for the people who make the best of the way things turn out.
text_raw: Things turn out the best for the people who make the best of the way things turn out.
author: John Wooden

provenance.notes: Wooden used this line constantly in his talks and books and it is one of his signature maxims, so the attribution is not wrong in spirit. But Wooden was a habitual quoter — he credited many of his sayings to his father Joshua and to older sources — and near-identical folk formulations of 'make the best of the way things turn out' circulated in American newspapers before his coaching fame. Safest reading: Wooden is the popularizer, possibly not the originator. Cannot place a first printing.

text: The history of literature is not the history of authors and their careers, but the history of 'Spirit as the producer and consumer of literature.'
text_raw: "The history of literature is not the history of authors and their careers, but the history of 'Spirit as the producer and consumer of literature.' "
author: Jorge Luis Borges

provenance.earliest_print_source: "The Flower of Coleridge" ("La flor de Coleridge"), in Other Inquisitions, Jorge Luis Borges, 1952
provenance.notes: Borges did not say this — he quoted it. 'The Flower of Coleridge' opens by citing Paul Valery: around 1938 Valery wrote that the history of literature should not be the history of the authors and the accidents of their careers or of their works, but rather the history of the Spirit as producer or consumer of literature. The internal quotation marks in the corpus text are the tell that something is being relayed. Credit belongs to Valery, with Borges as the conduit. | Suggested reattribution: Paul Valery (quoted by Jorge Luis Borges in "The Flower of Coleridge", Other Inquisitions, 1952)

text: The history of the universe is an infinite sacred book that all men write and read and try to understand, and in which they are also written.
text_raw: The history of the universe is an infinite sacred book that all men write and read and try to understand, and in which they are also written.
author: Jorge Luis Borges

provenance.notes: Reads as Borges's own prose from Other Inquisitions (1952), most likely 'On the Cult of Books', where he traces the idea of the world-as-book through Mallarme and Leon Bloy and summarizes Bloy's conception in almost exactly these terms. Caution: as with q_0839, Borges's essays are dense with relayed voices, and this sentence may be his restatement of Bloy rather than a standalone claim of his own. I am confident it is Borges's sentence; less confident which essay, so no print source named.

text: The world is ‘the infinite effect of an infinite cause’ and divinity is near ‘because it is in us even more than we ourselves are in us.’
text_raw: “The world is ‘the infinite effect of an infinite cause’ and divinity is near ‘because it is in us even more than we ourselves are in us.’ ”
author: Jorge Luis Borges & Giordano Bruno

provenance.notes: A composite, and the dual credit line is actually the right call. The two quoted fragments are Giordano Bruno's — from De la causa, principio e uno (1584) and the companion work on the infinite universe — while the connective framing is Borges's, in the essay 'Pascal's Sphere' (Other Inquisitions, 1952), where he narrates Bruno's exhilaration at the infinite before turning to Pascal's dread. So the words are Bruno via Borges's translation and paraphrase. Confident about the shape of this; not confident enough about which Bruno treatise supplies which fragment to print a citation.

text: The goal of life is to make your heartbeat match the beat of the universe, to match your nature with Nature.
text_raw: The goal of life is to make your heartbeat match the beat of the universe, to match your nature with Nature.
author: Joseph Campbell

provenance.notes: Campbell's idiom and one of his recurring themes — aligning individual nature with Nature, the heartbeat/cosmic-rhythm figure he used in both lectures and interviews. Most often cited to A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living (ed. Diane K. Osbon, 1991), which is itself a compilation of remarks from workshops rather than a primary text. Plausibly authentic, but I cannot confirm the source, so no citation.

text: If the path before you is clear, you're probably on someone else's.
text_raw: If the path before you is clear, you're probably on someone else's.
author: Joseph Campbell

provenance.notes: This is a compressed, aphorized version of the longer remark recorded at q_0849 ('If you see your path laid out in front of you...'). Campbell said something in this vein, but I know of no text where he said it this tersely — the one-liner looks like an internet-era tightening of the Osbon-compiled passage. Sentiment authentic, wording probably not his. Recommend preferring the longer form and dropping this as a derivative duplicate.

text: We must be willing to let go of the life we have planned, so as to have the life that is waiting for us.
text_raw: We must be willing to let go of the life we have planned, so as to have the life that is waiting for us.
author: Joseph Campbell

provenance.notes: One of the most heavily misattributed lines in the Campbell corpus. The Joseph Campbell Foundation has publicly addressed it and points to E. M. Forster as the source; Campbell appears to have quoted or adapted it rather than coined it. A variant closer to Campbell's own phrasing ('We must let go of the life we have planned, so as to accept the one that is waiting for us') circulates from A Joseph Campbell Companion. I cannot name the Forster work from memory, so the reattribution below is offered as the documented candidate, not as a verified citation. | Suggested reattribution: E. M. Forster (per the Joseph Campbell Foundation's own correction; specific work unconfirmed)

text: “The big question is whether you are going to be able to say a hearty yes to your adventure.
text_raw: “The big question is whether you are going to be able to say a hearty yes to your adventure.
author: Joseph Campbell

provenance.notes: Authentically Campbell's voice and theme — the refusal or acceptance of the call to adventure — and I associate it with the Moyers conversations in The Power of Myth (1988), though it also circulates from the Osbon Companion. I cannot pin which, so no citation. Data note: the text begins with a stray opening curly quote and has no closing one, an ingestion artifact that should be stripped.

text: If you see your path laid out in front of you -- Step one, Step two, Step three -- you only know one thing... it is not your path. Your path is created in the moment of action. If you can see it laid out in front of you, you can be sure it is someone else's path. That is why you see it so clearly.
text_raw: If you see your path laid out in front of you -- Step one, Step two, Step three -- you only know one thing... it is not your path. Your path is created in the moment of action. If you can see it laid out in front of you, you can be sure it is someone else's path. That is why you see it so clearly.
author: Joseph Campbell

provenance.notes: The longer, primary form of the saying compressed at q_0844, and the one I would keep. Usually cited to A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living (ed. Diane K. Osbon, 1991), a compilation of Campbell's workshop remarks rather than something he wrote for print. Consistent with his idiom and I have no reason to doubt it, but a compiled-from-talks source is weaker provenance than a book he authored, so I am staying below the promotion bar and naming no citation.

text: So yield to what is coming. We're in a free fall into future. We don't know where we're going. Things are changing so fast and always when you're going through a long tunnel anxiety comes along. And all you have to do to transform your hell into a paradise is to turn your fall into a voluntary act. I mean it's a very interesting shift of perspective, and that's all it is. Joyful participation in the sorrows and everything changes.
text_raw: So yield to what is coming. We're in a free fall into future. We don't know where we're going. Things are changing so fast and always when you're going through a long tunnel anxiety comes along. And all you have to do to transform your hell into a paradise is to turn your fall into a voluntary act. I mean it's a very interesting shift of perspective, and that's all it is. Joyful participation in the sorrows and everything changes.
author: Joseph Campbell

provenance.notes: Unmistakably Campbell speaking rather than writing — the asides ('I mean it's a very interesting shift of perspective') mark it as a lecture or interview transcript — and it closes on 'joyful participation in the sorrows', his signature rendering of the Buddhist formula and a phrase he used repeatedly. The 'free fall into future' passage circulates from his late talks and interviews. Authentic in voice and vocabulary; I cannot identify the specific recording or transcript, so no source named.

text: The privilege of a lifetime is being who you are.
text_raw: The privilege of a lifetime is being who you are.
author: Joseph Campbell

provenance.notes: Consistently and near-universally attributed to Campbell, who used the line in late interviews and lectures; it is commonly cited from A Joseph Campbell Companion: Reflections on the Art of Living (ed. Diane K. Osbon, 1991), but I cannot confirm that locus from memory, so I leave the print source null. A common variant reads 'the privilege of a lifetime is being who you are' vs. 'is to be who you are' -- the shorter form here is the one Campbell is usually quoted as saying. Note: identical text to q_0854 in this batch (duplicate record).

text: You become mature when you become the authority for your own life.
text_raw: You become mature when you become the authority for your own life.
author: Joseph Campbell

provenance.notes: Attribution to Campbell is consistent across quote collections and matches his recurring theme that the mythic 'call' includes assuming authority over one's own life; the sentiment appears in his Pathways to Bliss lectures. I cannot place this exact sentence in a specific published text, so I hold it below the promotion bar rather than assign a source I cannot confirm.

text: The privilege of a lifetime is being who you are.
text_raw: The privilege of a lifetime is being who you are.
author: Joseph Campbell

provenance.notes: Exact duplicate of q_0851's batch-mate q_0852 -- same text, same author, differing only in the empty category field. Same verdict: widely and consistently attributed to Campbell, commonly cited from A Joseph Campbell Companion (1991), but I cannot confirm that locus from training knowledge. Recommend deduplicating against q_0852 downstream.

text: Spiritual growth is not made in reaction against, for all striving against imposed restrictions is imaginary. Spiritual growth is accomplished by inclination toward. We grow like the sunflower, following the light.
text_raw: "Spiritual growth is not made in reaction against, for all striving against imposed restrictions is imaginary. Spiritual growth is accomplished by inclination toward. We grow like the sunflower, following the light."
author: Joy Houghton

provenance.notes: I have no knowledge of a writer named Joy Houghton and cannot place this passage in any published work. It circulates in inspirational-quote compilations with no traceable origin. I cannot confirm the attribution, cannot refute it, and will not guess at an alternative author. Honest answer: unknown.

text: Strength is the capacity to break a chocolate bar into four pieces with your bare hands - and then just eat one of the pieces.
text_raw: Strength is the capacity to break a chocolate bar into four pieces with your bare hands - and then just eat one of the pieces.
author: Judith Viorst

provenance.notes: Very widely attributed to Judith Viorst, and the voice fits her humorous essays and light verse (Love and Guilt and the Meaning of Life, Etc.; her Redbook columns). Attribution is consistent across sources, which is mild evidence, but I cannot place it in a specific book, column, or year, so I cannot raise this above unverified.

text: Life's circumstances sometimes seem overwhelming, but we must remember the amazing power of love. Just as the ripples in the ocean shape and form the land - from the cliffs to the tiny grains of sand - so do our actions, words, and thoughts shape and form our reality. Even more, ripples joining one another form tidal waves that change the planet. If we make sure that our every thought, word, and action are based in love then the ripples we create will bring about positive change for a positive future.
text_raw: Life's circumstances sometimes seem overwhelming, but we must remember the amazing power of love. Just as the ripples in the ocean shape and form the land - from the cliffs to the tiny grains of sand - so do our actions, words, and thoughts shape and form our reality. Even more, ripples joining one another form tidal waves that change the planet. If we make sure that our every thought, word, and action are based in love then the ripples we create will bring about positive change for a positive future.
author: Julia Butterfly

provenance.notes: 'Julia Butterfly' is Julia Butterfly Hill, the activist who lived two years in the redwood 'Luna.' The ripple-and-love theme is consistent with her public speaking and with The Legacy of Luna (2000), but I cannot place this specific passage in that book or in a documented speech. The author name should likely be normalized to 'Julia Butterfly Hill.'

text: Suppose you scrub your ethical skin until it shines, but there is no music. Then what?
text_raw: Suppose you scrub your ethical skin until it shines, but there is no music. Then what?
author: Kabir

provenance.notes: This reads as Robert Bly's English version of Kabir rather than a literal translation -- the diction ('scrub your ethical skin until it shines', 'but there is no music') is Bly's, from his Kabir renderings (The Kabir Book, 1977), which were themselves reworkings of Tagore's translations. So the sentiment is Kabir's tradition but the wording is Bly's. I recall the line in that Bly collection but not with enough certainty to cite it as a verified source. Consider crediting 'Kabir, versions by Robert Bly.'

text: We choose our joys and sorrows long before we experience them.
text_raw: We choose our joys and sorrows long before we experience them.
author: Kahlil Gibran

provenance.notes: The aphoristic single-sentence form is characteristic of Sand and Foam (1926), and I recall this line among Gibran's aphorisms there. Attribution to Gibran is consistent everywhere it appears. I stop short of naming the book as a verified source because I cannot confirm the locus, but I consider the authorship itself well supported.

text: Generosity is giving more than you can, and pride is taking less than you need.
text_raw: Generosity is giving more than you can, and pride is taking less than you need.
author: Kahlil Gibran

provenance.notes: A well-known Gibran aphorism, in the paradoxical two-clause form typical of Sand and Foam (1926), where I believe it appears. Attribution to Gibran is consistent and I have no evidence pointing elsewhere; I withhold the print citation because I cannot confirm the volume.

text: To love is to receive a glimpse of heaven.
text_raw: To love is to receive a glimpse of heaven.
author: Karen Sunde

provenance.notes: Karen Sunde is a real American playwright, and this line circulates in quotation dictionaries under her name, but I cannot connect it to any of her plays, essays, or interviews. Short aphorisms of this kind in quote compilations frequently carry unsourced attributions. Attribution is plausible but effectively untraceable from what I know.

text: An avoidance of true communication is tantamount to a relinquishment of my self-being; if I withdraw from it I am betraying not only the other but myself.
text_raw: An avoidance of true communication is tantamount to a relinquishment of my self-being; if I withdraw from it I am betraying not only the other but myself.
author: Karl Jaspers

provenance.notes: Authentically Jaspersian in both content and translation register -- 'self-being' is the standard English rendering of Selbstsein in E. B. Ashton's translation of Jaspers, and the claim that refusing communication betrays both other and self is central to Jaspers's account of existential communication in Philosophie (1932), vol. 2 (Existenzerhellung). I believe that is the source but cannot confirm the volume or page, so I leave the citation field null rather than assert it.

text: Only to the extent that we expose ourselves over and over again to annihilation can that which is indestructible arise within us.
text_raw: Only to the extent that we expose ourselves over and over again to annihilation can that which is indestructible arise within us.
author: Karlfried Gras Von Durkheim

provenance.notes: This is the best-known line associated with the German Zen teacher and psychotherapist Karlfried Graf Durckheim (Graf Karlfried von Durckheim-Montmartin), and it matches his central theme of transformation through the 'exercise' of dying to the ego; it is usually cited from The Way of Transformation, though I cannot confirm that locus. The author field is garbled: 'Karlfried Gras Von Durkheim' should read 'Karlfried Graf Durckheim' ('Graf' is the German title Count, not a given name). Flagged as a name correction, not a change of author. | Suggested reattribution: Karlfried Graf Durckheim

text: If you obey all the rules, you miss all the fun.
text_raw: If you obey all the rules, you miss all the fun.
author: Katharine Hepburn

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Katharine Hepburn and entirely in character for her public persona, but I cannot trace it to her memoir Me: Stories of My Life (1991), to a documented interview, or to any dated source. Short, quotable lines attached to famous personalities are a standard misattribution pattern, so I keep this below the promotion bar despite the consistency of the attribution.

text: Peace is not won by those who fiercely guard their differences, but by those who with open minds and hearts seek out connections.
text_raw: "Peace is not won by those who fiercely guard their differences, but by those who with open minds and hearts seek out connections."
author: Katherine Paterson

provenance.notes: Katherine Paterson is a real and much-quoted author (Bridge to Terabithia; two-time Newbery winner) who wrote and spoke often on peace, difference, and empathy, so the attribution is plausible and probably comes from a speech, acceptance address, or essay collection such as Gates of Excellence or A Sense of Wonder. I cannot identify the specific occasion or text.

text: When you can't have what you want, it's time to start wanting what you have.
text_raw: When you can't have what you want, it's time to start wanting what you have.
author: Kathleen A. Sutton

provenance.notes: I have no knowledge of Kathleen A. Sutton and cannot place her or this sentence. The sentiment is a commonplace that appears in many forms across proverb collections and self-help writing, which makes a single named originator unlikely to be verifiable. Honest answer: source unknown.

text: Lack of money is no obstacle. Lack of an idea is an obstacle.
text_raw: Lack of money is no obstacle. Lack of an idea is an obstacle.
author: Ken Hakuta

provenance.notes: Ken Hakuta is the Wacky WallWalker marketer known as 'Dr. Fad,' and the line fits his self-presentation and his 1988 book on inventing fads; it is consistently attributed to him in business-quote collections. I cannot confirm a book, article, or interview as the origin, so the attribution stays unverified.

text: The answer is never the answer. What’s really interesting is the mystery. If you seek the mystery instead of the answer, you’ll always be seeking. I’ve never seen anybody really find the answer – they think they have, so they stop thinking. The need for mystery is greater than the need for the answer.
text_raw: The answer is never the answer. What’s really interesting is the mystery. If you seek the mystery instead of the answer, you’ll always be seeking. I’ve never seen anybody really find the answer – they think they have, so they stop thinking. The need for mystery is greater than the need for the answer.
author: Ken Kesey

provenance.notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Ken Kesey, and the phrasing and stance match his interview voice; it appears to come from a spoken interview rather than his published fiction. I cannot identify the interview, outlet, or year, and spoken-source quotes of this kind often drift in wording, so I hold this at unverified despite the consistency of the attribution.

text: A loving person lives in a loving world. A hostile person lives in a hostile world. Everyone you meet is your mirror.
text_raw: A loving person lives in a loving world. A hostile person lives in a hostile world. Everyone you meet is your mirror.
author: Ken Keyes Jr.

provenance.notes: A signature Ken Keyes Jr. formulation; 'everyone you meet is your mirror' is one of the phrases most closely associated with him and with Handbook to Higher Consciousness (1972), where I believe the passage appears. Attribution to Keyes is consistent and I know of no competing claimant, but I cannot confirm the book or edition, so I leave the print source null.

text: The only thing that wants to get rid of the ego is the ego.
text_raw: The only thing that wants to get rid of the ego is the ego.
author: Ken Wilber

provenance.notes: Consistent with Ken Wilber's recurring argument that ego-fighting is itself an ego project, a point he makes in No Boundary and in the One Taste journals, and the paradoxical compression is his style. I cannot place this exact sentence in a specific book, and similar formulations circulate in Advaita and Zen teaching contexts, so the wording may be a paraphrase of Wilber rather than a direct quotation.

text: With courage you will dare to take risks, have the strength to be compassionate, and the wisdom to be humble. Courage is the foundation of integrity.
text_raw: With courage you will dare to take risks, have the strength to be compassionate, and the wisdom to be humble. Courage is the foundation of integrity.
author: Keshavan Nair

provenance.notes: Attributed consistently to Keshavan Nair, and the content -- courage as the ground of integrity, joined to compassion and humility -- matches the argument of his A Higher Standard of Leadership: Lessons from the Life of Gandhi (1994), which is the likely source. I cannot confirm the passage in that book, so I do not assert the citation.

text: Keep me away from the wisdom which does not cry, the philosophy which does not laugh, and the greatness which does not bow before children.
text_raw: Keep me away from the wisdom which does not cry, the philosophy which does not laugh, and the greatness which does not bow before children.
author: Khalil Gibran

provenance.notes: A widely circulated Gibran line whose triadic structure and tone are genuinely his; it is often traced to his Arabic-period writings in English translation (collections such as A Tear and a Smile / The Broken Wings tradition) rather than to The Prophet. Because the translation source is unsettled and translated aphorisms are prone to drift, I keep this at attributed without a citation. Author spelling should be normalized to 'Kahlil Gibran' for consistency with q_0860 through q_0863 in this batch.

text: It is no measure of health to be well adjusted to a profoundly sick society.
text_raw: It is no measure of health to be well adjusted to a profoundly sick society.
author: Krishnamurti

provenance.notes: Enormously widespread attribution to J. Krishnamurti, and consistent with his recurring theme that conformity to a diseased society is not sanity. However, I cannot place this exact sentence in any of his published books or transcribed talks. The wording has the compressed, aphoristic feel of a later condensation of a longer passage rather than a verbatim line. Some circulating versions cite 'Commentaries on Living' but the passages there differ. Honest verdict: attribution is plausible and near-universal, verbatim sourcing is absent from my knowledge.

text: When you judge, you lose love.
text_raw: When you judge, you lose love.
author: Krishnamurti

provenance.notes: I cannot place this five-word line anywhere in Krishnamurti's corpus. It gestures at a real Krishnamurti theme (judgment/evaluation as an obstacle to seeing, cf. his 'observing without evaluating' formulations), but the phrasing is not one I recognize from his talks or books. Reads like a social-media compression of his ideas. No traceable source.

text: When a man moves away from nature his heart becomes hard.
text_raw: When a man moves away from nature his heart becomes hard.
author: Lakota proverb

provenance.earliest_print_source: Land of the Spotted Eagle, Luther Standing Bear, 1933
provenance.notes: Not an anonymous proverb. This is a lightly reworded line from Luther Standing Bear (Oglala Lakota), whose 'Land of the Spotted Eagle' (1933) contains the passage rendered as 'Man's heart, away from nature, becomes hard.' The 'Lakota proverb' label is the usual folk-anonymization of a named Native author, which strips him of credit. Confidence figure reflects the weak 'Lakota proverb' attribution; my confidence in the Standing Bear reattribution is considerably higher (~0.7), though the corpus wording is a paraphrase rather than his exact sentence. | Suggested reattribution: Luther Standing Bear

text: Love is found in loving.
text_raw: Love is found in loving.
author: Lama Surya Das

provenance.notes: Lama Surya Das is a real American Dzogchen teacher and author ('Awakening the Buddha Within,' 1997), and the sentiment fits his register, but I cannot locate this four-word aphorism in any of his books or talks that I know. It is also generic enough to have many independent authors. No traceable source.

text: Leadership is not so much about technique and methods as it is about opening the heart. Leadership is about inspiration — of oneself and of others. Great leadership is about human experiences, not processes. Leadership is not a formula or a program, it is a human activity that comes from the heart and considers the hearts of others. It is an attitude, not a routine.
text_raw: "Leadership is not so much about technique and methods as it is about opening the heart. Leadership is about inspiration — of oneself and of others. Great leadership is about human experiences, not processes. Leadership is not a formula or a program, it is a human activity that comes from the heart and considers the hearts of others. It is an attitude, not a routine."
author: Lance Secretan

provenance.notes: Lance Secretan is a real leadership author ('Reclaiming Higher Ground,' 1997; 'Inspirational Leadership,' 1999) and this passage matches his documented thesis that leadership is an inspirational and heart-centered human activity rather than a technique or process. The length and paragraph structure suggest it was excerpted from one of his books, which raises my confidence in the attribution above the floor. But I cannot identify which book or confirm the wording, so no citation is recorded.

text: Those who flow as life flows know they need no other force.
text_raw: Those who flow as life flows know they need no other force.
author: Lao Tzu

provenance.notes: Does not correspond to any chapter of the Tao Te Ching in the standard translations I know (Legge, Waley, Feng/English, Mitchell, Lau, Addiss/Lombardo). The English is modern and idiomatic ('flow as life flows'), characteristic of the large body of free-floating pseudo-Lao Tzu circulating online. It may be a loose New Age rendering distantly inspired by the water imagery of ch. 8 or ch. 78, but I cannot connect it to a source text or a named translator.

text: Time is a created thing. To say 'I don't have time,' is like saying, 'I don't want to.'
text_raw: Time is a created thing. To say 'I don't have time,' is like saying, 'I don't want to.'
author: Lao Tzu

provenance.notes: Not in the Tao Te Ching. No chapter treats time as a 'created thing,' and the register — a self-help reframe about scheduling and willingness, complete with quoted colloquial speech ('I don't have time') — is unmistakably modern American. This circulates heavily in productivity writing as Lao Tzu, which is a textbook case of a modern maxim borrowing an ancient name for authority. I do not know who actually wrote it, so I offer no reattribution.

text: The bad leader is he who the people despise. The good leader is he who the people praise. The great leader is he who the people say, we did it ourselves.
text_raw: The bad leader is he who the people despise. The good leader is he who the people praise. The great leader is he who the people say, we did it ourselves.
author: Lao Tzu

provenance.earliest_print_source: Tao Te Ching, ch. 17 (traditionally attributed to Laozi, c. 4th century BCE)
provenance.notes: A modern managerial paraphrase built on genuine material. Tao Te Ching ch. 17 ranks rulers — the best barely known, then loved and praised, then feared, then despised — and closes 功成事遂，百姓皆謂我自然, commonly rendered 'when the work is done, the people say we did it ourselves.' The corpus wording compresses and reorders that into a three-tier leadership maxim; this formulation is popular in leadership literature (John Heider's 'The Tao of Leadership,' 1985, is one well-known vehicle for such renderings) and is not a translation. Holding at 0.70 rather than higher because the source thought is authentic but the sentence is not Lao Tzu's.

text: Give a man a fish and you feed him for the day. Teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime.
text_raw: Give a man a fish and you feed him for the day. Teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime.
author: Lao Tzu

provenance.earliest_print_source: Mrs. Dymond, Anne Isabella Ritchie, 1885
provenance.notes: Not Lao Tzu, and not a Chinese proverb. Nothing resembling it appears in the Tao Te Ching. The earliest known form traced by quotation researchers is in Anne Isabella Ritchie's novel 'Mrs. Dymond' (1885): 'if you give a man a fish he is hungry again in an hour; if you teach him to catch a fish you do him a good turn.' The saying has since been variously credited to Lao Tzu, Maimonides, and Confucius, all without support. Confidence value reflects the Lao Tzu attribution, which I regard as clearly wrong; my confidence in the Ritchie origin is high (~0.8). | Suggested reattribution: Anne Isabella Ritchie (Mrs. Thackeray Ritchie), Mrs. Dymond, 1885

text: Kindness in words creates confidence. Kindness in thinking creates profoundness. Kindness in giving creates love.
text_raw: "Kindness in words creates confidence. Kindness in thinking creates profoundness. Kindness in giving creates love."
author: Lao Tzu

provenance.notes: I cannot match this triad to any chapter of the Tao Te Ching. Its parallel structure faintly echoes ch. 8, which lists virtues by domain ('in dwelling, be close to the land; in dealing with others, be gentle and kind; in speech, be true...'), but that passage does not repeat 'kindness' and does not produce 'confidence,' 'profoundness,' or 'love' as outcomes. 'Profoundness' in particular is not a word that appears in any translation I know. Most likely a modern reworking that drifted far enough from ch. 8 to count as a separate composition. Attribution to Lao Tzu is weak.

text: Seek not happiness too greedily, and be not fearful of unhappiness.
text_raw: Seek not happiness too greedily, and be not fearful of unhappiness.
author: Lao Tzu

provenance.notes: I cannot place this in the Tao Te Ching or in the Zhuangzi. The sentiment is broadly Daoist in flavor (equanimity toward fortune and misfortune, cf. the reversals of ch. 58), but the archaic-sounding English construction 'Seek not... and be not' suggests a paraphraser imitating scriptural diction rather than a translation of a specific line. No traceable source.

text: Loving someone deeply gives you strength, while being deeply loved gives you courage.
text_raw: "Loving someone deeply gives you strength, while being deeply loved gives you courage."
author: Lao Tzu

provenance.notes: Not in the Tao Te Ching. This is one of the most heavily circulated pseudo-Lao Tzu lines on the internet, and the usual form is 'Being deeply loved by someone gives you strength, while loving someone deeply gives you courage' — note that the corpus version has the two clauses swapped, so it is a garbled variant of an already baseless attribution. Even the standard form has no identified author. Recommend removal or reattribution to 'Anonymous' if kept.

text: To see things in the seed, that is genius.
text_raw: To see things in the seed, that is genius.
author: Lao Tzu

provenance.notes: I cannot find this sentence in Tao Te Ching translations. There is a real thematic neighbor in ch. 52, 見小曰明 ('seeing the small is called clarity/insight'), and ch. 64's counsel to deal with things while they are still latent, so a very free paraphrase is conceivable. But 'genius' is a European category alien to the text's vocabulary, which argues for a Western aphorist's composition later hung on Lao Tzu's name. Weak attribution.

text: For peace of mind, we need to resign as general manager of the universe.
text_raw: For peace of mind, we need to resign as general manager of the universe.
author: Larry Eisenberg

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Larry Eisenberg across quotation collections, and the attribution has been stable long enough that it is unlikely to be pure invention. Complicating factor: at least two public figures share the name (the science-fiction writer and short-story author, and a clergyman), and I cannot determine which is meant or identify an originating publication. Attribution plausible, sourcing absent.

text: It's not the load that breaks you down; it's the way you carry it.
text_raw: It's not the load that breaks you down; it's the way you carry it.
author: Lena Horne

provenance.notes: Very widely attributed to Lena Horne, often loosely to an interview in her later career, and the attribution is stable and specific enough to take seriously. However, I cannot confirm a primary source, and proverbial formulations of the same idea (it is not the burden but the manner of carrying it) circulated before her. Plausible that she said it and gave it currency rather than originated it. Below the promotion bar until a primary source is found.

text: Curiosity about life in all its aspects, I think, is still the secret of great creative people.
text_raw: Curiosity about life in all its aspects, I think, is still the secret of great creative people.
author: Leo Burnett

provenance.notes: Consistently and specifically credited to Leo Burnett throughout advertising literature, where his speeches and internal memos are unusually well preserved and were collected posthumously (notably in '100 LEO's: Wit and Wisdom from Leo Burnett,' 1995). The hedged, conversational phrasing — 'I think,' 'is still' — reads like transcribed speech rather than a manufactured aphorism, which supports authenticity. I cannot confirm the specific speech or page, so no citation is recorded and this sits just below the promotion bar.

text: We are no longer puppets being manipulated by outside powerful forces; we become the powerful force ourselves.
text_raw: We are no longer puppets being manipulated by outside powerful forces; we become the powerful force ourselves.
author: Leo Buscaglia

provenance.notes: Matches Leo Buscaglia's documented themes and first-person-plural style, and my sense is that it comes from his writing on self-determination, plausibly 'Personhood' (1978). Attribution is widespread and I have no reason to doubt it, but I cannot identify the book or confirm the wording, and Buscaglia's popularity means his name attracts unsourced uplift. Recording as unverified.

text: Only when we give joyfully, without hesitation or thought of gain, can we truly know what love means.
text_raw: Only when we give joyfully, without hesitation or thought of gain, can we truly know what love means.
author: Leo Buscaglia

provenance.notes: Consistent with Buscaglia's central subject and voice; likely from 'Love' (1972) or 'Living, Loving and Learning' (1982), but I cannot confirm which or verify the wording. Attribution is widespread and plausible rather than evidenced. Same caveat as q_0897: his name is a magnet for unsourced sentiment about love.

text: Music is the shorthand of emotion
text_raw: Music is the shorthand of emotion
author: Leo Tolstoi

provenance.notes: Attributed to Tolstoy almost universally and for a long time, which gives it more weight than a recent internet attribution, but I cannot locate it in his works. It is not a line I can place in 'What Is Art?' (1897), his major statement on the subject, and it may originate in a letter, a diary entry, a recorded conversation, or a secondary account — or in a translator's compression of a longer passage. Also note the author name is spelled 'Leo Tolstoi'; the corpus should probably normalize to the standard 'Leo Tolstoy.' Attribution plausible, sourcing unconfirmed.

text: A human can be healthy without killing animals for food. If you eat meat, you participate in taking animal life merely for the sake of your appetite.
text_raw: A human can be healthy without killing animals for food. If you eat meat, you participate in taking animal life merely for the sake of your appetite.
author: Leo Tolstoy

provenance.notes: Tolstoy was a committed vegetarian from 1885 and argued exactly this in his 1892 essay 'The First Step' (Pervaya stupen), written as a preface to the Russian edition of Howard Williams's 'The Ethics of Diet'. The usual circulating wording is 'A man can live and be healthy without killing animals for food; therefore, if he eats meat, he participates in taking animal life merely for the sake of his appetite' — the corpus text is a gender-neutralized paraphrase of that. I cannot place the sentence at a specific page or confirm it is a direct translation rather than a summary of his argument, so I am not asserting a primary source. Attribution to Tolstoy is consistent across sources and entirely in character; the exact provenance is not.

text: The miracle is this — the more we share, the more we have.
text_raw: The miracle is this — the more we share, the more we have.
author: Leonard Nimoy

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Leonard Nimoy across quote collections and often cited alongside his poetry (he published several volumes, e.g. 'You & I', 1973, and 'Warmed by Love'). The sentiment and the aphoristic style fit his published verse. I cannot place it in a specific book, poem, interview, or speech from my training knowledge, and it may be a line lifted from a longer poem. No competing attribution that I know of, so the author is plausible but unverified.

text: Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication.
text_raw: Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication.
author: Leonardo Da Vinci

provenance.notes: This is a well-known false attribution. The line does not appear anywhere in Leonardo's notebooks or the Trattato della Pittura, and the Italian version circulating online ('La semplicita e l'ultima sofisticazione') is a back-translation from English, which is itself strong evidence of modern origin. Wikiquote lists it under Leonardo's disputed/misattributed section. Its popularity comes largely from twentieth-century advertising use, notably the 1977 Apple II brochure, where it appeared as a tagline. I do not reliably know the true earliest coiner, so I am not naming one rather than guessing.

text: From an early age, I have abjured the use of meat, and the time will come when men will look upon the murder of animals as they look upon the murder of men.
text_raw: From an early age, I have abjured the use of meat, and the time will come when men will look upon the murder of animals as they look upon the murder of men.
author: Leonardo Da Vinci

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci, Dmitry Merezhkovsky, 1900 (Russian; English translation 1902)
provenance.notes: A documented case of fiction laundered into a quotation. The 'time will come when men will look upon the murder of animals as they now look upon the murder of men' line comes from Dmitry Merezhkovsky's historical novel 'The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci' (1900), where it is dialogue invented for the character of Leonardo. It appears in no surviving Leonardo manuscript. Leonardo's actual vegetarianism is separately evidenced — chiefly Andrea Corsali's 1515 letter to Giuliano de' Medici describing him as eating no meat — but that is not this sentence. Wikiquote files it as misattributed. | Suggested reattribution: Dmitry Merezhkovsky (fictional dialogue in 'The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci', 1900)

text: Wanting something is not enough. You must hunger for it. Your motivation must be absolutely compelling in order to overcome the obstacles that will invariably come your way.
text_raw: Wanting something is not enough. You must hunger for it. Your motivation must be absolutely compelling in order to overcome the obstacles that will invariably come your way.
author: Les Brown

provenance.notes: Standard Les Brown motivational material, attributed to him consistently and without competing claimants. Most plausibly from his book 'Live Your Dreams' (1992) or his speaking material, but I cannot confirm a page or a specific talk, so I am leaving the print source null. Living-speaker quotes of this kind are rarely sourced in the aggregators that carry them; the attribution is likely right, the citation is unestablished.

text: Any fool can run towards the light. It takes a master with courage to turn and face the darkness and shine his own light there.
text_raw: Any fool can run towards the light. It takes a master with courage to turn and face the darkness and shine his own light there.
author: Leslie Fieger

provenance.notes: Leslie Fieger is a New Thought / self-development author known for the DELFIN Knowledge System trilogy. Quotes attributed to him circulate almost exclusively through quotation aggregators and mailing-list signatures rather than through cited books. I have no independent knowledge of this line in any of his published texts and cannot confirm or refute it. Low-profile author means low misattribution risk but also no verification path from training knowledge.

text: Utilizing your conscious mind to direct the subconscious mind to enter into communication and harmony with the universal mind is the secret of personal power.
text_raw: "Utilizing your conscious mind to direct the subconscious mind to enter into communication and harmony with the universal mind is the secret of personal power."
author: Leslie Fieger

provenance.notes: Same situation as the other Fieger line. The vocabulary — conscious mind directing subconscious mind into harmony with universal mind — is squarely the New Thought idiom of Fieger's DELFIN material, so the attribution is stylistically plausible. I cannot place it in a specific book or lesson and will not invent one. No competing attribution known.

text: For fast acting relief, try slowing down.
text_raw: For fast acting relief, try slowing down.
author: Lily Tomlin

provenance.notes: A signature Tomlin one-liner, attributed to her with great consistency. Important caveat: the great majority of Lily Tomlin's stage and television material was written by Jane Wagner, her longtime collaborator and later spouse, so 'Lily Tomlin said it' often means 'Jane Wagner wrote it and Lily Tomlin performed it'. I cannot determine which show or special this line came from, so I cannot say whether Wagner authored this specific joke. Attribution to Tomlin as speaker is safe; attribution as author is not.

text: I can handle reality in small doses, but as a lifestyle, it's much too confining.
text_raw: I can handle reality in small doses, but as a lifestyle, it's much too confining.
author: Lily Tomlin

provenance.notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Lily Tomlin, and I believe it belongs to the Trudy the bag lady material from 'The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe' (Broadway, 1985) — the same show that produced 'Reality is nothing but a collective hunch'. If that placement is right, the written author is Jane Wagner, who wrote the entire show; Tomlin performed it. I am not confident enough in the placement to state the show as a source or to file a formal reattribution, but the Wagner authorship question should be flagged before this is promoted.

text: The difference between holding on to a hurt or releasing it with forgiveness is like the difference between laying your head down at night on a pillow filled with thorns or a pillow filled with rose petals.
text_raw: The difference between holding on to a hurt or releasing it with forgiveness is like the difference between laying your head down at night on a pillow filled with thorns or a pillow filled with rose petals.
author: Loren Fincher

provenance.notes: I have no knowledge of Loren Fincher as an author, speaker, or public figure, and no knowledge of this line from any published source. It has the cadence of inspirational-newsletter or greeting-card writing and circulates, as far as I can tell, only through quote aggregators. Cannot confirm the person exists as attributed, cannot identify a real author, and will not guess. This is an honest 'I don't know'.

text: Architecture is the thoughtful making of space.
text_raw: Architecture is the thoughtful making of space.
author: Louis Khan

provenance.notes: Genuine Kahn in substance, but two corrections are needed. First, the author's name is misspelled in the corpus: it is Louis I. Kahn (1901-1974), not 'Louis Khan'. Second, Kahn's formulation is plural — 'Architecture is the thoughtful making of spaces' — and it opens his contribution to Perspecta 4 (Yale architectural journal, 1957), continuing 'It is the creating of spaces that evoke a feeling of appropriate use.' I am confident of the sentence and of Kahn as its author; I am less certain of the exact issue and year, so I have left the print source null rather than risk a wrong citation. Fix the surname regardless of promotion outcome. | Suggested reattribution: Louis I. Kahn (spelling correction, not a change of author)

text: A writer, or for that matter any artist, is continually putting demands on the subconscious and producing results.
text_raw: A writer, or for that matter any artist, is continually putting demands on the subconscious and producing results.
author: Louis L’Amour

provenance.notes: Attributed to Louis L'Amour consistently and with no competing claimant. The most likely home is his memoir 'Education of a Wandering Man' (1989), which contains extended reflection on reading, writing, and how the mind works on problems below awareness — but I cannot confirm the sentence is in that book, so I am not citing it as a source. The observation is characteristic of his prose about the writing craft. Plausible author, unestablished citation.

text: Love yourself first and everything else falls into line. You really have to love yourself to get anything done in this world.
text_raw: Love yourself first and everything else falls into line. You really have to love yourself to get anything done in this world.
author: Lucille Ball

provenance.notes: Attributed to Lucille Ball consistently, apparently originating in a magazine interview in which she described her 'everyday religion'. Note for the corpus editor: this is a truncated duplicate of q_0924, which carries the fuller and more likely original form beginning 'I have an everyday religion that works for me.' One of the two should be dropped, and the fuller version is the better record. Attribution plausible; no primary citation available to me.

text: I'm not funny. What I am is brave.
text_raw: I'm not funny. What I am is brave.
author: Lucille Ball

provenance.notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Lucille Ball, usually in the context of interviewers asking how she developed her physical comedy. The sentiment matches her documented account of learning comedy as craft rather than possessing it as a gift. I cannot place it in a specific interview, and it may derive from her posthumously published autobiography 'Love, Lucy' (1996), but I will not cite that without confirmation. No competing attribution known.

text: Not everything that is faced can be changed, but nothing can be changed until it is faced.
text_raw: Not everything that is faced can be changed, but nothing can be changed until it is faced.
author: Lucille Ball

provenance.earliest_print_source: 'As Much Truth As One Can Bear', James Baldwin, New York Times Book Review, 14 January 1962
provenance.notes: This is James Baldwin, not Lucille Ball, and the misattribution is not close. The line comes from Baldwin's 1962 New York Times Book Review essay 'As Much Truth As One Can Bear', on the responsibilities of American writers; it is one of his most frequently quoted sentences and is well documented in Baldwin scholarship and collections. It has nothing to do with Ball, and the corpus has additionally filed it under 'humor', which compounds the error. Strong recommendation: reattribute to Baldwin or drop. | Suggested reattribution: James Baldwin

text: A man who correctly guesses a woman's age may be smart, but he's not very bright.
text_raw: A man who correctly guesses a woman's age may be smart, but he's not very bright.
author: Lucille Ball

provenance.notes: A vaudeville-era stock gag about guessing a woman's age, of the kind that circulates freely and attaches itself to whichever comedian is being quoted. It is attributed to Lucille Ball in aggregators but I have no evidence she originated it, and jokes of this shape predate her career. Weak attribution; I cannot name a true originator, which is typical for anonymous stage material.

text: I was shy for several years in my early days in Hollywood until I figured out that no one really gave a damn if I was shy or not, and I got over my shyness.
text_raw: I was shy for several years in my early days in Hollywood until I figured out that no one really gave a damn if I was shy or not, and I got over my shyness.
author: Lucille Ball

provenance.notes: Reads as genuine first-person interview material rather than a manufactured aphorism, and the content matches the documented arc of Ball's early years as a contract player in Hollywood before her success. That specificity is mild evidence of authenticity — invented quotes rarely include this kind of ordinary biographical detail. Still, I cannot identify the interview or publication, so the citation is unestablished.

text: You see much more of your children once they leave home.
text_raw: You see much more of your children once they leave home.
author: Lucille Ball

provenance.notes: A free-floating domestic quip attributed to Lucille Ball in quote collections. I have no source for it and no strong reason to think it originated with her; observations of this form are common in mid-century newspaper humor columns and get reassigned to famous names. Weak attribution, no identifiable origin.

text: Luck? I don't know anything about luck. I've never banked on it, and I'm afraid of people who do. Luck to me is something else: Hard work -- and realizing what is opportunity and what isn't.
text_raw: Luck? I don't know anything about luck. I've never banked on it, and I'm afraid of people who do. Luck to me is something else: Hard work -- and realizing what is opportunity and what isn't.
author: Lucille Ball

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Lucille Ball and structured like genuine transcribed interview speech — the self-interrupting 'Luck? I don't know anything about luck' opening, the correction mid-thought, the dash. Manufactured quotations tend to be smoother than this. The sentiment also matches her well-documented insistence that her career came from work rather than fortune. I cannot identify the interview, so no citation.

text: I have an everyday religion that works for me. Love yourself first, and everything else falls into line. You really have to love yourself to get anything done in this world.
text_raw: I have an everyday religion that works for me. Love yourself first, and everything else falls into line. You really have to love yourself to get anything done in this world.
author: Lucille Ball

provenance.notes: The fuller and probably original form of the line duplicated at q_0917; the 'I have an everyday religion that works for me' opening is the part that usually gets trimmed off in circulation, and its presence here suggests this version is closer to the source. Attributed to Ball consistently, apparently from a magazine interview. I cannot identify the publication. Recommend keeping this version and dropping q_0917. Also note it is filed under 'humor' but is not a joke — the category looks wrong.

text: One of the things I learned the hard way was that it doesn't pay to get discouraged. Keeping busy and making optimism a way of life can restore your faith in yourself.
text_raw: One of the things I learned the hard way was that it doesn't pay to get discouraged. Keeping busy and making optimism a way of life can restore your faith in yourself.
author: Lucille Ball

provenance.notes: Attributed to Lucille Ball consistently across collections, with the reflective interview cadence of her later-career remarks about resilience in show business. No competing attribution known to me and nothing suspicious about it, but also no traceable source — I cannot name an interview, article, or book. Plausible but uncited. Like several others in this run it is filed under 'humor' despite being straightforwardly earnest.

text: I would rather regret the things that I have done than the things that I have not.
text_raw: I would rather regret the things that I have done than the things that I have not.
author: Lucille Ball

provenance.notes: Very widely and consistently attributed to Lucille Ball, usually in the form 'I'd rather regret the things I've done than regret the things I haven't done.' I cannot place a primary interview, memoir passage, or dated print appearance from training knowledge. The sentiment also belongs to a large family of older 'regret what you didn't do' maxims (compare the apocryphal Twain 'Twenty years from now' line), which raises the baseline risk that this was retrofitted onto a famous name. Plausible but unverified.

text: The drops of rain make a hole in the stone not by violence, but by oft falling.
text_raw: The drops of rain make a hole in the stone not by violence, but by oft falling.
author: Lucretius

provenance.notes: The IDEA is genuinely Lucretian: De Rerum Natura I.313 has 'stilicidi casus lapidem cavat' — the fall of dripping water hollows the stone. But this specific English wording, with the 'not by violence, but by oft falling' antithesis, is not a standard translation of that line; I recall it as English homiletic phrasing associated with Hugh Latimer's mid-16th-century preaching ('the drop of rain maketh a hole in the stone, not by violence, but by oft falling'). Related but distinct is Ovid's 'gutta cavat lapidem' (Ex Ponto IV.10.5). So the attribution is half-right: Lucretius for the thought, an English preacher's rhetoric for the sentence. Flagging rather than reattributing because my recall of the Latimer wording is good but not certain.

text: When one is frightened of the truth... then it is never the whole truth than one has an inkling of.
text_raw: When one is frightened of the truth... then it is never the whole truth than one has an inkling of.
author: Ludwig Wittgenstein

provenance.notes: I recall a remark of this shape in Wittgenstein's Culture and Value (Vermischte Bemerkungen), the posthumous collection of personal notebook remarks from the 1930s-40s, running roughly 'When you are frightened of the truth (as I am now) then it is never the whole truth that you have an inkling of.' The 'than' in the corpus text is a transcription corruption of 'that', and the ellipsis marks an elided parenthetical. I am reasonably confident the remark is authentic Wittgenstein but cannot name page or dated entry, so I am not citing a print source and am holding confidence below the promotion bar. Worth a human check against Culture and Value.

text: Self-creation is an act of fire.
text_raw: Self-creation is an act of fire.
author: M. C. Richards

provenance.notes: M. C. (Mary Caroline) Richards, potter and poet, wrote Centering in Pottery, Poetry, and the Person (1962), The Crossing Point, and Toward Wholeness; this aphorism is stylistically consistent with her work and with Centering's themes of self-formation through craft. I cannot place the line in a specific book or page from training knowledge, and short epigrammatic fragments like this circulate easily without provenance. Attribution is plausible and I have no evidence against it, but nothing supports it either.

text: Pain is inevitable. Suffering is optional.
text_raw: Pain is inevitable. Suffering is optional.
author: M. Kathleen Casey

provenance.notes: This is a modern English distillation of a Buddhist teaching (the second arrow, Sallatha Sutta), not a translation of any canonical text. The 'M. Kathleen Casey' credit propagates through 20th-century recovery and daily-meditation literature and through quote aggregators, but I cannot identify a book, page, or date for it, and Casey herself is a thinly documented figure easily confused with Karen Casey (Each Day a New Beginning, Hazelden). The line was popularized in the wider culture by Haruki Murakami's What I Talk About When I Talk About Running (2007), where he presents it as an anonymous runners' mantra rather than crediting Casey. Attribution is a convention, not evidence.

text: Only those who attempt the absurd will achieve the impossible.
text_raw: Only those who attempt the absurd will achieve the impossible.
author: M.C. Escher

provenance.notes: Circulates under Escher's name in design and business collections, but I know a closely matching line from Miguel de Unamuno — 'Solo el que ensaya lo absurdo es capaz de conquistar lo imposible' / 'Only he who attempts the absurd is capable of achieving the impossible' — which reads as the likelier origin. I cannot place the sentence in Escher's own writings (his essays and letters are fairly well documented and this is not a phrasing I associate with them). My Unamuno recall is solid on the Spanish wording but I cannot name the specific work, so the reattribution is offered as probable, not established, and the Escher attribution should not be promoted. | Suggested reattribution: Miguel de Unamuno (probable, not established)

text: Everything in life can be nourishing. Everything can bless us, but we've got to be there for the blessing to occur. Being present with quality is a decision we are invited to make each day.
text_raw: Everything in life can be nourishing. Everything can bless us, but we've got to be there for the blessing to occur. Being present with quality is a decision we are invited to make each day.
author: Macrina Wiederkehr

provenance.notes: Macrina Wiederkehr (1939-2020), Benedictine sister and author of A Tree Full of Angels (1988), Seasons of Your Heart, and Behold Your Life. The passage is idiomatically hers — the vocabulary of blessing, presence, and daily decision matches her devotional prose — and I have no reason to doubt the attribution. But I cannot identify which of her books it comes from, and prose excerpts from devotional writers are frequently re-cut and re-punctuated by anthologists. Attribution plausible, source unplaced.

text: We live in a world of theophanies. Holiness comes wrapped in the ordinary. There are burning bushes all around you. Every tree is full of angels. Hidden beauty is waiting in every crumb. Life wants to lead you from crumbs to angels, but this can happen only if you are willing to unwrap the ordinary by staying with it long enough to harvest its treasure.
text_raw: “We live in a world of theophanies. Holiness comes wrapped in the ordinary. There are burning bushes all around you. Every tree is full of angels. Hidden beauty is waiting in every crumb. Life wants to lead you from crumbs to angels, but this can happen only if you are willing to unwrap the ordinary by staying with it long enough to harvest its treasure.”
author: Macrina Wiederkehr

provenance.earliest_print_source: A Tree Full of Angels: Seeing the Holy in the Ordinary, Macrina Wiederkehr, 1988
provenance.notes: Strong internal evidence: the passage contains both halves of the book's own title — 'Every tree is full of angels' and the seeing-the-holy-in-the-ordinary theme — and theophany-in-the-ordinary is the organizing argument of A Tree Full of Angels (Harper & Row, 1988). This is the single most-anthologized Wiederkehr passage and the attribution is consistent wherever it appears. I am confident in the book but cannot give a page, and I am citing from recall rather than from a copy in front of me, so I am stopping short of 'verified'.

text: Love looks upon the world peacefully and accepts. The ego searches for shortcomings and weaknesses. Love watches for any sign of strength. It sees how far each one has come and not how far he has to go. How simple it is to love, and exhausting it is always to find fault, for every time we see a fault we think something needs to be done about it. Love knows that nothing is ever needed but more love.
text_raw: "Love looks upon the world peacefully and accepts. The ego searches for shortcomings and weaknesses. Love watches for any sign of strength. It sees how far each one has come and not how far he has to go. How simple it is to love, and exhausting it is always to find fault, for every time we see a fault we think something needs to be done about it. Love knows that nothing is ever needed but more love."
author: Maharishi

provenance.notes: 'Maharishi' is a title, not an author — presumably Maharishi Mahesh Yogi is intended, but the corpus entry does not say so, and the passage does not read like his teaching or like translated Indian devotional prose. The idiom is modern American therapeutic-spiritual English ('the ego searches for shortcomings', 'nothing is ever needed but more love') and sits much closer to the A Course in Miracles milieu — Jampolsky, Prather, Williamson and their imitators — than to Vedic commentary. I cannot identify the actual author, and I will not guess one. The attribution as it stands is unusable and the text should not be promoted under this name.

text: The best way to find youself is to lose yourself in the service of others.
text_raw: The best way to find youself is to lose yourself in the service of others.
author: Mahatma Gandhi

provenance.notes: One of the more defensible Gandhi attributions: the sentiment is squarely his (seva as self-realization) and the line is generally treated as sourced in his writings rather than as folk attribution. I cannot name the volume of the Collected Works or the Young India issue, so I am not citing a source. Held at 0.6 rather than higher because Gandhi is a misattribution magnet and 'widely cited with consistent wording' is weaker evidence for him than for almost any other author. Note the corpus text has a typo: 'youself' should be 'yourself'.

text: The future depends on what you do today.
text_raw: The future depends on what you do today.
author: Mahatma Gandhi

provenance.notes: The form usually treated as closer to Gandhi is 'The future depends on what we do in the present.' The 'what you do today' version in the corpus is a later, punchier simplification of that, of the kind motivational-poster culture produces. I cannot place either form in a primary Gandhi text.
