Given how heavily Gandhi's name attracts unsourced aphorisms, and given that this specific wording appears to be a rewrite rather than the earliest form, it should not be promoted.

text: If I believe I cannot do something, it makes me incapable of doing it. But when I believe I can, then I acquire the ability to do it, even if I did not have the ability in the beginning.
text_raw: If I believe I cannot do something, it makes me incapable of doing it. But when I believe I can, then I acquire the ability to do it, even if I did not have the ability in the beginning.
author: Mahatma Gandhi

provenance.notes: This is a modern condensation of q_0938 in the same batch ('Man often becomes what he believes himself to be...'), which is the longer and better-documented form of the same passage. The underlying thought is authentically Gandhi's, but this compressed first-person rewrite is not his sentence. Recommend the corpus keep q_0938 and treat this as a duplicate paraphrase rather than a separate quote.

text: Man often becomes what he believes himself to be. If I keep on saying to myself that I cannot do a certain thing, it is possible that I may end by really becoming incapable of doing it. On the contrary, if I have the belief that I can do it, I shall surely acquire the capacity to do it even if I may not have it at the beginning.
text_raw: Man often becomes what he believes himself to be. If I keep on saying to myself that I cannot do a certain thing, it is possible that I may end by really becoming incapable of doing it. On the contrary, if I have the belief that I can do it, I shall surely acquire the capacity to do it even if I may not have it at the beginning.
author: Mahatma Gandhi

provenance.notes: This longer form is the one that appears in serious Gandhi collections and is generally treated as sourced to his own writings, with stable wording across citations — a good sign, since spurious Gandhi lines tend to drift. The prose rhythm ('Man often becomes what he believes himself to be', 'On the contrary...') is consistent with his English. I cannot name the volume of the Collected Works or the periodical and date, so no print source is cited and I am holding just below the promotion bar. A human check against the Collected Works would likely confirm it.

text: Keep my word positive. Words become my behaviors. Keep my behaviors positive. Behaviors become my habits. Keep my habits positive. Habits become my values. Keep my values positive. Values become my destiny.
text_raw: Keep my word positive. Words become my behaviors. Keep my behaviors positive. Behaviors become my habits. Keep my habits positive. Habits become my values. Keep my values positive. Values become my destiny.
author: Mahatma Gandhi

provenance.notes: This is the 'thoughts become words, words become actions, habits become values, values become destiny' chain, one of the most durable false Gandhi attributions. No Gandhi source exists for it. Its ancestor is the 19th-century English maxim 'Sow a thought, reap an act; sow an act, reap a habit; sow a habit, reap a character; sow a character, reap a destiny', variously credited to Charles Reade and to Samuel Smiles and itself of contested origin; the modern positive-thinking chain is a 20th-century self-help reworking that later acquired Gandhi's name. I can identify the family the saying descends from but not a single true author, so I am leaving the reattribution null rather than guessing. Should not appear in the corpus under Gandhi.

text: There is more to life than increasing its speed.
text_raw: There is more to life than increasing its speed.
author: Mahatma Gandhi

provenance.notes: Ubiquitous under Gandhi's name, especially in slow-living and productivity writing, but I cannot place it in any primary text and I associate it with the unsourced tier of the Gandhi quote literature rather than the documented tier. The epigram's shape — a single modern aphorism about 'speed' — fits mid-to-late 20th-century Western anxieties about pace more naturally than Gandhi's own idiom. Plausible in sentiment, unsupported in provenance.

text: There is no path to peace. Peace is the path.
text_raw: There is no path to peace. Peace is the path.
author: Mahatma Gandhi

provenance.notes: The documented origin of this formula is the American pacifist A. J. Muste, who said 'There is no way to peace; peace is the way' — a line strongly associated with him in the 1960s and quoted in coverage around his death in 1967. The corpus's 'no path to peace / peace is the path' is a variant of Muste's sentence, and the Gandhi credit appears to be later drift onto a bigger name, a pattern well documented for pacifist aphorisms. I am confident enough in the Muste attribution to name it, though I cannot cite the specific speech or article. | Suggested reattribution: A. J. Muste

text: I have learned through bitter experience the one supreme lesson: to conserve my anger; and as heat conserved is transmitted into energy, even so, our anger controlled, can be transmitted into a power that can move the world.
text_raw: I have learned through bitter experience the one supreme lesson: to conserve my anger; and as heat conserved is transmitted into energy, even so, our anger controlled, can be transmitted into a power that can move the world.
author: Mahatma Gandhi

provenance.notes: I believe this is authentic Gandhi, from his journalism of the 1920s (the Young India period), and it is one of the Gandhi passages that circulates with a real source trail rather than as a bare aphorism. Two textual notes for the corpus: the authentic wording is 'transmuted', not 'transmitted' — the corpus text has the corruption twice, which flattens the heat/energy metaphor — and 'a power which can move the world' is the more usual ending. Recommend correcting to 'transmuted' before any promotion. Not citing a dated source because I cannot pin the issue.

text: My life is my message.
text_raw: My life is my message.
author: Mahatma Gandhi

provenance.notes: Well attested by the standards of Gandhi quotation. The line comes with a consistent anecdote — Gandhi, pressed by a journalist for a message and having no time to talk, wrote 'My life is my message' on a scrap of paper — and it is established enough to have been used as the title of Narayan Desai's multi-volume Gandhi biography. I cannot fix the date or the journalist with confidence, so no print source is cited, but the attribution itself is solid.

text: It is unwise to be too sure of one's own wisdom. It is healthy to be reminded that the strongest might weaken and the wisest might err.
text_raw: It is unwise to be too sure of one's own wisdom. It is healthy to be reminded that the strongest might weaken and the wisest might err.
author: Mahatma Gandhi

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Gandhi with stable wording, and I associate it with his own writing rather than with the aggregator tier — the balanced construction ('the strongest might weaken and the wisest might err') and the theme of humility before one's own certainty are characteristic. It appears in the standard Gandhi anthologies of the All Men Are Brothers type. I cannot name the original article or speech, so it stays below the promotion bar pending a check against the Collected Works.

text: Be the change you want to see in the world.
text_raw: Be the change you want to see in the world.
author: Mahatma Gandhi

provenance.notes: The single most famous thing Gandhi never said in these words. No source exists in his writings or speeches. The genuine passage it compresses is 'If we could change ourselves, the tendencies in the world would also change. As a man changes his own nature, so does the attitude of the world change towards him' — a different and more careful claim. The imperative-slogan wording appears to originate in 1970s American self-help; Arleen Lorrance's The Love Project material (c. 1974) carried 'Be the change you want to see happen', and the Gandhi credit attached later. Brian Morton's widely read 2011 New York Times piece 'Falser Words Were Never Spoken' laid this out. I name Lorrance as probable origin of the phrasing, but the sentiment is a fair paraphrase of Gandhi, so the corpus may prefer to carry the authentic longer passage instead. Do not promote under Gandhi as written. | Suggested reattribution: Arleen Lorrance (probable origin of the wording); the underlying sentiment paraphrases Gandhi

text: The greatness of a nation and its moral progress can be judged by the way its animals are treated.
text_raw: The greatness of a nation and its moral progress can be judged by the way its animals are treated.
author: Mahatma Gandhi

provenance.notes: Extremely widely quoted — it is a fixture of animal-welfare campaigning — but I know it as one of the Gandhi lines for which no source in the Collected Works has been located, and it is commonly listed in the unsourced or disputed tier of Gandhi quotation. Related sentiments do appear in his writing on cow protection and ahimsa, which is likely how the attribution took hold. Ubiquity here is a function of the cause it serves, not of evidence.

text: Consciously or unconsciously, every one of us does render some service or other. If we cultivate the habit of doing this service deliberately, our desire for service will steadily grow stronger, and will make, not only our own happiness, but that of the world at large.
text_raw: Consciously or unconsciously, every one of us does render some service or other. If we cultivate the habit of doing this service deliberately, our desire for service will steadily grow stronger, and will make, not only our own happiness, but that of the world at large.
author: Mahatma Gandhi

provenance.notes: Reads as authentic: it is long, syntactically unpolished, argumentative rather than epigrammatic, and it develops a thought about seva step by step — all features that spurious Gandhi quotes lack, since fabrications tend to be short and quotable. The wording is stable across the citations I recall. I cannot place the source text, so this is a judgment from style and internal evidence rather than from provenance, and I am keeping it below the promotion bar until someone checks the Collected Works.

text: An eye for an eye makes the whole world blind.
text_raw: "An eye for an eye makes the whole world blind."
author: Mahatma Gandhi

flags.suspect_reason: No Gandhi source; appears first in Louis Fischer's 1950 biography as paraphrase.

provenance.notes: The pre-flag is correct. No Gandhi source exists. The earliest credited appearances run through mid-20th-century secondary literature — Louis Fischer's The Life of Mahatma Gandhi (1950) carries a version of the thought as biographer's paraphrase rather than as a transcribed Gandhi sentence — and the line reached mass currency through Attenborough's Gandhi (1982), which drew on Fischer. The underlying reversal of lex talionis is older than Gandhi and circulated independently in English. Fischer is the likeliest proximate source of the wording, but as a paraphraser rather than an author, so I am recording that in notes rather than naming him as the quote's author.

text: The weak can never forgive. Forgiveness is the attribute of the strong.
text_raw: The weak can never forgive. Forgiveness is the attribute of the strong.
author: Mahatma Gandhi

provenance.notes: Generally treated as authentic Gandhi and traced to his periodical writing of the early 1930s; the wording is stable across citations and the aphorism-plus-gloss structure matches his editorial style. I cannot name the issue or date, so no print source is given. Held at 0.62 for the standing Gandhi caution — the line is short and quotable, the profile of quotes that drift — but I have no positive evidence against it.

text: My teaching does not require anyone to become homeless or resign the world unless he wants to, but it does require everyone to free himself from the illusion that he is a permanent self and to act with integrity while giving up his craving for pleasure.
text_raw: My teaching does not require anyone to become homeless or resign the world unless he wants to, but it does require everyone to free himself from the illusion that he is a permanent self and to act with integrity while giving up his craving for pleasure.
author: Majjhima Nikaya

provenance.notes: Not a canonical translation. The Majjhima Nikaya credit points at a 152-sutta collection without naming a sutta, and this English does not match any translation tradition I know — not Horner, not Nanamoli/Bodhi. Telltales: 'illusion that he is a permanent self' is a doctrinal gloss on anatta in modern comparative-religion register, not sutta idiom, and the sutta form (address to named interlocutors, formulaic repetition, similes) is entirely absent. This reads as a Western summary of Buddhist teaching later given a scriptural label — a common pattern in inspirational anthologies. Treat the citation as decorative; I cannot identify the actual writer.

text: Too many people overvalue what they are not and undervalue what they are.
text_raw: Too many people overvalue what they are not and undervalue what they are.
author: Malcolm Forbes

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Malcolm Forbes across quotation collections, and it matches the aphoristic register of his 'Fact and Comment' column in Forbes magazine and the 'Thoughts on the Business of Life' compilations. I cannot place a specific issue, page, or book from training knowledge, so the attribution rests on secondary consistency rather than a primary source. No competing claimant that I know of.

text: Fools never learn from their mistakes. Smart people learn from their mistakes. Wise people learn from other people's mistakes.
text_raw: Fools never learn from their mistakes. Smart people learn from their mistakes. Wise people learn from other people's mistakes.
author: Marc Allen

provenance.notes: Marc Allen (New World Library founder, author of 'Visionary Business' and 'The Millionaire Course') is a plausible modern popularizer, but the three-tier fool/smart/wise structure is a long-standing proverbial form with many older analogues, notably the aphorism commonly given to Bismarck ('Fools say they learn by experience; I prefer to profit by others' experience') and the 'learn from the mistakes of others, you can't live long enough to make them all yourself' family attributed variously to Eleanor Roosevelt, Groucho Marx, and Hyman Rickover. I cannot confirm that Allen originated this wording, and I will not guess a true source.

text: The days are too short even for love; how can there be enough time for quarreling?
text_raw: The days are too short even for love; how can there be enough time for quarreling?
author: Margaret Gatty

provenance.notes: Margaret Gatty (1809-1873), author of 'Parables from Nature' and 'The Book of Sun-Dials' (1872), is the name attached to this line in quotation collections, and the epigrammatic form is consistent with the sundial mottoes she gathered. But I cannot confirm whether she wrote it, translated it, or merely recorded it from an older inscription, and I have no page or edition to cite. Deliberately leaving the print source null rather than guessing at The Book of Sun-Dials.

text: We are continually faced with great opportunities which are brilliantly disguised as unsolvable problems.
text_raw: We are continually faced with great opportunities which are brilliantly disguised as unsolvable problems.
author: Margaret Mead

provenance.notes: The well-documented form of this line belongs to John W. Gardner (Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare; founder of Common Cause): 'We are continually faced by great opportunities brilliantly disguised as insoluble problems,' associated with his mid-1960s writing and speeches. The saying has also drifted to Lee Iacocca and Charles Swindoll, and the Margaret Mead version appears in collections without any source in her published anthropological work. I know of no Mead text containing it. Confidence figure reflects the strength of the Mead attribution, which is weak. | Suggested reattribution: John W. Gardner

text: When we are grateful for the good we already have, we attract more good into our life. On the other hand, when we are ungrateful, we tend to shut ourselves off from the good we might otherwise experience.
text_raw: When we are grateful for the good we already have, we attract more good into our life. On the other hand, when we are ungrateful, we tend to shut ourselves off from the good we might otherwise experience.
author: Margaret Stortz

provenance.notes: Margaret Stortz is a Religious Science / New Thought minister and author, and the sentiment fits that tradition's gratitude-and-attraction idiom, but I have no specific book, article, or sermon in training knowledge that carries this passage. I cannot rule out that it circulates from an anthology or daily-reader compilation. No competing attribution known; the honest answer here is that I cannot place it.

text: Being considerate of others will take you further in life than a college degree.
text_raw: "Being considerate of others will take you further in life than a college degree."
author: Marian Wright Edelman

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Marian Wright Edelman and consistent in voice and content with the numbered life lessons in 'The Measure of Our Success: A Letter to My Children and Yours' (1992), which is where I believe it originates. I am not certain enough of the lesson number or wording in that book to record it as a citation, so the print source stays null. No competing claimant.

text: Miracles occur naturally as expressions of love. The real miracle is the love that inspires them. In this sense everything that comes from love is a miracle.
text_raw: Miracles occur naturally as expressions of love. The real miracle is the love that inspires them. In this sense everything that comes from love is a miracle.
author: Marianne Williamson

provenance.earliest_print_source: A Course in Miracles, Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976 - Text, Ch. 1, 'Principles of Miracles', principle 3
provenance.notes: This is not original to Marianne Williamson. It is, essentially verbatim, the third of the Fifty Miracle Principles that open the Text of A Course in Miracles: 'Miracles occur naturally as expressions of love. The real miracle is the love that inspires them. In this sense everything that comes from love is a miracle.' Williamson's 'A Return to Love' (1992) is a commentary on ACIM and quotes the Course extensively, which is how the line came to be tagged with her name. The attribution to her is a quoter-for-author error. | Suggested reattribution: A Course in Miracles (Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976)

text: Most of the time, we fall in love but can’t remain there. The world then calls the state we were in a delusion or infatuation ... But we merely lacked, or someone else lacked, the emotional skills to hold on to the magic when the morning came. ... In truth, we can go to the moon and retain its magic for a lifetime.
text_raw: "Most of the time, we fall in love but can’t remain there. The world then calls the state we were in a delusion or infatuation ... But we merely lacked, or someone else lacked, the emotional skills to hold on to the magic when the morning came. ... In truth, we can go to the moon and retain its magic for a lifetime."
author: Marianne Williamson

provenance.notes: The voice, vocabulary, and subject matter are strongly consistent with Williamson's writing on romantic love, most plausibly 'Enchanted Love: The Mystical Power of Intimate Relationships' (1999) rather than 'A Return to Love.' The ellipses indicate the text was stitched from a longer passage, which is typical of a real book excerpt but also makes it hard to match. I cannot confirm the book or page from training knowledge, so no citation is recorded.

text: The practice of forgiveness is our most important contribution to the healing of the world.
text_raw: The practice of forgiveness is our most important contribution to the healing of the world.
author: Marianne Williamson

provenance.notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Marianne Williamson, and forgiveness-as-world-healing is a central and repeated theme of her work. I cannot locate a specific book or page. One caution given q_0961 in this same batch: Williamson's writing is saturated with A Course in Miracles material, so there is a residual risk that a line like this restates Course teaching; I do not recognize it as verbatim ACIM, but I flag the possibility rather than certify the attribution above the promotion bar.

text: If a man devotes himself to the instructions of his own unconscious, it can bestow this gift [of renewal], so that suddenly life, which has been stale and dull, turns into a rich unending inner adventure, full of creative possibilities.
text_raw: If a man devotes himself to the instructions of his own unconscious, it can bestow this gift [of renewal], so that suddenly life, which has been stale and dull, turns into a rich unending inner adventure, full of creative possibilities.
author: Marie-Louise von Franz

provenance.notes: I believe this comes from Marie-Louise von Franz's chapter 'The Process of Individuation' in 'Man and His Symbols' (C. G. Jung, ed., 1964), which is her best-known writing in English and matches this passage's theme of renewal through attending to the unconscious. The editorial bracket '[of renewal]' suggests the corpus entry was taken from a careful print quotation rather than a meme. I am not confident enough of the chapter or page to record it as a citation, so the print source stays null and the attribution rests on style and subject match plus consistent secondary citation.

text: Fear is a question: What are you afraid of, and why? Just as the seed of health is in illness, because illness contains information, our fears are a treasure house of self-knowledge if we explore them.
text_raw: Fear is a question: What are you afraid of, and why? Just as the seed of health is in illness, because illness contains information, our fears are a treasure house of self-knowledge if we explore them.
author: Marilyn Ferguson

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Marilyn Ferguson, author of 'The Aquarian Conspiracy' (1980) and editor of the Brain/Mind Bulletin, and the framing of fear as information matches her idiom. The passage's length and structure suggest an excerpt from her writing rather than an aphorism assembled by anthologists. I cannot confirm the book or issue, so no citation is recorded.

text: Ultimately we know deeply that the other side of every fear is a freedom.
text_raw: Ultimately we know deeply that the other side of every fear is a freedom.
author: Marilyn Ferguson

provenance.notes: One of the most-reproduced lines credited to Marilyn Ferguson, with consistent attribution but, as far as I know, no cited source anywhere in that circulation. Short aphorisms of this kind are the ones most likely to be detached from an author or absorbed from workshop culture, so consistent repetition is weak evidence on its own. Plausibly hers - it reads like a condensation of the same material as q_0966 - but unverified.

text: If everything feels under control, you’re just not driving fast enough.
text_raw: If everything feels under control, you’re just not driving fast enough.
author: Mario Andretti

provenance.notes: Solidly and consistently attributed to Mario Andretti in interviews and racing literature, though I cannot name the original interview or date. Important wording caveat: the canonical form is 'If everything seems under control, you're not going fast enough.' The recorded text ('feels under control ... just not driving fast enough') is a drifted variant. Recommend normalizing to the standard wording before promotion.

text: History doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme.
text_raw: History doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme.
author: Mark Twain

flags.suspect_reason: No Twain source; earliest attributions to Twain post-date his death by decades.

provenance.notes: The pre-flag is correct. No such line appears in Twain's published work, letters, or notebooks, and the attributions to him begin decades after his death in 1910 - the earliest instance I know of is a 1970 John Robert Colombo 'found poem' that presents 'History never repeats itself but it rhymes' as a Twain saying, which is a repetition of the claim rather than evidence for it. I cannot identify a true originator, so no reattribution is offered; classifying as apocryphal rather than likely_misattributed for exactly that reason. See also q_0975, a near-duplicate of this entry.

text: Do the thing you fear most and the death of fear is certain.
text_raw: Do the thing you fear most and the death of fear is certain.
author: Mark Twain

flags.suspect_reason: No Twain source found in his published work or letters.

provenance.notes: The pre-flag is correct: no source in Twain's published work or correspondence. The same sentence circulates just as often under Ralph Waldo Emerson's name, and that attribution is equally unsourced - Emerson's actual related line, from 'Heroism,' is 'Always do what you are afraid to do,' which he credits to his aunt Mary Moody Emerson. Because both major claimants fail and I cannot identify a real origin, apocryphal with no reattribution.

text: Twenty years from now you will be more disappointed by the things you didn't do than by the things you did. So throw off the bowlines. Sail away from the safe harbor. Explore. Dream.
text_raw: Twenty years from now you will be more disappointed by the things you didn't do than by the things you did. So throw off the bowlines. Sail away from the safe harbor. Explore. Dream.
author: Mark Twain

flags.suspect_reason: No Twain source. First appears in 1990s self-help material attributed to H. Jackson Brown Jr.'s mother.

provenance.earliest_print_source: P.S. I Love You, H. Jackson Brown Jr., 1990
provenance.notes: The pre-flag matches what I know. Nothing in Twain's corpus contains this, and 'throw off the bowlines / sail away from the safe harbor' is not his register. The earliest documented appearance is in H. Jackson Brown Jr.'s 'P.S. I Love You' (1990), a collection of sayings from his mother, Sarah Frances Brown; the Twain tag attached afterwards and spread through 1990s self-help and graduation-speech material. Recording the true origin here because it is documented, not inferred - but note that Brown's book presents it as his mother's saying, so 'H. Jackson Brown Jr.' is the compiler rather than strictly the author. | Suggested reattribution: Sarah Frances Brown, as recorded by her son H. Jackson Brown Jr. in P.S. I Love You (1990)

text: Worrying about something is like paying interest on a debt you don't even know if you owe.
text_raw: Worrying about something is like paying interest on a debt you don't even know if you owe.
author: Mark Twain

provenance.notes: Not pre-flagged, but it should have been. No Twain source exists for this. It is a wordy variant of the unsourced 'Worrying is like paying a debt you don't owe,' which circulates under Twain, Will Rogers, and others without a citation for any of them. The one genuinely documented aphorism in this family belongs to William Ralph Inge, Dean of St Paul's: 'Worry is interest paid on trouble before it falls due.' The recorded wording differs enough that I will not reattribute it to Inge, but his line is the likely ancestor of the metaphor. Recommend flagging this entry as suspect.

text: History doesn't repeat itself, but it rhymes.
text_raw: History doesn't repeat itself, but it rhymes.
author: Mark Twain

provenance.notes: Same verdict as q_0970, of which this is a near-duplicate differing only by the word 'does' - the corpus is carrying both variants and should deduplicate. No Twain source; attributions post-date his 1910 death by decades, with the earliest I know of being John Robert Colombo's 1970 found poem. No identifiable true author, hence apocryphal with no reattribution.

text: The human race has one really effective weapon, and that is laughter.
text_raw: The human race has one really effective weapon, and that is laughter.
author: Mark Twain

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Mysterious Stranger, Mark Twain, 1916 (posthumous)
provenance.notes: The idea is genuinely Twain's, from the Satan monologue in the Mysterious Stranger manuscripts: the human race 'has unquestionably one really effective weapon - laughter.' The exact sentence as quoted here is a smoothed condensation rather than Twain's printed wording, and the 1916 text itself was editorially assembled by Paine and Duneka from Twain's drafts. Correct author, imprecise wording.

text: Age is an issue of mind over matter. If you don't mind, it doesn't matter.
text_raw: Age is an issue of mind over matter. If you don't mind, it doesn't matter.
author: Mark Twain

provenance.notes: Not found in Twain's works or letters; Twain attributions for this line are late and unsupported. The 'if you don't mind, it doesn't matter' pun on mind/matter circulated as a stock joke well before it was pinned to any famous name. It is most commonly credited to Satchel Paige ('Age is a question of mind over matter...'), but Paige popularized rather than originated it, so I am not asserting a replacement author.

text: Don't go around saying the world owes you a living. The world owes you nothing. It was here first.
text_raw: Don't go around saying the world owes you a living. The world owes you nothing. It was here first.
author: Mark Twain

provenance.notes: I cannot place this in any Twain text - not in the novels, essays, letters, or notebooks I know. It reads like a newspaper-filler aphorism that later collected a Twain byline, the standard pattern for spurious Twain. I do not have a confident true origin, so I am recording honest uncertainty rather than a reattribution.

text: When I was a boy of 14, my father was so ignorant I could hardly stand to have the old man around. But when I got to be 21, I was astonished at how much the old man had learned in seven years.
text_raw: When I was a boy of 14, my father was so ignorant I could hardly stand to have the old man around. But when I got to be 21, I was astonished at how much the old man had learned in seven years.
author: Mark Twain

provenance.notes: A classic spurious Twain. It appears in no Twain work; documented appearances postdate his 1910 death, and it is biographically impossible as autobiography - John Marshall Clemens died when Samuel Clemens was eleven, so there was no father to rediscover at twenty-one. Origin unknown; the joke circulated anonymously in periodicals before acquiring Twain's name.

text: The secret to success is making your vocation your vacation.
text_raw: The secret to success is making your vocation your vacation.
author: Mark Twain

provenance.notes: No Twain source known to me. The vocation/vacation pun circulates in several forms ('Make your vocation your vacation') attached to various names, and I cannot trace any of them to a document. Twain's name here looks like the usual gravitational pull of a famous humorist on an unowned wordplay.

text: You can't depend on your eyes when your imagination is out of focus.
text_raw: "You can't depend on your eyes when your imagination is out of focus."
author: Mark Twain

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Twain across quote collections and stylistically plausible for him; I have a weak recollection of it sitting in one of the late novels but cannot place the work or chapter with enough confidence to name it, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing. Author plausible, citation unconfirmed.

text: Kindness is a language which the deaf can hear and the blind can see.
text_raw: "Kindness is a language which the deaf can hear and the blind can see."
author: Mark Twain

provenance.notes: Widely printed over Twain's name but absent from his writings so far as I know; the Twain attribution surfaces decades after his death, and quote-tracing work on this line has failed to find any contemporaneous support. Related sentiments about kindness as a universal language predate the Twain version. True origin unknown to me.

text: The best way to cheer yourself up is to try to cheer somebody else up.
text_raw: "The best way to cheer yourself up is to try to cheer somebody else up."
author: Mark Twain

provenance.notes: Very consistently attributed to Twain and usually pointed at his notebooks, but I cannot confirm which entry or letter, and I have not seen it quoted with a page citation. Plausible but unconfirmed - keeping it below the promotion bar until someone checks the notebooks.

text: There is nothing that fear does not make men believe.
text_raw: There is nothing that fear does not make men believe.
author: Marquis de Vauvengras

provenance.earliest_print_source: Reflexions et maximes, Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues, 1746
provenance.notes: The maxim is Vauvenargues': 'Il n'est rien que la peur ne fasse croire,' from his Reflexions et maximes (published 1746 with the Introduction a la connaissance de l'esprit humain). The author field is misspelled and mistitled - it should read 'Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues', not 'Marquis de Vauvengras'. I am confident of the author, less so of the exact maxim number, so I have not cited one. | Suggested reattribution: Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues (author name is misspelled in the record)

text: Dreams are illustrations from the book your soul is writing about you.
text_raw: Dreams are illustrations from the book your soul is writing about you.
author: Marsha Norman

provenance.notes: Consistently credited to the playwright Marsha Norman with no competing claimants, and it circulated widely after appearing in magazine quote features in the 1990s. I cannot name the interview, play, or essay it came from, so the citation stays null. Author likely right, source unlocated.

text: Instead of frittering away your vibrancy with worry or distraction, realize your mind and body are inextricably united. What calms and tones up one, soothes and improves the other.
text_raw: Instead of frittering away your vibrancy with worry or distraction, realize your mind and body are inextricably united. What calms and tones up one, soothes and improves the other.
author: Marsha Sinetar

provenance.notes: Attributed to Marsha Sinetar, whose subject matter (right livelihood, mind-body integration, contemplative practice) fits the content well - most likely from one of her books such as Do What You Love, the Money Will Follow (1987) or Ordinary People as Monks and Mystics (1986), but I cannot confirm which and will not guess a title.

text: When flowing water meets with obstacles on its path, a blockage in its journey, it pauses. It increases in volume and strength, filling up in front of the obstacle and eventually spilling past it... Emulate the example of the water: pause and build up your strength until the obstacle no longer represents a blockage.
text_raw: When flowing water meets with obstacles on its path, a blockage in its journey, it pauses. It increases in volume and strength, filling up in front of the obstacle and eventually spilling past it... Emulate the example of the water: pause and build up your strength until the obstacle no longer represents a blockage.
author: Marsha Sinetar

provenance.notes: Attributed to Marsha Sinetar in quote collections; the water-and-obstacle imagery reads like her commentary on an I Ching hexagram, which is consistent with her writing, but I cannot place the book or page. The ellipsis in the text indicates it is already an excerpt from a longer passage, which makes verification harder rather than easier.

text: There are no passengers on spaceship earth. We are all crew.
text_raw: There are no passengers on spaceship earth. We are all crew.
author: Marshall McLuhan

provenance.notes: Widely and consistently credited to McLuhan, but I know of no primary citation - no book, lecture, or interview I can point to. Complicating it: 'Spaceship Earth' is Buckminster Fuller's frame (Operating Manual for Spaceship Earth, 1969), and the line is sometimes handed to Fuller instead. McLuhan is the more common attribution and is plausible, but the evidence I have is secondary repetition, not a source.

text: We look at the dance to impart the sensation of living in an affirmation of life, to energize the spectator into keener awareness of the vigor, the mystery, the humor, the variety, and the wonder of life.
text_raw: We look at the dance to impart the sensation of living in an affirmation of life, to energize the spectator into keener awareness of the vigor, the mystery, the humor, the variety, and the wonder of life.
author: Martha Graham

provenance.notes: Genuine-sounding Graham and consistently attributed to her, from her writing on modern dance in the 1930s-50s. Note a probable transcription corruption: the standard wording is 'We look FOR the dance to impart the sensation of living in an affirmation of life,' not 'look at the dance.' I cannot name the essay or collection with confidence, so no citation.

text: There is only one of you in the world, just one. And if that is not fulfilled, then something has been lost.
text_raw: There is only one of you in the world, just one. And if that is not fulfilled, then something has been lost.
author: Martha Graham

provenance.notes: A variant rendering of the same de Mille conversation behind q_0999 ('because there is only one of you in all time'). It circulates as a standalone Graham line, but I cannot match it word for word to de Mille's text, so it may be a paraphrase in transmission rather than a distinct utterance. Author right, exact wording unverified.

text: True self simply refers to the aspect of our being that is completely aware of its expanded nature no matter what we may be experiencing in our lives.
text_raw: "True self simply refers to the aspect of our being that is completely aware of its expanded nature no matter what we may be experiencing in our lives."
author: Martia Nelson

provenance.notes: Martia Nelson is a real author whose best-known book is 'Coming Home: The Return to True Self' (New World Library, 1993), and this line's vocabulary ('true self', 'expanded nature') is consistent with that book's subject. I cannot confirm from training knowledge that this exact sentence appears there, and I have no independent citation for it. Attribution is plausible but unverified.

text: A user interface is like a joke. If you have to explain it, it’s not that good.
text_raw: A user interface is like a joke. If you have to explain it, it’s not that good.
author: Martin LeBlanc, Iconfinder

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed across design literature and talks to Martin LeBlanc, founder of Iconfinder; it circulated widely from around 2013 as a LeBlanc line and I am not aware of any competing attribution. The underlying joke formula ('if you have to explain it, it isn't good') is much older, so LeBlanc's contribution is the UI application rather than the structure. No primary source (original tweet, post, or talk) that I can cite from memory, so this stays below the verified bar.

text: Science and religion are not so different except that in science, the ultimate sin is believing too strongly.
text_raw: Science and religion are not so different except that in science, the ultimate sin is believing too strongly.
author: Marvin Minsky

provenance.notes: The sentiment is very characteristic of Minsky, who repeatedly argued that scientific commitment must stay revisable and criticized belief held past the evidence. I have a weak recollection of this specific phrasing circulating as a Minsky line from an interview or a talk, but I cannot place a book, article, or date, and I will not guess at one. Plausible but unsourced.

text: For every failure, there is an alternate course of action. You just have to find it.
text_raw: For every failure, there is an alternate course of action. You just have to find it.
author: Mary Kay Ash

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Mary Kay Ash in business and motivational quote collections, and consistent in tone with her writing in 'Mary Kay on People Management' (1984) and her autobiography. I cannot locate the sentence in a specific book, speech, or company publication from training knowledge, and much of the Mary Kay Ash quote canon circulates through corporate motivational material without sourcing.

text: Creativity is inventing, experimenting, growing, taking risks, breaking rules, making mistakes, and having fun.
text_raw: "Creativity is inventing, experimenting, growing, taking risks, breaking rules, making mistakes, and having fun."
author: Mary Lou Cook

provenance.notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Mary Lou Cook, the Santa Fe calligrapher, peace activist, and volunteer-movement figure. The attribution is stable — I know of no competing claimant — but I can point to no book, article, or interview containing it; it appears to have entered circulation through quote anthologies and greeting-card style collections. Stable attribution, absent source.

text: Even though you may want to move forward in your life, you may have one foot on the brakes. In order to be free, we must learn how to let go. Release the hurt. Release the fear. Refuse to entertain your old pain. The energy it takes to hang onto the past is holding you back from a new life.
text_raw: Even though you may want to move forward in your life, you may have one foot on the brakes. In order to be free, we must learn how to let go. Release the hurt. Release the fear. Refuse to entertain your old pain. The energy it takes to hang onto the past is holding you back from a new life.
author: Mary Manin Morrissey

provenance.notes: Attributed with reasonable consistency to Mary Manin Morrissey, the New Thought minister and author of 'Building Your Field of Dreams' (1996) and 'No Less Than Greatness' (2001). The 'one foot on the brakes' image and the letting-go framing match her teaching. I cannot confirm which book, sermon, or newsletter it comes from, and much of her circulating quote material originates in unarchived talks and columns.

text: It's easy to feel grateful when we receive a raise, meet the love of our life, or watch our children succeed, but spiritual gratitude is not circumstantial. It arises from a true knowing that God is our Source. We can feel thankful for every day, even in the middle of life's challenges.
text_raw: "It's easy to feel grateful when we receive a raise, meet the love of our life, or watch our children succeed, but spiritual gratitude is not circumstantial. It arises from a true knowing that God is our Source. We can feel thankful for every day, even in the middle of life's challenges."
author: Mary Manin Morrissey

provenance.notes: Reads as authentic Morrissey — New Thought vocabulary, 'God is our Source' capitalized in the movement's convention — and is attributed to her wherever it appears. But this looks like material from a devotional column, newsletter, or Thanksgiving-season message rather than a book, and I cannot identify the original venue. No source, honest uncertainty.

text: If you have made mistakes, even serious ones, there is always another chance for you. What we call failure is not the falling down but the staying down.
text_raw: If you have made mistakes, even serious ones, there is always another chance for you. What we call failure is not the falling down but the staying down.
author: Mary Pickford

provenance.notes: Long attributed to Mary Pickford and consistent with the inspirational writing she published in the 1930s, notably 'Why Not Try God?' (1934) and 'My Rendezvous with Life' (1935), which are full of exactly this kind of counsel about failure and second chances. The second sentence ('failure is not the falling down but the staying down') also circulates as an anonymous proverb, which raises the possibility that Pickford was repeating a current saying rather than coining it. I cannot confirm the book or page.

text: Beauty can be seen in all things, seeing and composing the beauty is what separates the snapshot from the photograph.
text_raw: Beauty can be seen in all things, seeing and composing the beauty is what separates the snapshot from the photograph.
author: Matt Hardy

provenance.notes: This line saturates photography quote lists attributed to a bare 'Matt Hardy' with no identifying detail, no publication, and no date. I cannot establish who this Matt Hardy is — the name is shared by a well-known professional wrestler, who is almost certainly not the source, and by several photographers. No traceable origin; the attribution is a name floating free of a person. Treat as effectively anonymous.

text: Conflict is inevitable, but combat is optional.
text_raw: Conflict is inevitable, but combat is optional.
author: Max Lucado

provenance.notes: Commonly attributed to Max Lucado, the Christian author, and the aphoristic construction fits his style. The same line also circulates in conflict-resolution and mediation training material with no attribution at all, and occasionally credited to others, which suggests it may be a stock saying that attached to Lucado's name rather than a line he coined. I cannot place it in any of his books.

text: Accept yourself as you are. Otherwise you will never see opportunity. You will not feel free to move toward it; you will feel you are not deserving.
text_raw: Accept yourself as you are. Otherwise you will never see opportunity. You will not feel free to move toward it; you will feel you are not deserving.
author: Maxwell Maltz

provenance.notes: Attributed to Maxwell Maltz, the plastic surgeon who wrote 'Psycho-Cybernetics' (1960); the self-image thesis and the link between self-acceptance and perceived opportunity are core Maltz themes, so the attribution is coherent. I cannot confirm the sentence appears in Psycho-Cybernetics or his later books, and the large body of 'Maltz quotes' online includes material from later ghostwritten and revised editions.

text: The most delightful surprise in life is to suddenly recognize your own worth.
text_raw: The most delightful surprise in life is to suddenly recognize your own worth.
author: Maxwell Maltz

provenance.notes: Widely circulated as Maxwell Maltz and thematically consistent with Psycho-Cybernetics' argument about self-image and self-worth. No specific book, chapter, or date that I can confirm; this is one of the short aphorisms that spread through motivational compilations detached from any source text.

text: I long, as does every human being, to be at home wherever I find myself.
text_raw: I long, as does every human being, to be at home wherever I find myself.
author: Maya Angelou

provenance.notes: Genuinely Angelou's in voice and theme, and consistently cited to 'All God's Children Need Traveling Shoes' (1986), the memoir of her years in Ghana, whose central subject is exactly this longing for home. The better-known companion line from that book — 'The ache for home lives in all of us' — is firmly sourced there. I believe this sentence is from the same work but cannot confirm the passage, so I am leaving the print source field empty rather than asserting a citation I have not confirmed.

text: I think we all have empathy. We may not have enough courage to display it.
text_raw: I think we all have empathy. We may not have enough courage to display it.
author: Maya Angelou

provenance.notes: Attributed to Maya Angelou consistently and without competing claimants; it comes from her spoken remarks — interviews and public conversations in her later years, where she returned often to the theme that empathy is common and the courage to act on it is not. Spoken origin means no clean print citation; I cannot name the specific interview or date.

text: If you are always trying to be normal, you will never know how amazing you can be.
text_raw: If you are always trying to be normal, you will never know how amazing you can be.
author: Maya Angelou

provenance.notes: This is a social-media staple attributed to Angelou and it should be treated with suspicion. I cannot place it in any of her memoirs, poetry, essay collections, or documented interviews, and its register — short, motivational-poster cadence — is unlike her usual construction. Angelou is a strong misattribution magnet: lines by Mary Anne Radmacher, Rumi translators, and anonymous inspirational writers are routinely assigned to her, and 'Still I Rise' fame pulls unattributed uplift toward her name. I have no evidence of a true author, so I am not proposing a reattribution, but the attribution should not be treated as sound.

text: I believe talent is like electricity. We don't understand electricity. We use it.
text_raw: I believe talent is like electricity. We don't understand electricity. We use it.
author: Maya Angelou

provenance.notes: Angelou used this electricity analogy for talent in interviews, typically extending it — talent, like electricity, is not understood but used, and it makes no judgment about who uses it. The attribution is consistent and the extended form's survival in the record argues for authenticity rather than a manufactured aphorism. I recall it from an interview context but cannot identify the publication or year, so no citation.

text: I have found that among its other benefits, giving liberates the soul of the giver.
text_raw: "I have found that among its other benefits, giving liberates the soul of the giver."
author: Maya Angelou

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Angelou and usually cited to 'Wouldn't Take Nothing for My Journey Now' (1993), her collection of short essays, which contains a piece on giving and the giver. The sentence structure ('I have found that among its other benefits') matches that book's essayistic voice more than her memoir prose. I cannot confirm the passage, so the print source field is left empty rather than asserted.

text: I had to accept the assignment of my own existence. The responsibility of this seemed immense but in actuality my acceptance became the freedom to fly.
text_raw: I had to accept the assignment of my own existence. The responsibility of this seemed immense but in actuality my acceptance became the freedom to fly.
author: Meg Blackburn Losey

provenance.notes: Meg Blackburn Losey is a real author ('The Children of Now', 2007; 'Conversations with the Children of Now', 2008), and the line's vocabulary fits her genre. I have no knowledge of this specific sentence in her published work and cannot find any independent trace of it in what I know. Low confidence; the attribution may be correct but rests on nothing I can check.

text: God is not found in the soul by adding anything, but by a process of subtraction.
text_raw: God is not found in the soul by adding anything, but by a process of subtraction.
author: Meister Eckhart

provenance.notes: The thought is authentically Eckhartian — the via negativa, Abgeschiedenheit (detachment), and his insistence that the soul approaches God by emptying rather than acquiring are central to the German sermons. But this exact English sentence is a modern paraphrase, not a translation of an identifiable sermon passage, and it spread largely through twentieth-century popularizers (Blakney's 1941 translation, and later Matthew Fox's Creation Spirituality writings, which loosely render Eckhart for contemporary readers). Eckhart is a heavy paraphrase magnet: much of what circulates under his name is compression of his ideas rather than his words. Faithful to his theology, unverifiable as his wording.

text: As long as I am this or that, I am not all things.
text_raw: "As long as I am this or that, I am not all things."
author: Meister Eckhart

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Eckhart and consonant with his German sermons on detachment and poverty of spirit; the fuller form usually runs 'As long as I am this or that, or have this or that, I am not all things and I have not all things.' It circulates through 20th-century English translations (Blakney 1941 and later Matthew Fox anthologies), but I cannot name the specific sermon with confidence from training knowledge, so I am leaving the print source null rather than guessing a sermon number.

text: Christ’s birth is always happening. And yet if it doesn’t happen now, how can it help me? Everything depends on that.
text_raw: Christ’s birth is always happening. And yet if it doesn’t happen now, how can it help me? Everything depends on that.
author: Meister Eckhart

provenance.notes: The thought is unmistakably Eckhart's central Christmas-sermon theme — the eternal birth of the Word in the soul, and his repeated challenge 'what good is it to me that this birth is always happening, if it does not happen in me?' The wording here reads as a modern loose rendering (of the sort found in devotional anthologies such as Matthew Fox's Meditations with Meister Eckhart) rather than a scholarly translation. Authentic in substance, uncertain as an exact quotation, so I am holding it below the promotion bar.

text: Gratitude unlocks the fullness of life. It turns what we have into enough, and more. It turns denial into acceptance, chaos to order, confusion to clarity. It can turn a meal into a feast, a house into a home, a stranger into a friend. Gratitude makes sense of our past, brings peace for today, and creates a vision for tomorrow.
text_raw: Gratitude unlocks the fullness of life. It turns what we have into enough, and more. It turns denial into acceptance, chaos to order, confusion to clarity. It can turn a meal into a feast, a house into a home, a stranger into a friend. Gratitude makes sense of our past, brings peace for today, and creates a vision for tomorrow.
author: Melody Beattie

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Language of Letting Go, Melody Beattie, 1990
provenance.notes: Genuinely Beattie's, from her codependency-recovery daily-meditation writing; the attribution is consistent everywhere it appears and the voice matches her published work. The book citation is the one given in most reputable secondary sources, but I cannot confirm the page or rule out an earlier appearance in Beyond Codependency (1989), so treat the title as probable rather than confirmed. Note that q_1030 is a verbatim duplicate of this entry and should be deduplicated upstream.

It can turn a meal into a feast, a house into a home, a stranger into a friend. Gratitude makes sense of our past, brings peace for today, and creates a vision for tomorrow.
author: Melody Beattie

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Language of Letting Go, Melody Beattie, 1990
provenance.notes: Verbatim duplicate of q_1029 — same verdict. Genuinely Beattie's; the book citation is the standard one but unconfirmed at page level, and an earlier appearance in Beyond Codependency (1989) cannot be excluded. Recommend deduplicating against q_1029.

text: When we allow today to be as meaningful as possible and fill it with a positive, hopeful, and loving perspective, then we are much more likely to have a tomorrow, and it is more likely to also be good and healing.
text_raw: When we allow today to be as meaningful as possible and fill it with a positive, hopeful, and loving perspective, then we are much more likely to have a tomorrow, and it is more likely to also be good and healing.
author: Meredith L. Young-Sower

provenance.notes: The author's name is almost certainly Meredith L. Young-Sowers (Agartha, Angelic Messenger Cards, Spiritual Crisis), not 'Young-Sower' — worth correcting in the corpus. I have no independent knowledge of this passage in her published work; it circulates on gratitude and healing quote sites without a source. Honest answer is that I cannot place it.

text: The bad news is time flies. The good news is you're the pilot.
text_raw: The bad news is time flies. The good news is you're the pilot.
author: Michael Altshuler

provenance.notes: Uniformly attributed to Michael Altshuler, an American motivational speaker, and I know of no competing claimant — but the attribution rests entirely on quote aggregators and graduation-speech roundups, not on a book, talk transcript, or dated first appearance I can point to. Plausible but unsourced.

text: If you don't know where you are going, any path will get you there.
text_raw: If you don't know where you are going, any path will get you there.
author: Michael Gerber

provenance.notes: Confidence reflects the strength of the Gerber attribution, which is weak. This is a floating proverb that long predates Michael Gerber; it is the popular paraphrase of the Cheshire Cat exchange in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865) — 'if you don't much care where you want to get to, then it doesn't matter which way you go' — and also circulates in Yogi Berra's form ('you'll end up someplace else'). Gerber may well have used it in E-Myth-era writing, but quoting is not coining. No original-author claim should be recorded for him. | Suggested reattribution: Popular paraphrase of Lewis Carroll's Cheshire Cat passage, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865); not original to Michael Gerber

text: I am careful not to confuse excellence with perfection. Excellence, I can reach for; perfection is God's business.
text_raw: I am careful not to confuse excellence with perfection. Excellence, I can reach for; perfection is God's business.
author: Michael J. Fox

provenance.earliest_print_source: Lucky Man: A Memoir, Michael J. Fox, 2002
provenance.notes: This is one of Fox's signature lines and matches the register of his Parkinson's-era memoir; my recollection places it in Lucky Man (2002), which is also the citation given in most secondary sources. I cannot confirm the page, and Fox has repeated the line in interviews, so the memoir may be a repetition rather than the first appearance. Strong on authorship, softer on the exact source.

text: The world is your mirror and your mind is a magnet. What you perceive in this world is largely a reflection of your own attitudes and beliefs. Life will give you what you attract with your thoughts think, act and talk negatively and your world will be negative. Think and act and talk with enthusiasm and you will attract positive results.
text_raw: The world is your mirror and your mind is a magnet. What you perceive in this world is largely a reflection of your own attitudes and beliefs. Life will give you what you attract with your thoughts think, act and talk negatively and your world will be negative. Think and act and talk with enthusiasm and you will attract positive results.
author: Michael LeBeuf

provenance.notes: The name is misspelled — the author credited is Michael LeBoeuf (Working Smart; The Greatest Management Principle in the World; How to Win Customers and Keep Them for Life). The passage is consistently attributed to him on quote sites but I cannot place it in any of his books, and the text as given is garbled ('what you attract with your thoughts think, act and talk negatively'), which is a common signature of aggregator-copied material. Unsourced.

text: Allow the heavens and stars to praise your ability to become no-thing in a comfortable state of forgiving mindlessness. From this location God exists as your partner and you dance together as one spirit inside the rhythm of the cosmos.
text_raw: "Allow the heavens and stars to praise your ability to become no-thing in a comfortable state of forgiving mindlessness. From this location God exists as your partner and you dance together as one spirit inside the rhythm of the cosmos."
author: Michael Levy

provenance.notes: Michael Levy is a contemporary inspirational poet and author (Point of Life), and the style here matches that body of work, so the attribution is plausible. But I have no knowledge of the specific book or poem it comes from, and a living aggregator-circulated author of this kind is exactly the case where I should not manufacture a citation.

text: The affairs of the world will go on forever. Do not delay the practice of meditation.
text_raw: "The affairs of the world will go on forever. Do not delay the practice of meditation."
author: Milarepa

provenance.notes: Consistently and traditionally ascribed to Milarepa (11th-century Tibetan yogi), and entirely in keeping with the counsel in the Mila Grubum (The Hundred Thousand Songs of Milarepa). But I cannot identify which song or which translation this English wording comes from, and Tibetan devotional sayings are heavily paraphrased in circulation. Plausible attribution, unlocated text.

text: I love everything that flows.
text_raw: I love everything that flows.
author: Milton

provenance.earliest_print_source: Tropic of Cancer, Henry Miller, 1934
provenance.notes: Confidence refers to the recorded attribution to 'Milton,' which appears to be a parsing error rather than a real claim about John Milton. The line is Henry Miller's, from the celebrated passage in Tropic of Cancer (1934): 'I love everything that flows...' — and Miller's own sentence contains the phrase 'said the great blind Milton of our times,' his epithet for James Joyce. Almost certainly the corpus captured the word 'Milton' out of that clause. Note this sits adjacent to q_1040, also a Miller entry with a truncated author field, which supports the parsing-error reading. | Suggested reattribution: Henry Miller

text: Design and art are independent coordinates that provide their greatest satisfactions when experienced simultaneously.
text_raw: Design and art are independent coordinates that provide their greatest satisfactions when experienced simultaneously.
author: Milton Glaser

provenance.notes: Thematically very Glaser — the art/design relationship was a lifelong preoccupation of his, running through Art Is Work (2000) and his lectures and essays — but I cannot match this exact sentence to any of his published writing or talks. The formulation 'independent coordinates' is distinctive enough that I would expect to recall it if it were a well-known Glaser line. Plausible, unverified.

text: Whoever knows himself knows God.
text_raw: Whoever knows himself knows God.
author: Mohammed

provenance.notes: This is the famous Sufi maxim 'man arafa nafsahu faqad arafa rabbahu' — 'he who knows himself knows his Lord' — widely quoted in Sufi literature (Ibn Arabi among many others) and often presented as a hadith. Classical hadith scholars rejected it: it appears in none of the canonical collections, and al-Nawawi, Ibn Taymiyya and al-Zarkashi among others judged it not established as a saying of the Prophet. It is sometimes ascribed instead to the early Sufi Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi. Attributing it flatly to Muhammad is not defensible. | Suggested reattribution: Sufi maxim of uncertain origin, sometimes ascribed to Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi; not a canonical hadith

text: Service to others is the rent you pay for your room here on earth.
text_raw: "Service to others is the rent you pay for your room here on earth."
author: Mohammed Ali

provenance.notes: The name should be Muhammad Ali. Ali did use this line and it appears on materials associated with him, but he did not originate it — 'service is the rent you pay for your room on this earth' is an older circulating aphorism with earlier claimants including Shirley Chisholm and Marian Wright Edelman ('service is the rent we pay for living'), and earlier still it has been credited to the missionary physician Wilfred Grenfell. I do not know the true earliest instance well enough to name one, so I am leaving the reattribution null and flagging Ali as popularizer rather than author.

text: Never use violence of any kind. Never threaten violence in any way. Never even think violent thoughts. Never argue because it attacks another’s opinion. Never criticize because it attacks another’s ego. And your success is guaranteed.
text_raw: "Never use violence of any kind. Never threaten violence in any way. Never even think violent thoughts. Never argue because it attacks another’s opinion. Never criticize because it attacks another’s ego. And your success is guaranteed."
author: Mohandas Gandhi

provenance.notes: Almost certainly not Gandhi. The register is late-20th-century American self-help — the escalating 'never / never / never' construction and especially the closing promise 'and your success is guaranteed' are wholly foreign to Gandhi, who framed ahimsa as a discipline and a truth-practice, not as a technique with a guaranteed payoff. I know of no passage resembling this in the Collected Works or in his letters and speeches. Gandhi is one of the strongest misattribution magnets in the corpus, and this has the hallmarks of a seminar handout attributed to him for authority. No true origin identifiable, so no reattribution offered.

text: One has to abandon altogether the search for security, and reach out to the risk of living with both arms. One has to court doubt and darkness as the cost of knowing.
text_raw: One has to abandon altogether the search for security, and reach out to the risk of living with both arms. One has to court doubt and darkness as the cost of knowing.
author: Morris L. West

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Shoes of the Fisherman, Morris L. West, 1963
provenance.notes: I recognize this as West's, and my recollection places it in The Shoes of the Fisherman (1963), where it belongs to a longer reflective passage that continues into a statement about accepting every consequence of living and dying. The attribution to West is consistent wherever the line appears. Holding at 0.7 because I am working from recall of the novel rather than a checked page, and West reused similar material across his fiction and essays.

text: The miracle is not that we do this work, but that we are happy to do it.
text_raw: The miracle is not that we do this work, but that we are happy to do it.
author: Mother Teresa

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Mother Teresa and fully in keeping with how she spoke about the Missionaries of Charity's work — joy as the surprising thing, not the labor. But I cannot locate it in a specific address, interview, or book; it circulates through devotional collections and secondhand quotation. Plausible and in-voice, but unsourced, so it stays below the promotion bar.

text: People are often unreasonable, illogical, and self centered; Forgive them anyway. If you are kind, people may accuse you of selfish, ulterior motives; Be kind anyway. If you are successful, you will win some false friends and some true enemies; Succeed anyway. If you are honest and frank, people may cheat you; Be honest and frank anyway. What you spend years building, someone could destroy overnight; Build anyway. If you find serenity and happiness, they may be jealous; Be happy anyway. The good you do today, people will often forget tomorrow; Do good anyway. Give the world the best you have, and it may never be enough; Give the world the best you've got anyway. You see, in the final analysis, it is between you and God; It was never between you and them anyway.
text_raw: People are often unreasonable, illogical, and self centered; Forgive them anyway. If you are kind, people may accuse you of selfish, ulterior motives; Be kind anyway. If you are successful, you will win some false friends and some true enemies; Succeed anyway. If you are honest and frank, people may cheat you; Be honest and frank anyway. What you spend years building, someone could destroy overnight; Build anyway. If you find serenity and happiness, they may be jealous; Be happy anyway. The good you do today, people will often forget tomorrow; Do good anyway. Give the world the best you have, and it may never be enough; Give the world the best you've got anyway. You see, in the final analysis, it is between you and God; It was never between you and them anyway.
author: Mother Teresa

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Silent Revolution: Dynamic Leadership in the Student Council, Kent M. Keith, 1968
provenance.notes: This is one of the best-documented misattributions in circulation. The text is an adapted version of 'The Paradoxical Commandments,' written by Kent M. Keith in 1968 while he was a Harvard undergraduate, published in his booklet The Silent Revolution: Dynamic Leadership in the Student Council. A shortened version titled 'Anyway' was posted on the wall of Mother Teresa's children's home in Calcutta, which is how her name became attached; it was later reprinted in books about her, cementing the error. The closing 'it is between you and God' line is part of that Calcutta adaptation. Keith's authorship is well established and he has written about it publicly. | Suggested reattribution: Kent M. Keith

text: The dying, the cripple, the mental, the unwanted, the unloved-- they are Jesus in disguise.
text_raw: The dying, the cripple, the mental, the unwanted, the unloved-- they are Jesus in disguise.
author: Mother Teresa

provenance.notes: The idiom is authentically hers — 'Jesus in his distressing disguise' was a formula Mother Teresa used repeatedly about the poor and the dying, and the sentence structure matches her spoken English. I cannot, however, tie this exact sentence to a dated address, interview, or book, and the wording varies across versions. Note also that the corpus text carries dated and dehumanizing phrasing ('the cripple, the mental') that may be a transcription of her idiom or an aggregator's corruption; worth a human editorial decision independent of the provenance question.

text: I'm not here to be successful. I'm here to be faithful.
text_raw: "I'm not here to be successful. I'm here to be faithful."
author: Mother Teresa

provenance.notes: Circulates most often as 'God has not called me to be successful; He has called me to be faithful,' consistently ascribed to Mother Teresa in devotional literature and quote collections. I cannot place it in any of her published writings, letters, or recorded addresses, and the wording varies noticeably between sources, which is a common signature of an oral/secondhand attribution. Plausible but unverified.

text: If you judge people, you have no time to love them.
text_raw: If you judge people, you have no time to love them.
author: Mother Teresa

flags.suspect_reason: Commonly attributed to her but no primary source.

provenance.notes: Agrees with the input flag. Extremely widely attributed to Mother Teresa and consistent with her recorded themes, but I know of no primary source — no speech, interview, or book of hers that I can place it in. It spread heavily through greeting-card and internet quote compilations. Honest answer: attribution is plausible and uncontested, evidence is absent.

text: We realize that what we are accomplishing is a drop in the ocean. But if this drop were not in the ocean, it would be missed.
text_raw: "We realize that what we are accomplishing is a drop in the ocean. But if this drop were not in the ocean, it would be missed."
author: Mother Teresa

provenance.notes: A genuine and consistently attributed Mother Teresa saying, though this is one of several circulating wordings. Better-known variants: 'I know that the work is only a drop in the ocean, but if the drop were not there, the ocean would be missing something,' and 'We ourselves feel that what we are doing is just a drop in the ocean. But the ocean would be less because of that missing drop.' Attribution is strong and uniform across sources; the specific phrasing here I cannot tie to a primary text, so I am holding below the 0.80 promotion bar.

text: We can not do great things, just small things with great Love.
text_raw: We can not do great things, just small things with great Love.
author: Mother Theresa

provenance.notes: One of the most durable and consistently attributed Mother Teresa lines; standard wording is 'We can do no great things, only small things with great love.' Attribution is uniform across decades of sources and she is recorded using the formulation in talks. The corpus entry has two hygiene problems: the author is misspelled 'Mother Theresa,' and the text is a garbled variant ('We can not do great things, just small things...') with inconsistent capitalization of 'Love.' I could not place the exact primary utterance, so this stays at strong-secondary rather than verified. | Suggested reattribution: Mother Teresa (author-name spelling correction only)

text: It is so clear it is very hard to see. You must know that the fire which you are seeking is the fire in your own lantern, and that your rice has been cooked from the very beginning.
text_raw: It is so clear it is very hard to see. You must know that the fire which you are seeking is the fire in your own lantern, and that your rice has been cooked from the very beginning.
author: Mu Mon-kwan

provenance.notes: 'Mu Mon-kwan' is not a person — it is a garbling of Mumonkan (無門關), the Japanese title of The Gateless Gate, the 1228 koan collection compiled by the Chinese Chan master Wumen Huikai (Japanese: Mumon Ekai). The underlying saying is Wumen's verse commentary, familiar in English from Paul Reps' Zen Flesh, Zen Bones as roughly: 'It is too clear and so it is hard to see. A dunce once searched for fire with a lighted lantern. Had he known what fire was, he could have cooked his rice much sooner.' The text here is a loose modern paraphrase, not any translation I recognize, so I am not citing the Mumonkan as the print source for this wording. The idea is authentically Wumen's; the sentence is not. | Suggested reattribution: Wumen Huikai (Mumon Ekai), The Gateless Gate / Mumonkan, c. 1228 — as a paraphrase, not a quotation

text: The man who has no imagination has no wings.
text_raw: "The man who has no imagination has no wings."
author: Muhammad Ali

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Muhammad Ali and stylistically plausible for him, but I cannot place it in a specific interview, press conference, or in The Greatest: My Own Story (1975). Ali is a moderate misattribution magnet — motivational copy written for and about him is routinely recirculated as his own words (see q_1057). Attribution here is uncontested but unsourced.

text: Impossible is just a word thrown around by small men who find it easier to live in the world they've been given than to explore the power they have to change it. Impossible is not a fact. It's an opinion. Impossible is potential. Impossible is temporary. Impossible is nothing.
text_raw: Impossible is just a word thrown around by small men who find it easier to live in the world they've been given than to explore the power they have to change it. Impossible is not a fact. It's an opinion. Impossible is potential. Impossible is temporary. Impossible is nothing.
author: Muhammad Ali

provenance.notes: This is advertising copy, not Ali. The passage is the manifesto text of the adidas 'Impossible Is Nothing' campaign launched in 2004, developed by the agency 180/TBWA, whose flagship spots featured Muhammad Ali (and archival footage of him alongside his daughter Laila). The final line 'Impossible is nothing' is the campaign tagline, which is the strongest tell. Ali's name and image were licensed to the campaign; the words were written for it. Widely recirculated as an Ali quotation ever since, including in books and on quote sites. I am confident the campaign is the origin and correspondingly low-confidence in the Ali attribution. | Suggested reattribution: adidas 'Impossible Is Nothing' campaign copy (agency 180/TBWA), 2004

text: Mindfulness means moment-to-moment, non-judgmental awareness. It is cultivated by refining our capacity to pay attention, intentionally, in the present moment, and then sustaining that attention over time as best we can. In the process, we become more in touch with our life as it is unfolding.
text_raw: "Mindfulness means moment-to-moment, non-judgmental awareness. It is cultivated by refining our capacity to pay attention, intentionally, in the present moment, and then sustaining that attention over time as best we can. In the process, we become more in touch with our life as it is unfolding."
author: Myla & Jon Kabat-Zinn

provenance.earliest_print_source: Everyday Blessings: The Inner Work of Mindful Parenting, Myla and Jon Kabat-Zinn, 1997
provenance.notes: The joint byline points to Everyday Blessings (Hyperion, 1997), which is Myla and Jon Kabat-Zinn's only co-authored book, so the source attribution is near-certain even though I cannot confirm the sentences verbatim against the text. The definition also closely tracks Jon Kabat-Zinn's standard formulation ('paying attention in a particular way: on purpose, in the present moment, and non-judgmentally,' Full Catastrophe Living, 1990 / Wherever You Go, There You Are, 1994), which is consistent with a co-authored restatement rather than a fabrication. Holding below 0.80 because the wording is unverified.

text: Each difficult moment has the potential to open my eyes and open my heart.
text_raw: Each difficult moment has the potential to open my eyes and open my heart.
author: Myla Kabat-Zinn

provenance.notes: Attributed to Myla Kabat-Zinn, most likely drawn from Everyday Blessings (1997), the book she co-wrote with Jon Kabat-Zinn, where she writes in her own voice in places. I cannot confirm the line appears there or anywhere else I can name. Myla Kabat-Zinn has a thin independent publication record, which makes the quote hard to source and easy to misassign between the two authors. Honest verdict: unverified.

text: Contentment is true wealth.
text_raw: Contentment is true wealth.
author: Nagarjuna

provenance.notes: The canonical form of this saying is Buddhist scripture, not Nagarjuna: Dhammapada 204, 'santuṭṭhī paramaṃ dhanaṃ' — 'contentment is the greatest wealth.' Nagarjuna does echo it in the Suhṛllekha (Letter to a Friend), where he cites the Buddha to the effect that contentment is the supreme form of wealth, so the ascription is not baseless — but it makes Nagarjuna a transmitter rather than the author, and this four-word English form matches the Dhammapada rendering, not a specific Suhṛllekha translation I can name. Attribution as it stands is weak. | Suggested reattribution: Dhammapada 204 (attributed to the Buddha); Nagarjuna restates it in the Suhṛllekha, quoting the Buddha

text: Great design is a multi-layered relationship between human life and its environment.
text_raw: Great design is a multi-layered relationship between human life and its environment.
author: Naoto Fukasawa

provenance.notes: Naoto Fukasawa is a real and well-documented Japanese industrial designer (MUJI, ±0, Naoto Fukasawa Design), and the sentiment matches his stated 'without thought' philosophy of design as embedded in everyday behavior and environment. The line circulates in design-quote collections, most plausibly extracted from an interview or from his Phaidon monograph (2007). I cannot place it in a specific text or interview, and designer quotes of this kind are frequently paraphrased in circulation.

text: It is in quiet that our best ideas occur to us. Don't make the mistake of believing that by a frantic kind of dashing around you are being your most effective and efficient self. Don't assume that you are wasting time when you take time out for thought.
text_raw: It is in quiet that our best ideas occur to us. Don't make the mistake of believing that by a frantic kind of dashing around you are being your most effective and efficient self. Don't assume that you are wasting time when you take time out for thought.
author: Napoleon Hill & W. Clement Stone
