The artists is first of all required to remove himself from human to celestial levels of appreciation; at this level and in a state of unification, no longer having in view anything external to himself, he sees and realizes, that is to say becomes, what he is afterwards to represent…”
author: Rama Choomarasawmy

provenance.notes: 'Rama Choomarasawmy' is not a real person — it is a phonetic corruption of Ananda K. Coomaraswamy (1877-1947), the Ceylonese-British metaphysician and art historian. The passage is characteristic Coomaraswamy, from his writing on traditional art and the artist's identification with the form contemplated; my recollection points toward The Transformation of Nature in Art (1934) or Christian and Oriental Philosophy of Art (1943), but I cannot fix the book, so no print source is recorded. Confidence in the author correction is high (~0.85); confidence in the recorded name as given is near zero. Note also 'The artists is' in the corpus text is a typo for 'The artist is'. | Suggested reattribution: Ananda K. Coomaraswamy

text: The fabled musk deer searches the world over for the source of the scent which comes from itself.
text_raw: The fabled musk deer searches the world over for the source of the scent which comes from itself.
author: Ramakrishna

provenance.notes: The musk-deer parable — the deer roaming in search of a fragrance emanating from its own navel — is a genuine and very old motif in Indian devotional literature, used by Kabir, by Ramakrishna, and in later Vedanta teaching. Ramakrishna did employ it, so the attribution is not baseless, but this compressed English sentence is an anthologist's paraphrase rather than a line from The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna as far as I can tell. The image is effectively traditional and predates any single speaker.

text: From silence came the ego, from the ego came thought, and from thought came speech. If speech is effective, how much more effective must be its source!
text_raw: From silence came the ego, from the ego came thought, and from thought came speech. If speech is effective, how much more effective must be its source!
author: Ramana Maharshi

provenance.notes: Consistent with Ramana Maharshi's recorded teaching on silence as the highest and most potent form of instruction, and I associate this passage with Talks with Sri Ramana Maharshi (Munagala Venkataramiah's transcripts) or Maharshi's Gospel. The usual ordering in his teaching runs silence to ego to thought to speech, matching this text. I cannot cite a specific talk number, so no print source is recorded.

text: If you are seeking creative ideas, go out walking. Angels whisper to a man when he goes for a walk.
text_raw: "If you are seeking creative ideas, go out walking. Angels whisper to a man when he goes for a walk."
author: Raymond Inmon

provenance.notes: 'Raymond Inmon' appears in my knowledge only as a name attached to this one sentence in motivational quote collections — no biography, no book, no other work, no dates. That pattern usually indicates either a private individual quoted once in a newsletter or a name that accreted to an orphan line. The quote itself is real and widely circulated; the attribution is untraceable. Honest answer here is that I do not know who said it.

text: Success is not the result of spontaneous combustion. You must set yourself on fire.
text_raw: Success is not the result of spontaneous combustion. You must set yourself on fire.
author: Reggie Leach

provenance.notes: Reggie Leach is a real person — NHL winger, 'the Riverton Rifle,' Philadelphia Flyers — and this line is attributed to him with near-total consistency across motivational anthologies, which is mild evidence. But I know of no interview, book, or speech where it originates, and no date. Sports one-liners of this kind are commonly attached to whichever athlete an anthologist had to hand. Plausible but unverified.

text: Spirit has placed a dream in your heart for a better world, starting with your family, extending to your work, community, country and stretching beyond your nation. Speak your truth and inspire others, for you are meant to make a significant and sizable difference.
text_raw: Spirit has placed a dream in your heart for a better world, starting with your family, extending to your work, community, country and stretching beyond your nation. Speak your truth and inspire others, for you are meant to make a significant and sizable difference.
author: Rev. Mary Manin Morrissey

provenance.notes: Mary Manin Morrissey is a real New Thought/Unity minister and author (Building Your Field of Dreams, 1996) and the language here — 'Spirit has placed a dream in your heart' — matches her register exactly, so the attribution is plausible. But it reads like newsletter or spoken-message material rather than a passage from a specific book, and I cannot locate it. No source recorded.

text: "You've got to pray like it's all up to God, and work like it's all up to you."
text_raw: "You've got to pray like it's all up to God, and work like it's all up to you."
author: Reverend Cecil Williams

provenance.notes: Cecil Williams of Glide Memorial in San Francisco may well have said this from the pulpit, but he did not originate it. The aphorism is centuries older and circulates in two mirrored forms: 'Pray as though everything depended on God, work as though everything depended on you,' commonly credited to Ignatius of Loyola and also to Augustine of Hippo. Scholarship on the Ignatian version (Joseph de Guibert and others) notes the two halves get swapped between retellings, which is itself evidence of a long oral history. Treat this as a traditional Christian saying quoted by Williams, not authored by him. | Suggested reattribution: Traditional Christian aphorism, commonly attributed to Ignatius of Loyola

text: Start with a style and you are in chains, start with an idea and you are free.
text_raw: Start with a style and you are in chains, start with an idea and you are free.
author: Richard Avedon

provenance.notes: Widely quoted under Richard Avedon's name in design and photography collections, and the sentiment fits a working photographer's outlook. I cannot place it in an Avedon interview, essay, or monograph, and I have some recollection of near-identical 'style is chains, ideas are freedom' formulations circulating under other designers' names, which weakens confidence. Attribution plausible but unsupported.

text: Sooner or later, those who win are those who think they can.
text_raw: Sooner or later, those who win are those who think they can.
author: Richard Bach

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Richard Bach and consonant with the Messiah's Handbook aphorisms in Illusions (1977), which is my best guess for the source. I am noticeably less confident than for the caterpillar line — I cannot confirm the book, and the sentiment is generic enough that it could belong to the broader 'those who think they can' tradition running back to Virgil's 'possunt quia posse videntur.' No print source recorded.

text: Reflection is one of the most underused yet powerful tools for success.
text_raw: Reflection is one of the most underused yet powerful tools for success.
author: Richard Carlson

provenance.notes: Richard Carlson is a real author (Don't Sweat the Small Stuff, 1997, and its many sequels) and this sentence is consistent with his advice register, but it is generic enough that it could come from almost any business or self-help writer. I cannot place it in a specific title or chapter. Plausible attribution, no evidence.

text: If I had to select one quality, one personal characteristic that I regard as being most highly correlated with success, whatever the field, I would pick the trait of persistence. Determination. The will to endure to the end, to get knocked down seventy times and get up off the floor saying, ‘Here comes number seventy-one.’
text_raw: If I had to select one quality, one personal characteristic that I regard as being most highly correlated with success, whatever the field, I would pick the trait of persistence. Determination. The will to endure to the end, to get knocked down seventy times and get up off the floor saying, ‘Here comes number seventy-one.’
author: Richard M DeVos

provenance.notes: Attributed with good consistency to Richard M. DeVos, Amway co-founder, and the 'Here comes number seventy-one' formulation is distinctive enough that it is unlikely to have drifted from another speaker. It matches the content of his motivational speaking and his book Believe! (1975), which is my best guess for the source, but I cannot confirm the book or a speech date, so no print source is recorded. Note the corpus name should probably be punctuated 'Richard M. DeVos'.

text: One of the saddest lines in the world is, 'Oh come now - be realistic.' The best parts of this world were not fashioned by those who were realistic. They were fashioned by those who dared to look hard at their wishes and gave them horses to ride.
text_raw: One of the saddest lines in the world is, 'Oh come now - be realistic.' The best parts of this world were not fashioned by those who were realistic. They were fashioned by those who dared to look hard at their wishes and gave them horses to ride.
author: Richard Nelson Bolles

provenance.notes: Attributed to Richard Nelson Bolles, author of What Color Is Your Parachute?, and it strongly matches his voice and his argument against 'realistic' career advice; my recollection is that it appears in the book, whose editions run annually from 1970, but I cannot pin an edition or page and will not guess a year. The closing image, 'gave them horses to ride,' echoes the old proverb 'if wishes were horses, beggars would ride,' which Bolles was plausibly inverting deliberately. Attribution stable, primary source unconfirmed.

text: Excellence in art is, ultimately, a function of wholeness as a human being.
text_raw: Excellence in art is, ultimately, a function of wholeness as a human being.
author: Richard Schechner

provenance.notes: Richard Schechner is a real and well-documented performance studies theorist (Environmental Theater, Performance Theory, Between Theater and Anthropology), but I cannot place this specific sentence in any of his writings. The register is more aphoristic than Schechner's usual analytic prose, which makes me mildly suspicious that it entered quote collections secondhand. No source located; not fabricating one.

text: When I say that ‘I love,’ it is not I who love, but in reality Love who acts through me. Love is not so much something I do as something that I am. Love is not a doing but a state of being - a relatedness, a connectedness to another mortal, an identification with her or him that simply flows within me and through me, independent of my intentions or my efforts.
text_raw: When I say that ‘I love,’ it is not I who love, but in reality Love who acts through me. Love is not so much something I do as something that I am. Love is not a doing but a state of being - a relatedness, a connectedness to another mortal, an identification with her or him that simply flows within me and through me, independent of my intentions or my efforts.
author: Robert A. Johnson

provenance.notes: Consistent in voice and content with Robert A. Johnson's Jungian writing on love, most plausibly 'We: Understanding the Psychology of Romantic Love' (1983), which argues precisely this distinction between love as a doing and love as a state of being. I have a genuine but not firm recollection of the passage from that book, and cannot confirm chapter or page, so I am leaving the print source null rather than asserting a citation I cannot stand behind. Attribution to Johnson itself is plausible and consistently reported.

text: There is no such thing as security. There are only varying degrees of risk.
text_raw: There is no such thing as security. There are only varying degrees of risk.
author: Robert Allen

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Robert G. Allen, the real-estate and 'Multiple Streams of Income' author, across business quote collections. The sentiment matches his investing rhetoric. However, every occurrence I know of is a quote-collection citation with no book or page, so this is secondary evidence only. Note the ambiguity of the bare name 'Robert Allen' — the corpus should probably disambiguate to Robert G. Allen.

text: Every rejection is valuable to those who persist.
text_raw: Every rejection is valuable to those who persist.
author: Robert Allen

provenance.notes: I cannot place this line in Robert G. Allen's published work. It circulates in motivational-quote lists with the bare name 'Robert Allen' attached. Generic enough in phrasing that it could belong to any number of sales/persistence writers. No traceable source; honest answer is that I do not know.

text: Herb True once said, “What people don’t realize is that successful people often have more failures than failures do. But they keep going.” You don’t drown by falling in the water. You drown by staying there.
text_raw: Herb True once said, “What people don’t realize is that successful people often have more failures than failures do. But they keep going.” You don’t drown by falling in the water. You drown by staying there.
author: Robert Allen

provenance.notes: This is a composite passage, not a single quote, and that matters. The inner quotation is credited in the text itself to Herb True (the Notre Dame marketing professor), and the 'more failures than failures do' line is indeed the one commonly attributed to him. The closing 'You don't drown by falling in the water. You drown by staying there' is widely attributed elsewhere to Edwin Louis Cole. The framing prose is plausibly Robert G. Allen quoting both, likely in one of his books, but I cannot confirm which. Recommend the corpus either drop this entry or split it, since attributing the whole block to Allen misrepresents two embedded attributions.

text: Our aspirations are our possibilities.
text_raw: Our aspirations are our possibilities.
author: Robert Browning

provenance.notes: Widely attributed to Robert Browning in nineteenth- and twentieth-century quote anthologies, but I cannot locate it in any specific poem or letter of his, and Browning's actual verse rarely reduces to a clean epigram like this. The same line also circulates attributed to Samuel Johnson in some collections, which is a classic signature of an unsourced anthology quote drifting between famous names. Attribution unresolved.

text: Progress is a nice word, but change is its motivator and change has enemies.
text_raw: Progress is a nice word, but change is its motivator and change has enemies.
author: Robert F. Kennedy

provenance.notes: I recall this line, usually punctuated as three sentences ('Progress is a nice word. But change is its motivator. And change has its enemies.'), from Robert F. Kennedy's Day of Affirmation Address at the University of Cape Town, 6 June 1966 — the same speech as the 'ripple of hope' passage. The attribution to RFK is consistent and I consider it sound. I am withholding the speech as a formal print source because I cannot confirm the exact verbatim placement from memory, which is the difference between 'attributed' and 'verified' here.

text: “For all my good intentions, there are days when things go wrong or I fall into old habits. When things are not going well, when I'm grumpy or mad, I'll realize that I've not been paying attention to my soul and I've not been following my best routine.”
text_raw: “For all my good intentions, there are days when things go wrong or I fall into old habits. When things are not going well, when I'm grumpy or mad, I'll realize that I've not been paying attention to my soul and I've not been following my best routine.”
author: Robert Fulghum

provenance.notes: The plainspoken, self-deprecating voice is very much Robert Fulghum's, and the content fits his essay collections (All I Really Need to Know I Learned in Kindergarten, From Beginning to End, Words I Wish I Wrote). But I cannot place the passage in a specific book, and it reads like it may come from an interview rather than a book. Plausible but unsourced.

text: Impossible situations can become possible miracles.
text_raw: Impossible situations can become possible miracles.
author: Robert H. Schuller

provenance.notes: Squarely in the idiom of Robert H. Schuller's 'possibility thinking' and consistently attributed to him in inspirational collections; the sentence is essentially a compressed statement of his central theme (cf. 'Tough Times Never Last, But Tough People Do!'). No specific book, sermon, or Hour of Power broadcast identified, so this rests on secondary evidence only.

text: Design creates culture. Culture shapes values. Values determine the future.
text_raw: Design creates culture. Culture shapes values. Values determine the future.
author: Robert L. Peters

provenance.notes: Robert L. Peters is a real Canadian graphic designer and past president of Icograda, and this three-clause line is his best-known statement — it is quoted consistently under his name throughout design literature and conference material, and he has spoken about it publicly as his own. I have no single originating publication or talk to cite, so it stays at 'attributed' rather than 'verified,' but the attribution itself is unusually stable for a design aphorism.

text: Saints are sinners who kept going.
text_raw: Saints are sinners who kept going.
author: Robert Louis Stevenson

provenance.notes: Very widely attributed to Robert Louis Stevenson (usually as 'Saints are sinners who kept on going'), but I cannot locate it in any of his essays, novels, letters, or prayers. Its circulation pattern — heavy in devotional and recovery literature, absent from Stevenson scholarship — is characteristic of an unsourced attribution attached to a famous literary name. I do not know a true origin, so I am not proposing a reattribution, but the Stevenson claim should be treated as doubtful.

text: Be master of your petty annoyances and conserve your energies for the big, worthwhile things. It isn't the mountain ahead that wears you out - it's the grain of sand in your shoe.
text_raw: Be master of your petty annoyances and conserve your energies for the big, worthwhile things. It isn't the mountain ahead that wears you out - it's the grain of sand in your shoe.
author: Robert Service

provenance.notes: The 'grain of sand in your shoe' image is attributed to the Yukon poet Robert W. Service in many quote collections, but I cannot find it in his verse or his memoirs, and the surrounding sentence ('Be master of your petty annoyances...') reads like self-help prose rather than Service. A near-identical formulation is widely credited to Muhammad Ali ('It isn't the mountains ahead to climb that wear you out; it's the pebble in your shoe'), which suggests a floating aphorism rather than a fixed authorship. Origin genuinely unclear; not proposing Ali either, since his version is also unsourced.

text: In our deepest moments of struggle, frustration, fear, and confusion, we are being called upon to reach in and touch our hearts. Then, we will know what to do, what to say, how to be. What is right is always in our deepest heart of hearts. It is from the deepest part of our hearts that we are capable of reaching out and touching another human being. It is, after all, one heart touching another heart.
text_raw: "In our deepest moments of struggle, frustration, fear, and confusion, we are being called upon to reach in and touch our hearts. Then, we will know what to do, what to say, how to be. What is right is always in our deepest heart of hearts. It is from the deepest part of our hearts that we are capable of reaching out and touching another human being. It is, after all, one heart touching another heart."
author: Roberta Sage Hamilton

provenance.notes: I have no knowledge of Roberta Sage Hamilton as a writer and can find no work of hers in my training. The passage appears to live entirely inside inspirational quote collections and greeting-card style compilations. The name may be real but obscure, or may itself be a corruption. No verification possible; this is an honest 'I do not know.'

text: The greatest crime in the world is not developing your potential. When you do what you do best, you are helping not only yourself, but the world.
text_raw: The greatest crime in the world is not developing your potential. When you do what you do best, you are helping not only yourself, but the world.
author: Roger Williams

provenance.notes: 'Roger Williams' is ambiguous and none of the candidates resolve it. The seventeenth-century founder of Rhode Island would not have written in this idiom of self-actualization; the biochemist Roger J. Williams and the pianist Roger Williams are both possible but I have no evidence for either. The vocabulary ('developing your potential') places the line in twentieth-century human-potential writing. Untraceable as given.

text: Be at peace with yourself. If you are not at peace with yourself, you are at peace with nothing.
text_raw: Be at peace with yourself. If you are not at peace with yourself, you are at peace with nothing.
author: Ron Rathbun

provenance.notes: Ron Rathbun is a real author — 'The Way Is Within: A Spiritual Journey' (1995) and related meditation writing — and this line is attributed to him with reasonable consistency in quote collections. I cannot confirm it against the book itself, and the sentiment is generic enough to have multiple independent origins. Plausible but unverified.

text: What you find in your mind is what you put there. Put good things in there.
text_raw: What you find in your mind is what you put there. Put good things in there.
author: Ron Rathbun

provenance.notes: Same author and same situation as the preceding entry: consistently attributed to Ron Rathbun in quote compilations, consistent with the plain instructional voice of 'The Way Is Within,' but with no source I can confirm. Weak evidence.

text: The world we are experiencing today is the result of our collective consciousness, and if we want a new world, each of us must start taking responsibility for helping create it.
text_raw: The world we are experiencing today is the result of our collective consciousness, and if we want a new world, each of us must start taking responsibility for helping create it.
author: Rosemary Fillmore Rhea

provenance.notes: Rosemary Fillmore Rhea is a real figure — granddaughter of Unity's founders Charles and Myrtle Fillmore, and a Unity broadcaster and author — and the New Thought vocabulary of 'collective consciousness' fits Unity writing closely. But I cannot place this sentence in any of her books or broadcasts. Attribution plausible on stylistic grounds only.

text: The golden age, which blind superstition situated behind or ahead of us is in us.
text_raw: The golden age, which blind superstition situated behind or ahead of us is in us.
author: Rousseau

provenance.notes: Attributed to Rousseau in quote collections, but I cannot locate it in the Discourses, Émile, the Social Contract, or the Reveries. Two warning signs: the English is awkward in the way that anthology-chain translations tend to be (the missing comma before 'is in us' is present in most circulating copies, indicating they all descend from one source), and the bare author name 'Rousseau' with no first name is typical of unsourced compilation entries. The sentiment is broadly Rousseauian, which is exactly what makes a misattribution easy. I do not know the true origin.

text: What bread looks like depends on whether you’re hungry or not.
text_raw: What bread looks like depends on whether you’re hungry or not.
author: Rumi

provenance.notes: Rumi is one of the strongest misattribution magnets in circulation, and the English Rumi corpus is dominated by Coleman Barks's loose renderings, which are not translations and often have no close counterpart in the Persian. I cannot match this line to any passage of the Masnavi or the Divan-e Shams that I know. The bread-and-hunger image is genuinely Rumi-adjacent in theme, which is not evidence. Treat as unverified pending a check against a scholarly translation (Nicholson or Arberry) with a book-and-line reference.

text: Let the beauty you love be what you do.
text_raw: Let the beauty you love be what you do.
author: Rumi

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
provenance.notes: From the Barks rendering beginning 'Today, like every other day, we wake up empty and frightened... Take down a musical instrument. Let the beauty we love be what we do. There are hundreds of ways to kneel and kiss the ground.' The corpus text alters 'we love' to 'you love', a common web variant. Barks worked from earlier English translations rather than the Persian, so the English wording is his; the underlying poem is genuinely Rumi's. Cannot place the Persian original (Divan-e Shams ghazal) from memory.

text: I have lived on the lip of insanity, wanting to know reasons, knocking on a door. It opens. I've been knocking from the inside!
text_raw: "I have lived on the lip of insanity, wanting to know reasons, knocking on a door. It opens. I've been knocking from the inside!"
author: Rumi

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
provenance.notes: A Barks rendering of a Rumi quatrain; I recall it in The Essential Rumi with consistent attribution across reputable Rumi collections. Wording is Barks' English, not a literal translation. No Persian source located from memory.

text: To grasp God’s beauty, you must become God.
text_raw: To grasp God’s beauty, you must become God.
author: Rumi

provenance.notes: I cannot place this line in any Rumi translation I know — not Barks, Nicholson, Arberry, or Helminski. The theological compression ('you must become God') is unlike the standard renderings, which speak of annihilation in the Beloved rather than becoming God. Possibly a loose paraphrase of a fana passage, possibly a modern invention. Honest answer: unknown.

text: A grain of sand left its father. Its father was a boulder. Only then was it introduced to an oyster, and became a pearl.
text_raw: A grain of sand left its father. Its father was a boulder. Only then was it introduced to an oyster, and became a pearl.
author: Rumi

provenance.notes: Cannot place this in any Rumi translation. The grain-of-sand-becomes-pearl motif is a stock modern inspirational image; the flat declarative diction here matches none of the standard English Rumi translators. Circulates on quote sites without any cited source. Likely a modern composition attached to Rumi's name, but I have no evidence of a true author.

text: Don’t be like the rider who gallops all night and never sees the horse that is beneath him.
text_raw: Don’t be like the rider who gallops all night and never sees the horse that is beneath him.
author: Rumi

provenance.notes: Rumi does use the rider-who-cannot-see-his-own-mount figure (the Mathnawi has teaching stories about a man searching for the animal he is riding), so the image is authentically Rumi's. But I cannot place this exact English sentence in any translation, and it reads like a paraphrase rather than a rendering. Image plausible, wording unverified.

text: The minute I heard my first love story, I started looking for you, not knowing how blind that was. Lovers don't finally meet somewhere. They're in each other all along.
text_raw: "The minute I heard my first love story, I started looking for you, not knowing how blind that was. Lovers don't finally meet somewhere. They're in each other all along."
author: Rumi

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
provenance.notes: A well-known Barks rendering of a Rumi quatrain, appearing in The Essential Rumi. Attribution to Rumi is consistent across reputable collections; the English phrasing ('Lovers don't finally meet somewhere. They're in each other all along.') is Barks'. Persian original not identified from memory.

text: The soul is here for its own joy.
text_raw: The soul is here for its own joy.
author: Rumi

provenance.notes: I recall this short line from Coleman Barks' Rumi versions and believe it appears in The Essential Rumi, but I am not confident enough in the specific volume to cite it as a print source. Attribution to Rumi (via Barks) is consistent in the sources I know; the underlying Persian is not identified.

text: Your task is not to seek for love, but merely to seek and find all the barriers within yourself that you have built against it.
text_raw: Your task is not to seek for love, but merely to seek and find all the barriers within yourself that you have built against it.
author: Rumi

provenance.notes: One of the most heavily circulated 'Rumi' lines on the internet and one of the most doubted. I cannot place it in Barks, Nicholson, Arberry, Helminski, or any other translation, and its vocabulary ('your task', 'barriers within yourself') is modern therapeutic English rather than Sufi poetics — it reads closer to twentieth-century self-help or A Course in Miracles-adjacent writing than to a thirteenth-century ghazal. I suspect it is not Rumi, but I cannot name a true author, so I am not asserting a reattribution.

text: Your body is woven from the light of heaven.
text_raw: Your body is woven from the light of heaven.
author: Rumi

provenance.notes: I have a weak recollection of this line in a Barks-style Rumi rendering (sometimes quoted with a following sentence about the body's purity), but I cannot confirm the volume or the Persian original. The imagery is consistent with Rumi's treatment of the body as woven of light. Attribution plausible, evidence thin.

text: The wound is the place where the Light enters you.
text_raw: The wound is the place where the Light enters you.
author: Rumi

provenance.notes: Among the most quoted Rumi lines in English, and consistently attributed to him via Coleman Barks' versions. However, Rumi scholars (Omid Safi among them) have noted that Barks' most famous lines often have no close Persian counterpart, and I cannot point to the ghazal or Mathnawi passage behind this one. Attribution is consistent but the sourcing chain stops at a modern English rendering, so I am not putting it above the promotion bar.

text: Every soul becomes gold when touched by the Beloved.
text_raw: Every soul becomes gold when touched by the Beloved.
author: Rumi

provenance.notes: Cannot place this line. Alchemical gold imagery is genuinely Rumi's territory (the Beloved as the philosopher's stone that transmutes copper to gold), but this specific one-sentence formulation appears only on quote aggregators with no source. Unknown.

text: Dance, when you’re broken open. Dance, if you’ve torn the bandage off. Dance in the middle of the fighting. Dance in your blood. Dance when you’re perfectly free.
text_raw: Dance, when you’re broken open. Dance, if you’ve torn the bandage off. Dance in the middle of the fighting. Dance in your blood. Dance when you’re perfectly free.
author: Rumi

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Essential Rumi, trans. Coleman Barks, 1995
provenance.notes: A recognized Coleman Barks rendering ('Dance, when you're broken open...'), appearing in The Essential Rumi and widely reprinted with consistent attribution to Rumi. English wording is Barks'; Persian original not identified from memory.

text: The pain is equal to the attachment.
text_raw: "The pain is equal to the attachment."
author: Sabrina Ward Harrison

provenance.notes: Sabrina Ward Harrison is a real author-artist (Spilling Open: The Art of Becoming Yourself, 1999; Brave on the Rocks, 2000), and this aphorism's register fits her handwritten-journal books. But I cannot place the line in a specific title, and the thought is a commonplace of Buddhist-inflected popular writing, so it could easily have drifted onto her name. Unconfirmed.

text: The key to immortality is first living a life worth remembering.
text_raw: The key to immortality is first living a life worth remembering.
author: Saint Augustine

provenance.notes: This does not read as Augustine in any register — not the Confessions, not the City of God, not the sermons — and 'a life worth remembering' as a route to 'immortality' inverts Augustine's actual theology, where immortality is God's gift and earthly fame is explicitly disparaged. The line circulates far more commonly attributed to Bruce Lee, in the sayings collected from his notebooks and popularized posthumously; that attribution is itself unverified, so I am flagging the Augustine attribution as wrong without asserting Lee as confirmed. | Suggested reattribution: Widely circulated as Bruce Lee (that attribution is itself unverified); not Augustine

text: Have no fear of perfection—you’ll never reach it.
text_raw: Have no fear of perfection—you’ll never reach it.
author: Salvador Dali

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Salvador Dali across quotation dictionaries and Dali literature, and the sentiment matches his public persona of grandiose self-deprecation. I cannot name the interview, book, or date of first appearance, so the sourcing chain is secondary only. Attribution steady, primary source not established.

text: Every submission to our fear enlarges its domain.
text_raw: Every submission to our fear enlarges its domain.
author: Samuel Johnson

provenance.notes: Johnson wrote at length on fear in The Rambler (No. 126 contains the well-known 'Fear is implanted in us as a preservative from evil; but its duty, like that of other passions, is not to overbear reason, but to assist it'), and this sentence is stylistically compatible with that essay. But the crisp epigrammatic form suggests a later condensation of Johnson's prose rather than his own sentence, and I cannot confirm the exact wording in any Rambler or Idler number. Plausible but unconfirmed; deliberately not citing a number I cannot verify.

text: It doesn't much signify whom one marries, for one is sure to find out the next morning that it was someone else.
text_raw: It doesn't much signify whom one marries, for one is sure to find out the next morning that it was someone else.
author: Samuel Rogers

provenance.earliest_print_source: Recollections of the Table-Talk of Samuel Rogers, Alexander Dyce, 1856
provenance.notes: A stock Regency epigram consistently credited to the poet and celebrated conversationalist Samuel Rogers (1763-1855), whose remarks survive chiefly through Dyce's posthumous Table-Talk. Quotation dictionaries routinely source Rogers quips to that volume and I believe this is one of them, but I cannot confirm the page or that this specific quip appears there rather than in another memoir of Rogers, so treat the citation as probable rather than checked.

text: The angry man will defeat himself in battle as well as in life.
text_raw: The angry man will defeat himself in battle as well as in life.
author: Samurai maxim

provenance.notes: Attributed only to an anonymous collective ('Samurai maxim'), which is not an attribution at all. I cannot trace it to Hagakure, the Book of Five Rings, Budoshoshinshu, or any classical bushido text, and the English is modern. Most 'samurai maxims' in circulation are twentieth-century Western compositions. Origin unknown.

text: View money and things not as something you create to fill a lack, but as tools to help you more fully express yourself and realize your potential.
text_raw: View money and things not as something you create to fill a lack, but as tools to help you more fully express yourself and realize your potential.
author: Sanaya Roman & Duane Pack

provenance.notes: Sanaya Roman and Duane Packer are real co-authors whose Creating Money: Keys to Abundance (1988) covers exactly this material, so the pairing of quote to authors is plausible. I cannot confirm this sentence appears in that book or in another of their titles. Also note the author field misspells the second name as 'Duane Pack' (should be Duane Packer) and so does not match q_1248's spelling.

text: Don’t discard your fantasies as merely wishful thinking. Honor them as messages from the deepest part of your being about what you can do and directions you can choose.
text_raw: Don’t discard your fantasies as merely wishful thinking. Honor them as messages from the deepest part of your being about what you can do and directions you can choose.
author: Sanaya Roman & Duane Packer

provenance.notes: Consistent in content and voice with the Roman/Packer Earth Life Series (Creating Money, Living with Joy, Spiritual Growth), but I cannot place the sentence in a specific volume or year. Real authors, plausible attribution, no confirmable source.

text: "All of your self-honoring choices will tend to promote your sense of dignity, personal and authentic power, and sense of balance. Sometimes the most self-honoring choices don't come easy and don't feel good at all; They may feel risky, difficult and uncertain. Other times the most self-honoring choices will feel completely natural to you -- they'll feel exhilarating, giving you a sense of liberation and joyous self-actualization."
text_raw: "All of your self-honoring choices will tend to promote your sense of dignity, personal and authentic power, and sense of balance. Sometimes the most self-honoring choices don't come easy and don't feel good at all; They may feel risky, difficult and uncertain. Other times the most self-honoring choices will feel completely natural to you -- they'll feel exhilarating, giving you a sense of liberation and joyous self-actualization."
author: Sandra Anne Taylor

provenance.notes: Sandra Anne Taylor is a real author (Quantum Success, Secrets of Attraction, Truth, Triumph and Transformation) and the vocabulary of 'self-honoring choices' and 'authentic power' fits that genre and era. I cannot locate this passage in any specific title of hers. Unconfirmed. The corpus text also retains stray enclosing quotation marks and an anomalous capital after a semicolon.

text: Sincere forgiveness isn't colored with expectations that the other person apologize or change. Don't worry whether or not they finally understand you. Love them and release them. Life feeds back truth to people in its own way and time...
text_raw: Sincere forgiveness isn't colored with expectations that the other person apologize or change. Don't worry whether or not they finally understand you. Love them and release them. Life feeds back truth to people in its own way and time...
author: Sara Paddison

provenance.notes: Widely circulated with consistent attribution to Sara Paddison, and usually to her book The Hidden Power of the Heart (Planetary Publications / HeartMath, 1992), which is a real title on exactly this subject. I have not confirmed the page or verified the excerpt against the text, so I am recording the attribution as consistent secondary evidence rather than citing the book as a checked source. The trailing ellipsis indicates the passage is truncated.

text: When you have compassion and surrender to your own heart, you are surrendering to the hidden power in your heart, God. You are surrendering to love, because God is Love, the cohesive force of the universe that connects us all. Surrender is not just a religious concept; it's a power tool for listening to the voice of your spirit and following its directions. When you surrender your head to your heart, you allow your heart to give you a wider, higher intelligence perspective. Remember the phrase, ‘The real teacher is within you.’ Very simply, that teacher is to be found in the common sense of your own heart.
text_raw: "When you have compassion and surrender to your own heart, you are surrendering to the hidden power in your heart, God. You are surrendering to love, because God is Love, the cohesive force of the universe that connects us all. Surrender is not just a religious concept; it's a power tool for listening to the voice of your spirit and following its directions. When you surrender your head to your heart, you allow your heart to give you a wider, higher intelligence perspective. Remember the phrase, ‘The real teacher is within you.’ Very simply, that teacher is to be found in the common sense of your own heart."
author: Sara Paddison

provenance.notes: Same author and same idiom as q_1250 — the heart-intelligence language ('surrender your head to your heart', 'the real teacher is within you') is characteristic HeartMath-school writing and consistent with Sara Paddison's The Hidden Power of the Heart (1992). But this longer passage is less commonly quoted than q_1250 and I cannot place it in a specific chapter or confirm it is not stitched together from separate paragraphs. Plausible, unconfirmed.

text: We can no longer afford to throw away even one ‘unimportant’ day by not noticing the wonder of it all. We have to be willing to discover and then appreciate the authentic moments of happiness available to all of us every day.
text_raw: We can no longer afford to throw away even one ‘unimportant’ day by not noticing the wonder of it all. We have to be willing to discover and then appreciate the authentic moments of happiness available to all of us every day.
author: Sarah Ban Breathnach

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Sarah Ban Breathnach and entirely consistent with her vocabulary in the Simple Abundance books ('authentic', noticing ordinary days). I believe it comes from Simple Abundance: A Daybook of Comfort and Joy (1995) or a companion volume, but I cannot place the specific entry or page from memory, so I am not asserting that citation. Attribution to Breathnach is plausible and uncontested; the sourcing is not established.

text: Life begets life. Energy creates energy. It is by spending oneself that one becomes rich.
text_raw: Life begets life. Energy creates energy. It is by spending oneself that one becomes rich.
author: Sarah Bernhardt

provenance.notes: Very widely and consistently attributed to Sarah Bernhardt in twentieth-century quotation anthologies, but in my recollection it circulates without a source citation — it is the kind of line that appears in quote dictionaries with only a name attached. Bernhardt did publish a memoir (Ma Double Vie / Memories of My Life, 1907), and the line would not be out of character, but I cannot confirm it appears there. Honest verdict: plausible, unsourced.

text: Man loves because he is love. He seeks joy, for he is joy. He thirsts for God for he is composed of God and he cannot exist without God.
text_raw: Man loves because he is love. He seeks joy, for he is joy. He thirsts for God for he is composed of God and he cannot exist without God.
author: Sathya Sai Baba

provenance.notes: Circulates widely in Sathya Sai Baba devotional literature and is stylistically characteristic of his discourses. His discourses were transcribed at length in the Sathya Sai Speaks series, so a genuine origin is plausible, but I cannot identify the specific discourse, date, or volume, and Sai Baba material is heavily paraphrased and re-edited in secondary circulation. No citation asserted.

text: Design is thinking made visible.
text_raw: Design is thinking made visible.
author: Saul Bass

provenance.notes: Ubiquitous on design quote lists under Saul Bass, but I know of no documented primary source — no interview, lecture, or published essay of his that I can point to containing this sentence. Design aphorisms attach themselves to famous designers (Bass, Rand, Eames) the way general aphorisms attach to Einstein, so the popularity of the pairing is not evidence. Cannot confirm or reattribute.

text: It is well known that the longer one postpones a pleasure, the greater the pleasure is when one finally gets it. Therefore, if one postpones it forever, the pleasure should be infinite.
text_raw: It is well known that the longer one postpones a pleasure, the greater the pleasure is when one finally gets it. Therefore, if one postpones it forever, the pleasure should be infinite.
author: Saul Gorn

provenance.notes: Saul Gorn was a real computer scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, known in hacker folklore for 'Saul Gorn's Compendium of Rarely Used Clichés.' This line reaches modern circulation almost entirely through the Unix fortune-cookie database, which is a weak provenance chain — fortune files carry many attributions that were never checked. I cannot place the line in anything Gorn actually published. Plausible but essentially unsourced.

text: I am a firm believer in optimism because without optimism, what else is there?
text_raw: I am a firm believer in optimism because without optimism, what else is there?
author: Saul Gorn

provenance.notes: Same fortune-file provenance problem as q_1256, and weaker: this is a generic optimism line with nothing distinctive tying it to Saul Gorn. I have no independent knowledge of Gorn saying or writing it, and I have a vague sense the sentence also circulates under other names, though I cannot confirm which and will not guess. Attribution should be treated as unsupported.

text: Step aside from all thinking, and there is nowhere you can’t go.
text_raw: Step aside from all thinking, and there is nowhere you can’t go.
author: Seng T'san, Third Zen Patriarch

provenance.notes: Almost certainly a translation of the Hsin Hsin Ming line more commonly rendered 'Stop talking and thinking, and there is nothing you will not be able to know' (Suzuki/Conze) — the sense and position in the poem match. But I cannot identify which translation produces this exact English, and 'step aside from all thinking' is loose enough that it may be a popular paraphrase rather than a published rendering. Source text is confident; this specific wording is not, so I am holding below the verified bar.

text: The death of fear is in doing what you fear to do.
text_raw: The death of fear is in doing what you fear to do.
author: Sequichie Comingdeer

provenance.notes: Sequichie Comingdeer was a real Cherokee teacher and author, and this line circulates consistently under his name in inspirational collections. I cannot place it in any book, lecture, or documented interview, and quotations attributed to Native American teachers are unusually prone to unsourced circulation and invented attribution. Attribution is uncontested but unsupported by anything I can point to.

text: Ultimately, what we are looking to is the deepest connection within ourselves. As we get more connected to that, we begin to feel in harmony with other people and with the rest of the world.
text_raw: Ultimately, what we are looking to is the deepest connection within ourselves. As we get more connected to that, we begin to feel in harmony with other people and with the rest of the world.
author: Shakti Gawain

provenance.notes: Consistent with Shakti Gawain's published voice and themes, and attributed to her without competition. Most likely from Living in the Light (1986) or an interview, but I cannot place it, and this is generic enough New Age phrasing that I would not bet on the specific book. No citation asserted.

text: Most of us are in touch with our intuition whether we know it or not, but we're usually in the habit of doubting or contradicting it so automatically that we don't even know it has spoken.
text_raw: Most of us are in touch with our intuition whether we know it or not, but we're usually in the habit of doubting or contradicting it so automatically that we don't even know it has spoken.
author: Shakti Gawain

provenance.notes: Distinctively Gawain in content — the doubting-and-contradicting-intuition observation is a central argument of Living in the Light (1986), and I believe the line comes from that book, but I cannot confirm the chapter or exact page from memory and so am not asserting the citation. Attribution to Gawain is strong on internal evidence; the print source is unestablished.

text: Evil (ignorance) is like a shadow - it has no real substance of its own, it is simply a lack of light. You cannot cause a shadow to disappear by trying to fight it, stomp[ing] on it, by railing against it, or any other form of emotional or physical resistance. In order to cause a shadow to disappear, you must shine light on it.
text_raw: Evil (ignorance) is like a shadow - it has no real substance of its own, it is simply a lack of light. You cannot cause a shadow to disappear by trying to fight it, stomp[ing] on it, by railing against it, or any other form of emotional or physical resistance. In order to cause a shadow to disappear, you must shine light on it.
author: Shakti Gawain

provenance.notes: Attributed consistently to Shakti Gawain and consistent with her work on light, shadow, and non-resistance. The shadow-and-light image itself is ancient and appears in many traditions, so the metaphor is not evidence of authorship — only this particular formulation would be. I cannot place the formulation in a specific Gawain title. Note the text carries a bracketed editorial fix ('stomp[ing]'), suggesting it was transcribed from a secondary source rather than a book.

text: The most positive and empowering way to relate to money is to let it be a teacher for you. Assume that whatever is happening in your financial reality is in some way a reflection of your internal process, something you can learn from, and something that can help you in your self-development.
text_raw: The most positive and empowering way to relate to money is to let it be a teacher for you. Assume that whatever is happening in your financial reality is in some way a reflection of your internal process, something you can learn from, and something that can help you in your self-development.
author: Shakti Gawain

provenance.notes: Subject matter points to Creating True Prosperity (1997), Gawain's book specifically about money and abundance, and the framing of money as a mirror of internal process is that book's core thesis. I cannot confirm the sentence appears there verbatim, so I am not asserting the citation. Attribution to Gawain is plausible and uncontested.

text: The people we are in relationship with are always a mirror, reflecting our own beliefs, and simultaneously we are mirrors reflecting their beliefs. So relationship is one of the most powerful tools for growth... if we look honestly at our relationships we can see so much about how we have created them.
text_raw: "The people we are in relationship with are always a mirror, reflecting our own beliefs, and simultaneously we are mirrors reflecting their beliefs. So relationship is one of the most powerful tools for growth... if we look honestly at our relationships we can see so much about how we have created them."
author: Shakti Gawain

provenance.notes: The relationships-as-mirror teaching is a signature Gawain theme, developed at length in Living in the Light (1986), and the passage reads like continuous prose from a book rather than a manufactured aphorism — the internal ellipsis suggests it was excerpted from a longer paragraph. Attribution is credible on internal evidence; I cannot verify the source, so no citation is asserted.

text: To discover one’s own divinity is to become incapable of denying it in others.
text_raw: To discover one’s own divinity is to become incapable of denying it in others.
author: Shalom Ormsby

provenance.notes: This is attributed to Shalom Ormsby, the owner and maintainer of this corpus, and appears to be an original line rather than a quotation from any published source. I have no training knowledge of it, which is the expected result for an unpublished original and is not evidence against it. My tooling cannot validate first-party authorship, so the low confidence here reflects the limits of my method, not doubt about the claim. This one should be settled by human confirmation at review time rather than by provenance research; if the author confirms it, it can be promoted directly.

text: There are times when we may fool ourselves. There are times when we can fool others. But we can never fool our body. It is the most sensitive barometer of our inner world.
text_raw: There are times when we may fool ourselves. There are times when we can fool others. But we can never fool our body. It is the most sensitive barometer of our inner world.
author: Sherrill Sellman

provenance.notes: Sherrill Sellman is a real author in the natural-health field (Hormone Heresy and related titles), and the body-as-barometer framing fits that domain. I cannot place the quote in any of her books or articles, and it circulates mainly through wellness quote collections, which are a low-reliability chain. Plausible, unsourced.

text: If you play it safe in life you've decided that you don't want to grow any more.
text_raw: If you play it safe in life you've decided that you don't want to grow any more.
author: Shirley Hufstedler

provenance.notes: Shirley Hufstedler — federal appellate judge and the first U.S. Secretary of Education — is consistently named as the source, and the line appears in compilations of quotations by American women, likely originating in an interview or speech. That kind of origin is real but hard to verify, and I cannot identify the occasion or publication. Attribution is stable across sources but rests on repetition rather than documentation.

text: Wherever you go you will find your teacher, as long as you have the eyes to see and the ears to hear.
text_raw: Wherever you go you will find your teacher, as long as you have the eyes to see and the ears to hear.
author: Shunryu Suzuki

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Shunryu Suzuki and characteristic of his teaching, likely from Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind or the later collection Not Always So. I cannot place it in either with enough confidence to name the book, so the print source is left null. Below the promotion bar on sourcing, not on plausibility.

text: Our subconscious minds have no sense of humor, play no jokes and cannot tell the difference between reality and an imagined thought or image. What we continually think about eventually will manifest in our lives.
text_raw: Our subconscious minds have no sense of humor, play no jokes and cannot tell the difference between reality and an imagined thought or image. What we continually think about eventually will manifest in our lives.
author: Sidney Madwed

provenance.notes: Sidney Madwed was a real motivational speaker and poet whose lines circulate widely on aggregator sites, and this one is consistently attributed to him, but I cannot place it in any book, article, or speech transcript I know of. The claim itself ('the subconscious cannot tell the difference between reality and imagination') is a stock New Thought / self-help proposition that predates Madwed by decades, so he may be restating rather than originating it. No citation available.

text: Thought is action in rehearsal.
text_raw: Thought is action in rehearsal.
author: Sigmund Freud

provenance.notes: The idea is genuinely Freud's: he described thinking as 'Probehandeln' — trial or experimental action — notably in 'Formulations on the Two Principles of Mental Functioning' (1911), where thought is characterized as experimental action carried out with small quantities of energy, and again in later work. 'Thought is action in rehearsal' is a compressed English aphorism of that concept rather than any translator's rendering I can point to in the Standard Edition. Attribution to Freud is sound at the level of idea; the exact wording is popularizer's phrasing, so I am holding this below the promotion bar.

text: I do not know what I am to the world, but to myself, I am but a small boy, playing on the seashore, searching for an ever more perfect pebble or seashell, while before me lies the great ocean of truth.
text_raw: "I do not know what I am to the world, but to myself, I am but a small boy, playing on the seashore, searching for an ever more perfect pebble or seashell, while before me lies the great ocean of truth."
author: Sir Isaac Newton

provenance.earliest_print_source: Memoirs of the Life, Writings, and Discoveries of Sir Isaac Newton, David Brewster, 1855
provenance.notes: Newton's seashore remark is well documented, but the corpus text is a loose paraphrase, not the recorded wording. The standard version: 'I do not know what I may appear to the world, but to myself I seem to have been only like a boy playing on the sea-shore, and diverting myself in now and then finding a smoother pebble or a prettier shell than ordinary, whilst the great ocean of truth lay all undiscovered before me.' Recorded by Joseph Spence (Anecdotes, collected in Newton's lifetime, published 1820) and given wide currency by Brewster's 1855 Memoirs. 'Searching for an ever more perfect pebble or seashell' is a modern rewrite. High confidence Newton said something very close to this; low confidence in this specific text, hence attributed rather than verified. Strongly recommend replacing with the canonical wording.

text: When we have done our best, we should wait the result in peace.
text_raw: When we have done our best, we should wait the result in peace.
author: Sir John Lubbock

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Sir John Lubbock (Lord Avebury) across quotation collections, and it is stylistically at home in his popular essay collections 'The Pleasures of Life' (1887) and 'The Use of Life' (1894). I believe it comes from one of those two, but I cannot state which with confidence, so I am not citing a source. Lubbock is not a misattribution magnet and the attribution is stable, which supports a moderate rating; the missing citation keeps it below the bar.

text: Everyone stumbles over the truth from time to time, but most people pick themselves up and hurry off as though nothing ever happened.
text_raw: Everyone stumbles over the truth from time to time, but most people pick themselves up and hurry off as though nothing ever happened.
author: Sir Winston Churchill

provenance.notes: Churchill is a documented misattribution magnet and this line has no primary source I can identify in his speeches, books, or letters. It circulates in two forms: 'Men occasionally stumble over the truth...' (the older form, found in mid-20th-century Churchill anecdote compilations) and the later gender-neutral 'Everyone stumbles...' variant used here. Churchill quotation scholarship treats sayings of this kind that surface only in compiled anecdote books with suspicion. Plausible but unconfirmed; the corpus text is in any case the later rewritten variant, not the earliest attributed form.

text: A lie gets halfway around the world before the truth has a chance to get its pants on.
text_raw: A lie gets halfway around the world before the truth has a chance to get its pants on.
author: Sir Winston Churchill

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Examiner, No. 14, Jonathan Swift, 1710
provenance.notes: The Churchill attribution is spurious. This is a modern variant of a saying with a long documented pedigree: Jonathan Swift wrote 'Falsehood flies, and the Truth comes limping after it' in The Examiner (1710), and the 'boots' form — 'A lie will go round the world while truth is pulling its boots on' — circulated in the 19th century, commonly credited to the preacher C. H. Spurgeon, who himself presented it as an old saying. 'Pants on' is a 20th-century Americanized rewrite. Versions of this line are also misattributed to Mark Twain, another magnet. There is no evidence Churchill originated it. | Suggested reattribution: Jonathan Swift (1710, earliest documented form); the 'boots' variant is commonly credited to C. H. Spurgeon in the 19th century

text: Two people have been living in you all your life. One is the ego, garrulous, demanding, hysterical, calculating; the other is the hidden spiritual being, whose still voice of wisdom you have only rarely heard or attended to - you have uncovered in yourself your own wise guide.
text_raw: Two people have been living in you all your life. One is the ego, garrulous, demanding, hysterical, calculating; the other is the hidden spiritual being, whose still voice of wisdom you have only rarely heard or attended to - you have uncovered in yourself your own wise guide.
author: Sogyal Rinpoche

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying, Sogyal Rinpoche, 1992
provenance.notes: The two-selves passage — the garrulous, demanding, hysterical, calculating ego versus the hidden spiritual being whose still voice of wisdom is rarely heard — is characteristic of and, to my knowledge, drawn from 'The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying' (1992). I am confident about the book but not about chapter or page, and the corpus text appears spliced: the closing clause ('you have uncovered in yourself your own wise guide') does not grammatically follow the preceding sentence and looks like material lifted from further down the same passage. Recommend re-checking against the book and repairing the ellipsis before promotion.

text: Be with what is, so that what is to be may become.
text_raw: Be with what is, so that what is to be may become.
author: Soren Kierkegaard

provenance.notes: I know of nothing in Kierkegaard's authorship resembling this, in any standard translation. The diction is modern therapeutic/mindfulness aphorism — the Gestalt 'paradoxical theory of change' register — not Kierkegaard's, whose treatment of becoming is far more elaborated and anguished. It reads like a coaching-literature line that acquired a prestigious name. I cannot identify the real originator, so I am not proposing a reattribution, but I would not promote this under Kierkegaard's name.

text: Each day beckons you to walk on the road of self-transcendence. When we transcend ourselves we do not compete with others, we compete only with our previous achievements. And each time we surpass our achievements, we get joy... Life is nothing but a perpetual possibility.
text_raw: Each day beckons you to walk on the road of self-transcendence. When we transcend ourselves we do not compete with others, we compete only with our previous achievements. And each time we surpass our achievements, we get joy... Life is nothing but a perpetual possibility.
author: Sri Chinmoy

provenance.notes: Self-transcendence and 'competing only with yourself' were central, endlessly repeated themes of Sri Chinmoy's talks and writings, and the vocabulary here is authentically his. But he published hundreds of volumes of aphorisms and transcribed lectures, and I cannot locate this specific text in any of them; the ellipsis suggests it has been assembled from more than one sentence. Attribution is plausible and stylistically consistent, but uncited.

text: Never confuse your mistakes with your value as a human being. You're a perfectly valuable, creative, worthwhile person simply because you exist. And no amount of triumphs or tribulations can ever change that. Unconditional self acceptance is the core of a peaceful mind.
text_raw: Never confuse your mistakes with your value as a human being. You're a perfectly valuable, creative, worthwhile person simply because you exist. And no amount of triumphs or tribulations can ever change that. Unconditional self acceptance is the core of a peaceful mind.
author: St. Francis de Sales

provenance.notes: Anachronistic. 'Unconditional self acceptance' is a term of art from Albert Ellis's Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy, and the whole passage — separating mistakes from intrinsic worth, 'a peaceful mind' — is 20th-century cognitive-therapy and self-esteem language with no counterpart in the devotional writing of a 17th-century bishop. Francis de Sales wrote about gentleness toward one's own faults, which is probably why his name attached itself here, but his framing is theological (worth grounded in God), not psychological. I cannot identify who actually wrote this, so I am proposing no reattribution; Ellis is the likely conceptual source rather than a confirmed author.

text: When you encounter difficulties and contradictions, do not try to break them, but bend them with gentleness and time.
text_raw: When you encounter difficulties and contradictions, do not try to break them, but bend them with gentleness and time.
author: St. Francis de Sales

provenance.notes: This one is genuinely at home in Francis de Sales: gentleness in the face of difficulty, and the counsel to bend rather than break, are signatures of his spiritual direction in 'Introduction to the Devout Life' and his letters. It appears in Catholic devotional compilations of his sayings, usually paired with 'Do not lose your inner peace for anything whatsoever.' I cannot pin it to a specific letter or chapter, and translation-era English makes exact matching hard, so no citation. Moderate confidence, unlike q_1292 which I judge to be a modern fabrication under the same name.

text: It's no use walking anywhere to preach anything unless our walking is our preaching.
text_raw: It's no use walking anywhere to preach anything unless our walking is our preaching.
author: St. Francis of Assisi

provenance.notes: This belongs to the same apocryphal cluster as 'Preach the Gospel at all times; when necessary, use words' — a line Franciscan scholars have repeatedly shown is absent from Francis's writings and from the early biographies. The 'walking is our preaching' version derives from a later retelling of an anecdote about Francis walking through town with a companion, and appears in modern devotional literature rather than in any source contemporary with him. Not found in the Writings of Francis or in Celano/Bonaventure as far as I know.

text: Start by doing what is necessary, then do what is possible, and suddenly you are doing the impossible.
text_raw: Start by doing what is necessary, then do what is possible, and suddenly you are doing the impossible.
author: St. Francis of Assisi

provenance.notes: No evidence connects this to Francis of Assisi. It does not appear in his authenticated writings or in the early Franciscan biographies, and the earliest instances I am aware of are 20th-century, in motivational and recovery literature, where it circulated for some time before Francis's name was attached. The rhetorical shape — necessary, possible, impossible — is a modern three-beat inspirational construction. Widely repeated, which is not evidence.

text: Nothing lowers the level of conversation more than raising the voice.
text_raw: Nothing lowers the level of conversation more than raising the voice.
author: Stanley Horowitz

provenance.notes: Stanley Horowitz is a real and otherwise obscure figure best known for a Reader's Digest contest-winning line about the seasons ('Winter is an etching, spring a watercolor...'). This aphorism is consistently credited to him in quotation collections, which suggests a shared original source — plausibly the same magazine-filler context — but I cannot identify a publication or date. Attribution is stable but entirely uncited.

text: Our ultimate freedom is the right and power to decide how anybody or anything outside ourselves will affect us.
text_raw: Our ultimate freedom is the right and power to decide how anybody or anything outside ourselves will affect us.
author: Stephen Covey

provenance.notes: Consistent with Covey's Habit 1 material on proactivity and the freedom to choose one's response, which he built explicitly on Viktor Frankl. The sentiment is authentically his and the attribution is stable, but I cannot place this exact sentence in 'The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People' (1989) or 'Principle-Centered Leadership' (1991), and Covey also said versions of this in many talks. Note the underlying idea traces to Frankl, not Covey.

text: Say yes to life, even though you know it will devour you. Because among the obstacles and, to be sure, the cruelties of life are signs that we are on a primary spiritual adventure (even though it seems to be taking place in what we regard as an unmistakably physical world).
text_raw: Say yes to life, even though you know it will devour you. Because among the obstacles and, to be sure, the cruelties of life are signs that we are on a primary spiritual adventure (even though it seems to be taking place in what we regard as an unmistakably physical world).
author: Stephen Larsen

provenance.notes: Stephen Larsen is a real author — Joseph Campbell's biographer, with Robin Larsen, of 'A Fire in the Mind' — and this passage is written in a Campbellian register, which is precisely the problem: 'say yes to life even though you know it will devour you' echoes Campbell's affirmation-of-life and 'joyful participation in the sorrows of the world' themes closely enough that the two men's names could easily have been swapped in transmission. I cannot place the text in Larsen's own books, nor confirm it as a Campbell quotation. Uncertain enough that I am proposing no reattribution.

text: Letting go of our suffering is the hardest work we will ever do. It is also the most fruitful. To heal means to meet ourselves in a new way - in the newness of each moment where all is possible and nothing is limited to the old.
text_raw: Letting go of our suffering is the hardest work we will ever do. It is also the most fruitful. To heal means to meet ourselves in a new way - in the newness of each moment where all is possible and nothing is limited to the old.
author: Stephen Levine

provenance.notes: Authentically Levine in vocabulary and cadence — 'letting go', meeting oneself anew, healing as distinct from curing are the core of his work with the dying. Most likely from 'Healing into Life and Death' (1987) or 'Who Dies?' (1982), but I cannot confirm which, so no citation. Attribution stable across sources and stylistically sound; uncited.

text: People ask what must they become to be loving. The answer is ‘nothing.’ It is a process of letting go of what you thought you had become and allowing your true nature to float to the surface naturally.
text_raw: People ask what must they become to be loving. The answer is ‘nothing.’ It is a process of letting go of what you thought you had become and allowing your true nature to float to the surface naturally.
author: Stephen Levine

provenance.notes: Same assessment as q_1299: the framing — that becoming loving is subtractive, a letting go of accreted self-concept rather than an achievement — is a recognizable Stephen Levine teaching, and the attribution is consistent wherever it appears. I cannot identify the book. Uncited, and the opening sentence's grammar ('People ask what must they become') suggests transcription from a talk rather than from print.

text: Every human has four endowments - self awareness, conscience, independent will and creative imagination. These give us the ultimate human freedom... The power to choose, to respond, to change.
text_raw: Every human has four endowments - self awareness, conscience, independent will and creative imagination. These give us the ultimate human freedom... The power to choose, to respond, to change.
author: Stephen R. Covey

provenance.notes: The four human endowments — self-awareness, conscience, independent will, creative imagination — are a genuine and distinctive Covey framework, presented in 'The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People' (1989) and developed further in 'Principle-Centered Leadership' (1991). Attribution to Covey is not in doubt. The circulating text, with its ellipsis, is a condensation rather than a verbatim sentence from either book, which is why I am not citing a page or crossing the promotion bar. Note this is the same author as q_1297, entered under a different name form ('Stephen Covey' vs 'Stephen R. Covey') — worth normalizing in the corpus.

text: You may be good, but what are you good for? You’ve got to be good for something. You’ve got to be about some project, some task that requires you to be humble and obedient to the universal principles of service.
text_raw: You may be good, but what are you good for? You’ve got to be good for something. You’ve got to be about some project, some task that requires you to be humble and obedient to the universal principles of service.
author: Stephen R. Covey

provenance.notes: Sounds like Covey speaking rather than writing — the direct second-person challenge and the appeal to 'universal principles' are his, but the loose, spoken syntax points to a seminar or interview rather than a book. I cannot place it in any of his published works. Plausible, uncited.

text: Every time I feel I'm losing my own focus, I ask myself one question: What am I trying to accomplish?
text_raw: Every time I feel I'm losing my own focus, I ask myself one question: What am I trying to accomplish?
author: Steve DeMasco

provenance.notes: Steve DeMasco is a real figure — Shaolin martial artist and author of 'The Shaolin Way' (2006) — and this line is consistently credited to him, plausibly from that book or from an interview around its publication. I cannot confirm the source. The quote is generic enough that stable attribution carries little evidential weight on its own.

text: Remember, most of the things you think you need are ego trips designed to bolster your image and your perception of security.... You'll waste a lot of energy satisfying your ego only to find that, as soon as it's got what it wants, it ignores all your efforts and promptly nails another list of demands to your forehead. The ego will always try to force you to slave for its vision. I wouldn't stand for that BS if I were you.
text_raw: Remember, most of the things you think you need are ego trips designed to bolster your image and your perception of security.... You'll waste a lot of energy satisfying your ego only to find that, as soon as it's got what it wants, it ignores all your efforts and promptly nails another list of demands to your forehead. The ego will always try to force you to slave for its vision. I wouldn't stand for that BS if I were you.
author: Stuart Wilde

provenance.notes: The voice is strongly consistent with Stuart Wilde (1946-2013) — the irreverent register, the ego-as-taskmaster conceit, the closing 'I wouldn't stand for that BS if I were you' — and the line circulates consistently under his name. It plausibly comes from Infinite Self (1996) or Silent Power, but I cannot place it in a specific book or page from training knowledge, so I will not name one.

text: When the heart grieves over what it has lost, the spirit rejoices over what it has left.
text_raw: When the heart grieves over what it has lost, the spirit rejoices over what it has left.
author: Sufi saying

provenance.notes: Circulates widely as an unsourced 'Sufi saying' or 'Sufi epigram' in English-language quotation collections. I know of no Sufi primary text, named poet, or translator behind it, and the polished English antithesis (heart grieves / spirit rejoices) reads like a modern anthology formulation. Generic tradition labels of this kind are effectively unverifiable.

text: It seems in every interaction there is something to learn if we can only see ourselves as students. If we can humble ourselves, and allow ourselves to see the world without our own beliefs and dogmas, then we could see so much beauty awaiting us in each moment.
text_raw: It seems in every interaction there is something to learn if we can only see ourselves as students. If we can humble ourselves, and allow ourselves to see the world without our own beliefs and dogmas, then we could see so much beauty awaiting us in each moment.
author: Sukh Chugh

provenance.notes: I have no knowledge of Sukh Chugh as a published author, and no recollection of this passage in any book, essay, or collection. The prose reads like contemporary personal-blog or social-media writing. Attribution may well be correct, but I have nothing to confirm it against.

text: Each body is a universe, as good a universe as you could conceive.
text_raw: Each body is a universe, as good a universe as you could conceive.
author: Swami Amar Jyoti

provenance.notes: Swami Amar Jyoti (1928-2001), founder of Truth Consciousness, published satsang discourses (Spirit of Himalaya, Retreat Into Eternity) and the line is idiomatically plausible for that body of work. I cannot place it in any specific discourse or volume, and it does not appear in quotation references I can recall.

text: We are what our thoughts have made us; so take care about what you think. Words are secondary. Thoughts live; they travel far.
text_raw: We are what our thoughts have made us; so take care about what you think. Words are secondary. Thoughts live; they travel far.
author: Swami Vivekananda

provenance.notes: Genuinely Vivekananda in substance and idiom; 'We are what our thoughts have made us' is a recurring formulation of his and the passage is consistently cited to the Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda. I cannot confirm the volume, lecture, or page from training knowledge, so I leave the print source blank rather than guess a locator. Held below the promotion bar for that reason.

text: Those who wish to sing always find a song.
text_raw: Those who wish to sing always find a song.
author: Proverb

provenance.notes: Usually labeled a Swedish proverb in English collections, sometimes simply 'proverb'. I know of no traceable earliest appearance, no Swedish original I can cite, and no scholarly proverb reference that dates it. An honest 'unknown'.

text: The shortest way to do many things is to do only one thing at a time.
text_raw: The shortest way to do many things is to do only one thing at a time.
author: Sydney Smiles

provenance.earliest_print_source: Self-Help, Samuel Smiles, 1859 (quoting the Rev. Richard Cecil)
provenance.notes: 'Sydney Smiles' is not a person; this is a corruption of Samuel Smiles, the Scottish author of Self-Help (1859). In Self-Help, Smiles quotes the maxim from the Rev. Richard Cecil, whose usual wording is 'The shortest way to do many things is to do only one thing at once' — so even under the corrected name Smiles is the transmitter, not the author. My recollection of the Self-Help citation is good but not page-level; the confidence figure reflects the weakness of the attribution as recorded, not of the reattribution. | Suggested reattribution: Richard Cecil, as quoted by Samuel Smiles in Self-Help (1859)

text: Time you enjoyed wasting is not wasted time.
text_raw: Time you enjoyed wasting is not wasted time.
author: T. S. Eliot

provenance.earliest_print_source: Phrynette Married, Marthe Troly-Curtin, 1912
provenance.notes: A well-documented misattribution. Eliot never wrote this; it appears in Marthe Troly-Curtin's novel Phrynette Married (1912) as 'Time you enjoy wasting is not wasted time', and Quote Investigator traced it there. Wikiquote lists it in the misattributed section of the Eliot page. Low confidence here reflects the near-certainty that the recorded attribution to Eliot is wrong. | Suggested reattribution: Marthe Troly-Curtin

text: Only those who will risk going too far can possibly find out how far one can go.
text_raw: Only those who will risk going too far can possibly find out how far one can go.
author: T. S. Eliot

provenance.earliest_print_source: Preface to Transit of Venus: Poems by Harry Crosby, T. S. Eliot, 1931
provenance.notes: Genuine Eliot. The line comes from his preface to Harry Crosby's posthumous collection Transit of Venus (Black Sun Press, 1931), and Wikiquote carries it as sourced. I am confident in the work and year but have not verified the exact wording against the preface, so I stop short of 'verified'.

text: Life extracts a price for less than full participation.
