text_raw: Life extracts a price for less than full participation.
author: Tarthang Tulku

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Tarthang Tulku in quotation collections and idiomatically consistent with his Dharma Publishing books (Skillful Means, Gesture of Balance, Knowledge of Freedom). I cannot locate it in a specific book or chapter, so no print source is offered.

text: Whether your life is meaningful or not depends on how much you value your present situation.
text_raw: Whether your life is meaningful or not depends on how much you value your present situation.
author: Tarthang Tulku

provenance.notes: Same situation as the preceding Tarthang Tulku line: plausible in voice and consistently attributed to him in secondary collections, but I can place it in no specific work. Slightly weaker than q_1319 because it circulates less and the phrasing is more generic.

text: Driven by the forces of love, the fragments of the world are seeking each other, so that the world may come into being.
text_raw: Driven by the forces of love, the fragments of the world are seeking each other, so that the world may come into being.
author: Teilhard de Chardin

provenance.notes: Authentically Teilhardian in both doctrine and phrasing — love as the physical energy that draws fragments toward convergence is central to his cosmology — and the line is consistently attributed to him. However, sources differ on the work (variously The Phenomenon of Man, Human Energy, and the essays collected in Toward the Future), and I cannot resolve which is correct or confirm the translation, so I name no source. Full name is Pierre Teilhard de Chardin.

text: Dancing faces you towards Heaven, whichever direction you turn.
text_raw: Dancing faces you towards Heaven, whichever direction you turn.
author: Terri Guillemets

provenance.notes: Terri Guillemets is a contemporary American quotation anthologist (The Quote Garden) who also writes original aphorisms, and this is one of hers rather than an anonymous line she collected. Attribution is consistent wherever it appears. Original publication is self-published online rather than in print, so there is no print source to cite and no independent scholarly confirmation.

text: Those who see themselves as whole make no demands.
text_raw: Those who see themselves as whole make no demands.
author: The Course in Miracles

provenance.notes: The sentence is idiomatically ACIM — wholeness, lack, and demand are its standard vocabulary — and it is consistently attributed to the Course. But ACIM is a large text with a precise numbering system (T-/W-/M- locators), and I cannot place this line at any chapter or section. Without a locator I will not assert the source. Also note the title is A Course in Miracles, not 'The Course in Miracles'.

text: Remember that not getting what you want is sometimes a wonderful stroke of luck.
text_raw: Remember that not getting what you want is sometimes a wonderful stroke of luck.
author: Dalai Lama

provenance.notes: This is an item from the chain-circulated list 'Instructions for Life in the New Millennium', which spread by email in the late 1990s under the Dalai Lama's name. The Office of the Dalai Lama has disclaimed the list; it is not his, and several of its items track secular American self-help writing (H. Jackson Brown Jr.'s Life's Little Instruction Book is often noted as a source of similar material). Wikiquote treats the list as misattributed. I cannot identify the actual author of this specific line, so I offer no reattribution. A classic misattribution magnet — treat any bare 'Dalai Lama' aphorism in this register with suspicion.

text: The wise use memories, but do not allow memories to use them.
text_raw: The wise use memories, but do not allow memories to use them.
author: The Vedas

provenance.notes: I know of no Vedic passage corresponding to this, in any standard translation. The epigram's shape — a chiasmus about using memory rather than being used by it — is a modern rhetorical form, and 'The Vedas' is exactly the kind of blanket ancient-authority label that gets attached to unsourced aphorisms. Very likely modern and pseudo-attributed, but since I cannot name a real author I am not calling it a misattribution outright.

text: What we need is more people who specialize in the impossible.
text_raw: What we need is more people who specialize in the impossible.
author: Theodore Roethke

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to the poet Theodore Roethke (1908-1963) across quotation collections, with no competing claimant that I know of. It most likely comes from his notebooks rather than the published poems — Straw for the Fire: From the Notebooks of Theodore Roethke (ed. David Wagoner, 1972) is the usual candidate — but I cannot confirm that, so I name no source. Consistent attribution without a locatable text keeps this below the promotion bar.

text: Whenever you are asked if you can do a job, tell' em, 'Certainly I can!' - and get busy and find out how to do it.
text_raw: Whenever you are asked if you can do a job, tell' em, 'Certainly I can!' - and get busy and find out how to do it.
author: Theodore Roosevelt

provenance.notes: Circulates widely in motivational compilations as Theodore Roosevelt, but I cannot place it in any of his speeches, letters, or books that I know. The colloquial 'tell 'em' phrasing is the kind of line that gets retrofitted onto TR as a can-do figurehead. No primary source known to me; honest answer is that the attribution is unsupported rather than disproven.

text: The problem is not that there are problems. The problem is expecting otherwise and thinking that having problems is a problem.
text_raw: The problem is not that there are problems. The problem is expecting otherwise and thinking that having problems is a problem.
author: Theodore Rubin

provenance.notes: Consistently and specifically attributed to Theodore Isaac Rubin, the American psychiatrist and author (1923-2019), across self-help and psychology anthologies. The construction and content match his popular writing on emotional life. I cannot identify which of his books it comes from, so no print citation. Note the corpus author field reads 'Theodore Rubin' — the full form 'Theodore Isaac Rubin' is the standard one and would reduce confusion with other Rubins.

text: The miracle is not to walk on water, but to walk with love on earth, as if your feet are kissing the ground. We must remember that our presence alone is a miracle. We must learn to say 'Yes' to the miracles of life.
text_raw: The miracle is not to walk on water, but to walk with love on earth, as if your feet are kissing the ground. We must remember that our presence alone is a miracle. We must learn to say 'Yes' to the miracles of life.
author: Inspired by Thich Nhat Hanh's teachings
author_raw: Inspired by Thich Nhat Hanh's teachings

provenance.notes: This is a composite paraphrase, not a verbatim Thich Nhat Hanh passage. Two authentic teachings of his are welded together here: the walking-on-water line from The Miracle of Mindfulness (1975), which runs roughly 'People usually consider walking on water or in thin air a miracle. But I think the real miracle is not to walk either on water or in thin air, but to walk on earth'; and the 'walk as if you are kissing the Earth with your feet' instruction associated with Peace Is Every Step (1991). The closing sentences about 'our presence alone is a miracle' and saying 'Yes' to the miracles of life I cannot place in his work at all. The corpus author field 'Inspired by Thich Nhat Hanh's teachings' is accurate framing, and the text should not be presented as a direct quotation.

text: At any moment, you have a choice, that either leads you closer to your spirit or further away from it.
text_raw: At any moment, you have a choice, that either leads you closer to your spirit or further away from it.
author: Inspired by Thich Nhat Hanh's teachings
author_raw: Inspired by Thich Nhat Hanh's teachings

provenance.notes: I cannot place this in Thich Nhat Hanh's writing, and the vocabulary is off for him — 'closer to your spirit or further away from it' is Western self-development diction, not the mindfulness/interbeing register he actually uses (he would speak of mindfulness, breath, the present moment, not 'your spirit'). Reads like a social-media caption that acquired a monk's name. No traceable source; no candidate true author identifiable, so no reattribution offered.

text: We have more possibilities available in each moment than we realize.
text_raw: We have more possibilities available in each moment than we realize.
author: Inspired by Thich Nhat Hanh's teachings
author_raw: Inspired by Thich Nhat Hanh's teachings

provenance.notes: Short, generic sentence widely circulated under Thich Nhat Hanh's name. The thought — that each moment holds more possibility than we notice — is consonant with his teaching, but the line is brief and unmarked enough that I cannot distinguish an authentic sentence from a paraphrase of one. No book, talk, or page reference known to me.

text: When we look deeply into the heart of a flower, we see clouds, sunshine, minerals, time, the earth, and everything else in the cosmos in it. Without clouds that could be no rain, and without rain there would be no flower.
text_raw: When we look deeply into the heart of a flower, we see clouds, sunshine, minerals, time, the earth, and everything else in the cosmos in it. Without clouds that could be no rain, and without rain there would be no flower.
author: Inspired by Thich Nhat Hanh's teachings
author_raw: Inspired by Thich Nhat Hanh's teachings

provenance.notes: The teaching is unmistakably Thich Nhat Hanh's — seeing clouds, sunshine, minerals, and time inside a single object is his signature illustration of interbeing, developed at length in The Heart of Understanding (1988), his commentary on the Heart Sutra, where the same move is made with a sheet of paper ('If you are a poet, you will see clearly that there is a cloud floating in this sheet of paper'). The flower variant appears across his talks. What I cannot confirm is that this exact wording is his rather than a paraphrase by an editor or reader, so I am holding below the promotion bar. Also note a transcription error in the corpus text: 'Without clouds that could be no rain' should read 'there could be no rain'.

text: As we cultivate peace and happiness in ourselves, we also nourish peace and happiness in those we love.
text_raw: As we cultivate peace and happiness in ourselves, we also nourish peace and happiness in those we love.
author: Inspired by Thich Nhat Hanh's teachings
author_raw: Inspired by Thich Nhat Hanh's teachings

provenance.notes: Consistent with Thich Nhat Hanh's recurring teaching that personal peace propagates outward to family and society — a theme carried through Being Peace (1987) and Peace Is Every Step (1991). I cannot confirm this specific sentence as his wording versus a summary of the teaching. No page-level source known to me.

text: Let him who wants to move and convince others be first moved and convince himself.
text_raw: Let him who wants to move and convince others be first moved and convince himself.
author: Thomas Carlyle

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Thomas Carlyle in nineteenth- and twentieth-century quotation dictionaries, usually in the form 'Let him who would move and convince others, be first moved and convinced himself.' The sentiment and the periodic sentence structure fit Carlyle's essayistic prose. I cannot identify the specific essay or volume, so no print citation; the attribution itself is old and stable, which is why this sits at 'attributed' rather than lower.

text: Having a strong desire or being successful does not mean that you are going to feel great all the time. No matter how enlightened I become, I will not be positive all the time. You have to understand the swing of the pendulum. It must swing back and forth. The only other alternative is to sit still in neutral, which is precisely what most people do.
text_raw: Having a strong desire or being successful does not mean that you are going to feel great all the time. No matter how enlightened I become, I will not be positive all the time. You have to understand the swing of the pendulum. It must swing back and forth. The only other alternative is to sit still in neutral, which is precisely what most people do.
author: Thomas D. Willhite

provenance.notes: Thomas D. Willhite (1940-1983) founded PSI Seminars, and this passage circulates within that human-potential lineage and its derivative literature, always under his name. The pendulum metaphor and the 'sit still in neutral' line match the seminar idiom of that world. Attribution is consistent but narrow — I know of no independent published source, and material from seminar transcripts is hard to verify. No citation offered.

text: Opportunity is missed by most people because it is dressed in overalls and looks like work.
text_raw: Opportunity is missed by most people because it is dressed in overalls and looks like work.
author: Thomas Edison

provenance.notes: One of the most-repeated Edison lines and one of the least documented. It does not appear in his notebooks or documented interviews as far as I know, and my recollection of the quotation-research literature is that attributions to Edison cluster well after his death in 1931, with earlier anonymous 'opportunity in overalls' sayings in circulation before his name attached to any of them. I do not have a confident earliest instance or a true author, so I am not calling it misattributed outright — but treat the Edison attribution as unsupported.

text: If we all did the things we are capable of doing, we would literally astound ourselves.
text_raw: "If we all did the things we are capable of doing, we would literally astound ourselves."
author: Thomas Edison

provenance.notes: Widely repeated as Edison, commonly in the variant 'If we did all the things we are capable of, we would literally astound ourselves.' I cannot place it in any of his writings, interviews, or authorized biographies. Edison is a strong misattribution magnet for terse work-ethic aphorisms. No source, no alternative author known to me.

text: Two things a man should never be angry at: what he can help, and what he cannot help.
text_raw: Two things a man should never be angry at: what he can help, and what he cannot help.
author: Thomas Fuller

provenance.notes: Attributed to Thomas Fuller, and the form is exactly that of the numbered maxims in Gnomologia: Adagies and Proverbs (1732), compiled by Thomas Fuller, M.D. (1654-1734) — as distinct from the earlier churchman Thomas Fuller (1608-1661), with whom he is routinely confused in quote collections. I could not confirm this specific maxim in Gnomologia from memory, so I am not asserting that citation. Also worth flagging: Gnomologia is a compilation of existing proverbs, so even a confirmed entry would make Fuller the collector rather than the author.

text: He that cannot forgive others breaks the bridge over which he must pass himself; for every man has need to be forgiven.
text_raw: He that cannot forgive others breaks the bridge over which he must pass himself; for every man has need to be forgiven.
author: Thomas Fuller

provenance.notes: This 'breaks the bridge over which he must pass himself' saying has a genuinely contested attribution: it appears in quotation dictionaries under Thomas Fuller and also under Edward Herbert, Lord Herbert of Cherbury (1583-1648), and I have seen it credited to George Herbert as well. I do not know which is earliest and cannot resolve the tangle from memory, so no reattribution is offered — but the Fuller attribution here should not be treated as settled.

text: Really big people are, above everything else, courteous, considerate and generous - not just to some people in some circumstances, but to everyone all the time.
text_raw: Really big people are, above everything else, courteous, considerate and generous - not just to some people in some circumstances, but to everyone all the time.
author: Thomas J. Watson

provenance.notes: Attributed to Thomas J. Watson Sr., the IBM founder, in business and leadership anthologies. Watson Sr. did speak and write extensively on conduct and courtesy as company doctrine, so the sentiment is in character, but I cannot tie this wording to a speech, a THINK-era publication, or any IBM document. Note also that Watson Sr. and his son Watson Jr. are frequently conflated in quote collections (see q_1354 in this same batch).

text: When you reach the end of your rope, tie a knot in it and hang on.
text_raw: When you reach the end of your rope, tie a knot in it and hang on.
author: Thomas Jefferson

provenance.notes: The Jefferson attribution is almost certainly wrong. To my knowledge this line appears on the Jefferson Monticello foundation's list of spurious quotations — it is not found anywhere in his correspondence or published writings, and the idiom is twentieth-century American rather than eighteenth-century. It is also commonly credited to Franklin D. Roosevelt, which is itself unverified. Best current understanding is an anonymous early-twentieth-century saying that later collected famous names; because I cannot name the real originator with confidence, I am leaving the reattribution field null rather than guessing FDR.

text: I'm a great believer in luck and I find the harder I work, the more I have of it.
text_raw: I'm a great believer in luck and I find the harder I work, the more I have of it.
author: Thomas Jefferson

provenance.notes: Not Jefferson. This is a documented spurious Jefferson quotation — it does not appear in his writings, and the Monticello foundation lists it among quotes wrongly ascribed to him. My recollection of Quote Investigator's research is that the earliest located version belongs to Coleman Cox, an American aphorist writing in the early 1920s, in the form 'I am a great believer in Luck. The harder I work, the more of it I seem to have'; the saying was later also pinned on Stephen Leacock and Samuel Goldwyn. I am naming Cox as the probable originator on the strength of that research but deliberately leaving earliest_print_source null, since I cannot confirm the exact volume and year without looking it up. | Suggested reattribution: Coleman Cox

text: The chief act of the will is not effort, but consent.
text_raw: The chief act of the will is not effort, but consent.
author: Thomas Keating

provenance.notes: A well-known formulation from Fr. Thomas Keating (1923-2018), the Trappist monk who developed Centering Prayer. The distinction between effort and consent is load-bearing in his method — consent to God's presence and action is the definitional move of Centering Prayer — and this sentence is quoted consistently under his name throughout contemplative literature. I cannot pin it to Open Mind, Open Heart, Invitation to Love, or a specific conference talk, so no print citation.

text: Motivation is an external, temporary high that pushes you forward. Inspiration is a sustainable internal glow which pulls you forward.
text_raw: "Motivation is an external, temporary high that pushes you forward. Inspiration is a sustainable internal glow which pulls you forward."
author: Thomas Leonard

provenance.notes: Attributed consistently to Thomas J. Leonard (1955-2003), the founder of Coach U and a principal architect of the professional coaching field. The motivation/inspiration contrast is a standard piece of his teaching and the wording is stable across coaching sources. I cannot connect it to The Portable Coach, his newsletters, or any dated publication, so the attribution stays unverified.

text: It's important to be heroic, ambitious, productive, efficient, creative, and progressive, but these qualities don't necessarily nurture soul. The soul has different concerns, of equal value: downtime for reflection, conversation, and reverie; beauty that is captivating and pleasuring; relatedness to the environs and to people; and any animal’s rhythm of rest and activity.
text_raw: “It's important to be heroic, ambitious, productive, efficient, creative, and progressive, but these qualities don't necessarily nurture soul. The soul has different concerns, of equal value: downtime for reflection, conversation, and reverie; beauty that is captivating and pleasuring; relatedness to the environs and to people; and any animal’s rhythm of rest and activity.”
author: Thomas Moore

provenance.notes: Strongly characteristic of Thomas Moore, the Jungian-influenced former monk who wrote Care of the Soul (1992). The argument — that heroic productivity is a real good but a different good from what the soul needs, and that soul wants reverie, beauty, relatedness, and rhythm — is the central thesis of that book and recurs in The Re-Enchantment of Everyday Life (1996). I believe this is authentic Moore prose rather than a paraphrase, but I cannot identify which book or page, so no citation and no promotion above the bar.

text: I think we would be able to live in this world more peaceably if our spirituality were to come from looking not just into infinity but very closely at the world around us - and appreciating its depth and divinity.
text_raw: "I think we would be able to live in this world more peaceably if our spirituality were to come from looking not just into infinity but very closely at the world around us - and appreciating its depth and divinity."
author: Thomas Moore

provenance.notes: Reads as spoken rather than written — the hedged opening ('I think we would be able to') suggests an interview or lecture transcript, and it is attributed to Thomas Moore in that form. The content matches his argument for a spirituality of the immediate and ordinary over an abstract or transcendent one. Without a named interview or program I cannot verify it.

text: We need people in our lives with whom we can be as open as possible. To have real conversation with people may seem like such a simple, obvious suggestion, but it involves courage and risk.
text_raw: "We need people in our lives with whom we can be as open as possible. To have real conversation with people may seem like such a simple, obvious suggestion, but it involves courage and risk."
author: Thomas Moore

provenance.notes: Consistent with Thomas Moore's writing on friendship and intimacy, the territory of Soul Mates: Honoring the Mysteries of Love and Relationship (1994), and attributed to him wherever I have encountered it. The concessive move ('may seem like such a simple, obvious suggestion, but') is his rhetorical habit. No specific source identifiable, so unverified.

text: Character is much easier kept than recovered.
text_raw: Character is much easier kept than recovered.
author: Thomas Paine

provenance.notes: Long and stably attributed to Thomas Paine, and the compressed antithesis is genuinely in his rhetorical style. It is usually cited to The American Crisis series (1776-1783), which I believe is correct, but I cannot confirm which number in the series and will not guess at one. Holding at 'attributed' on the strength of the consistent historical attribution rather than a located passage.

text: We can only be said to be alive in those moments when our hearts are conscious of our treasures.
text_raw: We can only be said to be alive in those moments when our hearts are conscious of our treasures.
author: Thornton Wilder

provenance.notes: Genuine Thornton Wilder, and among his most-quoted lines. My recollection places it in the novel The Woman of Andros (1930), spoken in the reflective register of that book rather than in Our Town, to which it is sometimes loosely assigned. Because I am working from memory and cannot confirm the passage, I have left earliest_print_source null rather than state a citation I cannot check — but the Wilder attribution itself is solid and the novel is the likely home.

text: Joy is the most infallible sign of the presence of God.
text_raw: Joy is the most infallible sign of the presence of God.
author: Tielhard de Chardin

provenance.notes: Extremely widely circulated under Teilhard de Chardin's name (also spelled correctly 'Teilhard'), but I cannot place it in any of his published works (The Divine Milieu, The Phenomenon of Man, Hymn of the Universe, letters). The same line, in French — 'La joie est le signe infaillible de la presence de Dieu' — is commonly credited to the French Catholic writer Leon Bloy, and that attribution appears at least as often in Catholic sources. I am not confident enough in the Bloy origin to reattribute outright, but the Teilhard attribution should not be treated as established.

text: Disbelief in magic can force a poor soul into believing in government and business.
text_raw: Disbelief in magic can force a poor soul into believing in government and business.
author: Tom Robbins

provenance.notes: Reads unmistakably like Tom Robbins and is consistently attributed to him, most often to the novel Even Cowgirls Get the Blues (1976). I recall the line in that context but cannot confirm the novel or page with enough certainty to call it verified. No competing attribution exists, which is a point in its favor.

text: If you're going to hold someone down you're going to have to hold on by the other end of the chain. You are confined by your own repression.
text_raw: If you're going to hold someone down you're going to have to hold on by the other end of the chain. You are confined by your own repression.
author: Toni Morrison

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Toni Morrison and consistent with her recurring argument that racism imprisons the oppressor as well as the oppressed. It circulates as an interview or lecture remark rather than a passage from her fiction or essays; I cannot identify the specific interview, date, or outlet. No competing attribution. Holding below the promotion bar for lack of a locatable source.

text: Terrible drought, crops dead, sheep dying. Spring dried out. No water. The Hopi, or the Christian, maybe the Moslem, they pray for rain. The Navajo has the proper ceremony done to restore himself to harmony with the drought. You see what I mean. The system is designed to recognize what’s beyond human power to change, and then to change the human’s attitude to be content with the inevitable.
text_raw: Terrible drought, crops dead, sheep dying. Spring dried out. No water. The Hopi, or the Christian, maybe the Moslem, they pray for rain. The Navajo has the proper ceremony done to restore himself to harmony with the drought. You see what I mean. The system is designed to recognize what’s beyond human power to change, and then to change the human’s attitude to be content with the inevitable.
author: Tony Hillerman

provenance.notes: Stylistically and substantively consistent with Tony Hillerman's Navajo Tribal Police novels — it reads as Joe Leaphorn (or Jim Chee) explaining the contrast between petitionary prayer and Navajo restorative ceremony, a theme Hillerman returns to repeatedly. I cannot identify which novel it comes from, and passages of dialogue lifted from novels are frequently reworded in circulation. Plausibly authentic, unverified as to source and exact wording.

text: Happiness is not about the fulfillment of desires; it's about honoring your heart along the way.
text_raw: Happiness is not about the fulfillment of desires; it's about honoring your heart along the way.
author: Trish Whynot

provenance.notes: Trish Whynot is a contemporary self-help author and holistic counselor; the line is consistent with her published work and I know of no competing attribution, which is typical for quotes from minor contemporary authors — they are rarely misattributed but also rarely sourced. I cannot point to a specific book or page. Low confidence reflects absence of evidence, not suspicion.

text: Failure is the condiment that gives success its flavor.
text_raw: Failure is the condiment that gives success its flavor.
author: Truman Capote

provenance.notes: Attributed to Truman Capote with unusual consistency across quotation collections, and the aphoristic style fits him. However, it circulates only as a free-floating epigram — I cannot connect it to a specific book, essay, or interview, and Capote's published prose is well indexed, so the absence of a source is a mild concern. Attribution is plausible and uncontested but not evidenced.

text: Water which is too pure has no fish.
text_raw: Water which is too pure has no fish.
author: Ts'ai Ken T'an

provenance.notes: 'Ts'ai Ken T'an' is not an author — it is the Wade-Giles title of the Caigentan (Vegetable Root Discourse), a late-Ming aphorism collection by Hong Zicheng (Hong Yingming), c. 1590. The saying itself is considerably older than that collection: the Chinese proverb 'shui zhi qing ze wu yu, ren zhi cha ze wu tu' (water too clear has no fish; a person too exacting has no companions) is recorded in Han-dynasty sources, notably Dongfang Shuo's 'Answering a Guest's Objections' as preserved in the Book of Han, and in the Da Dai Liji. So the line is a classical Chinese proverb that the Caigentan may transmit rather than originate. The author field should at minimum be corrected to name Hong Zicheng or be marked as a Chinese proverb. | Suggested reattribution: Classical Chinese proverb (Han-era; cf. Dongfang Shuo in the Book of Han) — not original to the Caigentan

text: FEAR: False Evidence Appearing Real.
text_raw: FEAR: False Evidence Appearing Real.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: An anonymous backronym long current in twelve-step recovery culture (Alcoholics Anonymous and related fellowships), where multiple expansions of FEAR circulate — 'False Evidence Appearing Real', 'Face Everything And Recover', 'Forget Everything And Run'. No identifiable originator; it is folk material and correctly listed as Unknown. Zig Ziglar and others popularized it but did not coin it as far as I know.

text: No one can go back and make a brand new start. Anyone can start from now and make a brand new ending.
text_raw: No one can go back and make a brand new start. Anyone can start from now and make a brand new ending.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: Usually credited to 'Carl Bard', a figure for whom no biographical record is generally produced — a pattern that often signals an invented or garbled attribution. A near-identical line is credited to Maria Robinson ('Nobody can go back and start a new beginning, but anyone can start today and make a new ending'), equally without a source. 'Unknown' is the honest label; I would not reattribute to either name.

text: If you don't take care of your body, where will you live?
text_raw: If you don't take care of your body, where will you live?
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: Widely credited to Kobi Yamada, the Compendium author, and it fits the aphoristic gift-book genre he works in; the attribution is common but I have seen no source citation for it. It also circulates freely as an anonymous saying. 'Unknown' is defensible; Yamada is the leading candidate but unconfirmed.

text: If you don't like something, change it. If you can't change it, change the way you think about it.
text_raw: If you don't like something, change it. If you can't change it, change the way you think about it.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: This exact wording ('change the way you think about it') is most often credited to the illustrator Mary Engelbreit, whose artwork popularized it. A closely related and better-sourced line is Maya Angelou's 'If you don't like something, change it. If you can't change it, change your attitude', which appears in her 1993 collection Wouldn't Take Nothing for My Journey Now. The two have cross-contaminated in circulation. Leaving as Unknown is safer than picking one.

text: Change is created by those whose imaginations are bigger than their circumstances.
text_raw: Change is created by those whose imaginations are bigger than their circumstances.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: I do not recognize this line or any attribution for it. It has the cadence of contemporary leadership or activist writing but I cannot place an author, book, or speech. Honest answer: unknown origin.

text: I can complain because rosebushes have thorns, or I can rejoice because thorn bushes have roses.
text_raw: I can complain because rosebushes have thorns, or I can rejoice because thorn bushes have roses.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: This is an English paraphrase of a genuine and much older line by the French writer Alphonse Karr, from Voyage autour de mon jardin (A Tour Round My Garden, 1845): some people grumble that roses have thorns; he is grateful that thorns have roses. The 'I can complain / I can rejoice' rewording is a later inspirational reformulation of unknown authorship, and it is also spuriously attributed to Abraham Lincoln — a classic Lincoln magnet attribution with no basis in his writings. Correctly listed as Unknown for this wording; the underlying thought is Karr's. | Suggested reattribution: Paraphrase of Alphonse Karr, Voyage autour de mon jardin (1845); NOT Lincoln

text: The pessimist complains about the wind, the optimist expects it to change, and the realist adjusts his sails.
text_raw: The pessimist complains about the wind, the optimist expects it to change, and the realist adjusts his sails.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: Almost always credited to William Arthur Ward, the American inspirational writer, and the attribution is consistent enough to be the leading candidate; Ward's aphorisms are, however, poorly sourced in general and this one circulates without a book or date. A sailing-metaphor variant is also attributed to Ward's contemporaries. Listing as Unknown is acceptable; Ward is the probable author but unverified.

text: The miracles of nature do not seem miracles because they are so common. If no one had ever seen a flower, even a dandelion would be the most startling event in the world.
text_raw: The miracles of nature do not seem miracles because they are so common. If no one had ever seen a flower, even a dandelion would be the most startling event in the world.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: I cannot place this. The dandelion/flower argument about wonder dulled by familiarity is a commonplace found in Chesterton, Emerson, and Carl Sagan among others, but this specific wording does not match any passage I can identify. Unknown origin.

text: In any contest between power and patience, bet on patience.
text_raw: In any contest between power and patience, bet on patience.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: In quotation anthologies this line is generally credited to 'W. B. Prescott', a name that appears attached to it and little else — the kind of thinly documented attribution that anthologies copy from one another. I cannot confirm the person or a print source, so I am not reattributing. Unknown is honest.

text: You have a unique mission to fulfill in this life, for you are capable of doing things that can be accomplished by no one else‚ and when you honor your own inner Light, keeping always attuned to the Divine Source, your purpose will continue to reveal itself, though shadows of darkness and doubt will sometimes befall your path. Keep going far enough, and you will always return to a place of shimmering light and warmth, and then shall you sense with certainty that you're traveling in the right direction, and will surely reach your destination in good time."
text_raw: You have a unique mission to fulfill in this life, for you are capable of doing things that can be accomplished by no one else‚ and when you honor your own inner Light, keeping always attuned to the Divine Source, your purpose will continue to reveal itself, though shadows of darkness and doubt will sometimes befall your path. Keep going far enough, and you will always return to a place of shimmering light and warmth, and then shall you sense with certainty that you're traveling in the right direction, and will surely reach your destination in good time."
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: Anonymous contemporary inspirational prose in the greeting-card / New Thought register (inner Light, Divine Source). No author, book, or tradition I can identify. Note also that the text carries a stray trailing double quotation mark and a corrupted character (a comma rendered as an encoding artifact after 'no one else'), suggesting it was scraped rather than transcribed from print.

text: To reflect is to reflect on the subtlest details of one's actions.
text_raw: To reflect is to reflect on the subtlest details of one's actions.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: Unrecognized. The phrasing has the flavor of a translated Buddhist or Brahma Kumaris 'thought for the day', but I cannot identify a text, teacher, or tradition. Unknown origin.

text: To laugh is to risk appearing the fool. To weep is to risk appearing sentimental. To reach out for another is to risk involvement. To expose feelings is to risk exposing your true self. To place your ideas, your dreams before a crowd is to risk their loss. To love is to risk not being loved in return. To live is to risk dying. To hope is to risk despair. To try is to risk failure. But risks must be taken, because the greatest hazard in life is to risk nothing.
text_raw: To laugh is to risk appearing the fool. To weep is to risk appearing sentimental. To reach out for another is to risk involvement. To expose feelings is to risk exposing your true self. To place your ideas, your dreams before a crowd is to risk their loss. To love is to risk not being loved in return. To live is to risk dying. To hope is to risk despair. To try is to risk failure. But risks must be taken, because the greatest hazard in life is to risk nothing.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: This is the widely circulated poem usually titled 'Risks'. It is most often credited to Leo Buscaglia, who quoted it in his lectures and books (Living, Loving and Learning), but he was a popularizer rather than the demonstrable author; the poem is also credited to Janet Rand and to William Arthur Ward, and frequently printed as anonymous. Because the competing claims cancel out and none carries a documented first printing that I can confirm, Unknown is the right label. Note the corpus version omits the poem's closing lines about the person who risks nothing.

text: Live each day as if it were your last, and one day you’ll be right.
text_raw: Live each day as if it were your last, and one day you’ll be right.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: A comic inversion of the ancient memento mori maxim (compare Marcus Aurelius and Seneca on living each day as if it were the last). The joke form circulates in many phrasings — 'and one day you'll be right', 'and one of these days you will be' — attributed variously to Jerry Rubin, Benny Hill, and others, none of which I can substantiate. Almost certainly a folk witticism with no fixed author.

text: You can never get enough of what you don’t really need.
text_raw: You can never get enough of what you don’t really need.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: Closely tracks a genuine Eric Hoffer aphorism — 'You can never get enough of what you don't really want' / 'what you don't need to make you happy' — which appears in his aphoristic writings and is consistently credited to him. The wording here ('what you don't really need') is a common variant that also circulates anonymously and in recovery and simple-living literature. Hoffer is the probable ultimate source, but the exact wording given is not his, so I am not reattributing.

text: It seems that we have to go to war every twenty years or so just to prove what we already know: there are no winners in war, only survivors.
text_raw: It seems that we have to go to war every twenty years or so just to prove what we already know: there are no winners in war, only survivors.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: Unrecognized. The sentiment 'there are no winners in war, only survivors' is a widespread commonplace with no single origin; the full sentence with the 'every twenty years' framing I cannot place to any author, speech, or novel. Unknown origin.

text: It’s impossible for an optimist to be pleasantly surprised.
text_raw: It’s impossible for an optimist to be pleasantly surprised.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: Unrecognized as a sourced quotation. It is the mirror image of a line associated with George F. Will — that the pleasant thing about being a pessimist is that you are constantly either proven right or pleasantly surprised — which is itself a widely circulated formulation of an older joke. This pessimist's-consolation gag has many anonymous variants; no identifiable author for this wording.

text: Even if you are on the right track, you'll get run over if you just sit there.
text_raw: Even if you are on the right track, you'll get run over if you just sit there.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: Popularly attributed to Will Rogers, but I know of no instance in his own writing or columns; the Will Rogers attribution appears decades after his 1935 death and quote researchers have treated it as unsupported. Anonymous newspaper-filler versions of the joke circulated in the early 20th century. Keeping the author as 'Unknown' is the honest choice; I cannot name a first printing.

text: Never be afraid to try something new. Remember, amateurs built the ark. Professionals built the Titanic.
text_raw: Never be afraid to try something new. Remember, amateurs built the ark. Professionals built the Titanic.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: Anonymous modern aphorism circulated widely in business/motivational material and on posters. I have seen it credited to various columnists and speakers, but no attribution I know of is consistent or documented. No traceable origin in my knowledge.

text: It takes five years to make an overnight success.
text_raw: It takes five years to make an overnight success.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: A show-business/startup proverb with many numeric variants ('five years', 'ten years', 'twenty years'). The best-documented relative is Eddie Cantor's line about taking twenty years to become an overnight success, but that is a different sentence and I cannot connect this five-year phrasing to any named author or first printing.

text: As artists, to cause awareness is our only strength.
text_raw: As artists, to cause awareness is our only strength.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: I cannot place this line. It has the register of a late-20th-century artist's statement or interview remark, but no author, work, or date is retrievable from my knowledge. Honest answer: unknown.

text: You vote for reality with your imagination.
text_raw: You vote for reality with your imagination.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: No recollection of this line from any author or work. It resembles aphorisms from contemporary creativity writing, but I can offer no attribution and will not guess.

text: If you don’t see God in all, then you don’t see God at all.
text_raw: "If you don’t see God in all, then you don’t see God at all."
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: Very widely circulated in Kundalini Yoga / 3HO circles as a saying of Yogi Bhajan (Harbhajan Singh Khalsa), where it appears in lecture transcripts and teaching collections. The attribution is consistent across that community but I cannot cite a specific dated lecture or printed volume, so it stays unverified. The sentiment also echoes older Sikh and Vedantic formulations, which makes an even earlier antecedent plausible. | Suggested reattribution: Yogi Bhajan (commonly credited; unconfirmed)

text: Sometimes naked, sometimes mad, now as a scholar, now as a fool, thus they appear on earth - the free ones!
text_raw: Sometimes naked, sometimes mad, now as a scholar, now as a fool, thus they appear on earth - the free ones!
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: This reads as an English rendering of a classical Sanskrit verse on the avadhuta / jivanmukta, and it is most often credited to Bhartrihari's Vairagya Shataka; it circulated in English-speaking spiritual circles partly through Ram Dass's use of it. I am reasonably but not firmly confident of the Bhartrihari source and cannot name the verse number or the translator, so the corpus author 'Unknown' is not wrong, merely incomplete. | Suggested reattribution: Bhartrihari, Vairagya Shataka (traditional Sanskrit; unconfirmed)

text: You have been hired by the universe to be yourself.
text_raw: You have been hired by the universe to be yourself.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: Unknown to me. Phrasing suggests contemporary coaching or workshop language rather than a published literary source. No attribution offered.

text: Reach high, for stars lie hidden in your soul. Dream deep, for every dream precedes the goal.
text_raw: Reach high, for stars lie hidden in your soul. Dream deep, for every dream precedes the goal.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: Consistently credited to Pamela Vaull Starr across greeting-card and anthology sources; the attribution is stable and specific enough to be worth recording, but I know of no primary publication, date, or verified biography confirming it. Stays below the promotion bar for that reason. | Suggested reattribution: Pamela Vaull Starr (commonly credited; unconfirmed)

text: See if you can stretch your heart and expand your love so that it touches not only those to whom you can give it easily, but also to those who need it more than you.
text_raw: “See if you can stretch your heart and expand your love so that it touches not only those to whom you can give it easily, but also to those who need it more than you.”
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: I cannot place this. It has the cadence of a devotional or pastoral exhortation and circulates in inspirational collections without a stable author. No attribution I can support.

text: Know love, know happiness. No love, no happiness.
text_raw: Know love, know happiness. No love, no happiness.
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: A homophone-play proverb ('know'/'no') of the same family as 'Know Jesus, know peace; no Jesus, no peace.' Anonymous formula, no traceable first author or printing.

text: Blessed are those who can laugh at themselves, for they will never cease to be amused.
text_raw: "Blessed are those who can laugh at themselves, for they will never cease to be amused."
author: Unknown

provenance.notes: One of the modern mock-beatitudes that circulate anonymously; I have seen it credited to several different clergy and humorists with no consistency. No documented origin in my knowledge.

text: When you see that God acts through you at every moment, in every movement of mind and body, you attain true freedom. When you realize the truth, and cling to nothing in the world, you enter eternal life.
text_raw: When you see that God acts through you at every moment, in every movement of mind and body, you attain true freedom. When you realize the truth, and cling to nothing in the world, you enter eternal life.
author: Upanishads

provenance.notes: Plausibly Upanishadic in substance — the closing clause echoes the Isha Upanishad's 'attains immortality / eternal life' (amrtam asnute) and the renunciation formula of Isha 1-2 — but this is a loose, heavily paraphrastic English rendering and I cannot match it to a specific Upanishad or verse. The theistic framing ('God acts through you') suggests a devotional translator's hand rather than a literal one. The generic attribution 'Upanishads' may well be right in spirit; it is not verifiable from what I know.

text: What sane person could live in this world and not be crazy?
text_raw: What sane person could live in this world and not be crazy?
author: Ursula LeGuin

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Lathe of Heaven, Ursula K. Le Guin, 1971 (recalled, not confirmed)
provenance.notes: I recall this line from Le Guin's The Lathe of Heaven, a novel whose whole subject is sanity and a world gone wrong, and the attribution to Le Guin is consistent wherever I have seen it quoted. I am confident it is hers; I am less confident of the exact novel and cannot cite chapter or page, so the source is flagged as recalled. Note also that the corpus spells the surname 'LeGuin' — the correct form is Ursula K. Le Guin.

text: The creative adult is the child who has survived.
text_raw: The creative adult is the child who has survived.
author: Ursula LeGuin

provenance.notes: This is a well-documented misattribution. Le Guin herself denied writing it, stating on her own website that the line was not hers and asking that it stop being credited to her; quote researchers traced the sentence to the mathematics educator Julian F. Fleron, who wrote a close version in his own work before it drifted onto Le Guin. Confidence 0.15 rates the (weak) attribution to Le Guin, not the misattribution finding, which I hold with reasonable strength. Recommend removing Le Guin as author. | Suggested reattribution: Julian F. Fleron

text: My imagination makes me human and makes me a fool; it gives me all the world and exiles me from it.
text_raw: My imagination makes me human and makes me a fool; it gives me all the world and exiles me from it.
author: Ursula LeGuin

provenance.notes: Attributed to Le Guin with reasonable consistency in quote collections, and the thought (imagination as both gift and exile) is characteristic of her essays on fantasy. But I cannot place it in a specific novel, essay, or address, and Le Guin is a magnet for plausible-sounding lines she did not write (see q_1397 in this same batch). Holding below the promotion bar until a text can be named.

text: The greatest religious problem today is how to be both a mystic and a militant; in other words how to combine the search for an expansion of inner awareness with effective social action, and how to feel one's true identity in both.
text_raw: The greatest religious problem today is how to be both a mystic and a militant; in other words how to combine the search for an expansion of inner awareness with effective social action, and how to feel one's true identity in both.
author: Ursula LeGuin

provenance.notes: Almost certainly not Ursula K. Le Guin. The vocabulary is that of academic religious studies — 'the greatest religious problem today', 'expansion of inner awareness', mysticism paired with social action — and Le Guin, a lifelong non-believer who wrote about Taoism in a very different register, is an implausible author. The likeliest explanation is a first-name collision with another Ursula in a quote list; the attribution I associate with this line is Ursula King, the scholar of mysticism and Teilhard de Chardin, whose subject matter matches exactly. I am not confident enough in that to enter it as a reattribution, so the field is left null. Recommend removing the Le Guin attribution regardless.

text: If you see a whole thing - it seems that it's always beautiful. Planets, lives.... But close up a world's all dirt and rocks. And day to day, life's a hard job, you get tired, you lose the pattern.
text_raw: If you see a whole thing - it seems that it's always beautiful. Planets, lives.... But close up a world's all dirt and rocks. And day to day, life's a hard job, you get tired, you lose the pattern.
author: Ursula LeGuin

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Dispossessed, Ursula K. Le Guin, 1974 (recalled, not confirmed)
provenance.notes: I recall this as Shevek's line in The Dispossessed — the imagery of a world that is beautiful whole and 'all dirt and rocks' close up fits Anarres and the novel's argument directly, and the diction ('you lose the pattern') is Le Guin's. Confident in the author, reasonably confident in the novel, unable to cite chapter or page from memory, so it is marked attributed rather than verified. Surname in the corpus should be corrected to Le Guin.

text: Just as surely as distress must follow self-deceit, healing must follow self-honesty.
text_raw: Just as surely as distress must follow self-deceit, healing must follow self-honesty.
author: Vernon Howard

provenance.notes: Vernon Howard (1918-1992) was a real and prolific American self-help and inner-work author, and this line is entirely consistent with his idiom and is consistently credited to him. I cannot name which of his many books it comes from, and his corpus is large enough that unattributed paraphrases circulate under his name, so this stays unverified.

text: Self-knowledge is the great power by which we comprehend and control our lives.
text_raw: Self-knowledge is the great power by which we comprehend and control our lives.
author: Vernon Howard

provenance.notes: Same assessment as q_1402: stable and plausible attribution to Vernon Howard, whose books turn on self-knowledge as the operative power, but no specific title, edition, or year that I can name. Honest verdict is attribution-without-source.

text: Experience is a hard teacher, because she gives the test first, the lesson afterwards.
text_raw: Experience is a hard teacher, because she gives the test first, the lesson afterwards.
author: Vernon Saunders

provenance.earliest_print_source: This Week magazine, 14 August 1960 (attributed to Vernon Law; recalled, not confirmed)
provenance.notes: The author name in the corpus is garbled. This is Vernon Sanders Law, the Pittsburgh Pirates pitcher and 1960 Cy Young winner — 'Vernon Saunders' appears to be his middle name mistaken for a surname. The saying is credited to him in a 1960 magazine piece and the attribution has been examined and upheld by quote researchers. Confident in the person; the exact publication date is from memory and should be checked before it is printed as fact. | Suggested reattribution: Vernon Sanders Law

text: Look at usual things with unusual eyes.
text_raw: Look at usual things with unusual eyes.
author: Vico Magistretti

provenance.notes: Widely repeated in design writing and exhibition material as a motto of the Milanese architect and designer Vico Magistretti (1920-2006), and it is consistent with how he described his method. I cannot trace it to a specific interview, lecture, or publication, and short designer mottos of this kind are frequently paraphrased in translation from Italian, so the wording may not be his exactly.

text: There is one thing stronger than all the armies in the world, and that is an idea whose time has come.
text_raw: There is one thing stronger than all the armies in the world, and that is an idea whose time has come.
author: Victor Hugo

provenance.earliest_print_source: Histoire d'un crime, Victor Hugo (written 1852, published 1877), conclusion: 'On resiste a l'invasion des armees; on ne resiste pas a l'invasion des idees.'
provenance.notes: Rooted in Hugo but not a translation of him. Hugo's actual sentence, at the close of Histoire d'un crime, is 'One resists the invasion of armies; one does not resist the invasion of ideas.' The familiar English form with 'stronger than all the armies in the world' and 'an idea whose time has come' is a loose 19th-century paraphrase that took on a life of its own in English-language oratory and journalism. Attributing the sentiment to Hugo is fair; presenting this wording as his words is not. Recommend flagging the text as a paraphrase, or replacing it with the accurate translation.

text: If you aren’t fired with enthusiasm, you will be fired with enthusiasm.
text_raw: If you aren’t fired with enthusiasm, you will be fired with enthusiasm.
author: Vince Lombardi

provenance.notes: A pun-shaped motivational quip ('fired with enthusiasm' / 'fired with enthusiasm') that circulates almost entirely in sales and management literature. I know of no Lombardi speech, book, or contemporaneous report containing it, and Lombardi died in 1970 while the line appears to spread in business contexts later. Lombardi is a magnet for coach-flavored aphorisms he did not originate. I cannot name the true source, so no reattribution is offered.

text: Your profession is not what brings home your weekly paycheck, your profession is what you're put here on earth to do, with such passion and such intensity that it becomes spiritual in calling.
text_raw: Your profession is not what brings home your weekly paycheck, your profession is what you're put here on earth to do, with such passion and such intensity that it becomes spiritual in calling.
author: Vincent van Gogh

provenance.notes: Not van Gogh. The vocabulary is anachronistic and un-translatable back into his idiom: 'weekly paycheck' and 'spiritual in calling' belong to modern American self-help prose, not to the 1870s-80s Dutch/French letters to Theo. I cannot recall this passage anywhere in the collected letters, which are exhaustively indexed. It reads like a 20th-century vocation-and-calling passage that acquired a van Gogh byline. I cannot identify the real author, so no reattribution.

text: I dream my painting and I paint my dream.
text_raw: I dream my painting and I paint my dream.
author: Vincent van Gogh

provenance.notes: One of the most-reproduced van Gogh lines and one of the least supported. I cannot place it in the letters, and my recollection is that reference collections file it as unsourced or disputed rather than citing a letter. Its epigrammatic symmetry is unlike his actual prose, which is discursive. Popular but evidentially empty; treat as unsourced unless a letter citation surfaces.

text: If you do not tell the truth about yourself you cannot tell it about other people.
text_raw: If you do not tell the truth about yourself you cannot tell it about other people.
author: Virginia Woolf

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Woolf and entirely consonant with her essays on autobiography and biography, but I cannot place the exact essay, diary entry, or letter. Plausible sources include the posthumous essay collections or the autobiographical writings, and I will not name one I cannot confirm. Attribution is likely correct; the citation is missing.

text: Every great person, every successful person, no matter what the field of endeavor, has known the magic that lies in these words: Every adversity has the seed of an equivalent or greater benefit.
text_raw: Every great person, every successful person, no matter what the field of endeavor, has known the magic that lies in these words: Every adversity has the seed of an equivalent or greater benefit.
author: W. Clement Stone

provenance.notes: Stone did use and promote this maxim — it is central to Success Through a Positive Mental Attitude (1960, with Napoleon Hill) and to his later books — but the core formula descends from Napoleon Hill's 'every adversity, every failure, every heartache carries with it the seed of an equal or greater benefit' (Think and Grow Rich, 1937). The framing sentence here reads like Stone quoting the maxim rather than coining it. Attribution to Stone is defensible; the underlying idea is Hill's, so I have not pinned a print source for this exact sentence.

text: Only a mediocre person is always at his best.
text_raw: Only a mediocre person is always at his best.
author: W. Somerset Maugham

provenance.notes: Circulates with competing attributions. The closely parallel 'only the mediocre are always at their best' is widely attributed to Jean Giraudoux, and variants appear under Maugham and other early-20th-century wits. I cannot locate the line in Maugham's own texts. Genuine attribution uncertainty rather than a clear misattribution, so no reattribution is offered.

text: Every atom belonging to you equally belongs to me.
text_raw: "Every atom belonging to you equally belongs to me."
author: Walt Whitman

provenance.earliest_print_source: 'Song of Myself', section 1, Leaves of Grass, Walt Whitman
provenance.notes: The idea and the author are certainly Whitman, but the wording is corrupted. The printed line, in section 1 of 'Song of Myself', is 'For every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you' — spoken by the poet to the reader. The corpus version reverses the direction and flattens 'as good belongs' into 'equally belongs'. Recommend replacing with the canonical wording before promotion; confidence is held below the bar because what is in the corpus is not what Whitman wrote.

text: Our lives improve only when we take chances... and the first and most difficult risk we can take is to be honest with ourselves.
text_raw: Our lives improve only when we take chances... and the first and most difficult risk we can take is to be honest with ourselves.
author: Walter Anderson

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Walter Anderson, the Parade magazine editor and author of self-development books in the 1990s. My best guess is that it comes from The Confidence Course (1997) or a related Parade column, but I cannot confirm which, so I leave the print source null rather than guess a title into the record. Author attribution is probably right; sourcing is thin.

text: If you realized that the nurtured spiritual part of yourself would accompany you on your eternal journey and that everything that you have labored so hard to accumulate would vanish the instant you depart this world, would it alter your daily agenda?
text_raw: If you realized that the nurtured spiritual part of yourself would accompany you on your eternal journey and that everything that you have labored so hard to accumulate would vanish the instant you depart this world, would it alter your daily agenda?
author: Walter Cooper

provenance.notes: I cannot place this quote or identify which Walter Cooper is meant — the name is shared by several people (a chemist, a broadcaster, others) and none is a figure I associate with devotional or inspirational writing. The prose is generic contemporary spiritual-motivational writing of the kind that circulates in anthologies and newsletters without provenance. Honest answer: unknown.

text: One's true religion is what one cares about most.
text_raw: One's true religion is what one cares about most.
author: Walter Starcke

provenance.notes: Walter Starcke was a real New Thought author (The Ultimate Revolution, The Third Appearance, It's All God), and this aphorism is consistent with his subject matter, so the attribution is at least plausible. But I cannot locate the line in any of his books and know it only as a free-floating quotation. Note the sentiment is a commonplace with older analogues (Tillich's 'ultimate concern', among others), which makes independent origination easy and attribution weak.

text: To be authentic is literally to be your own author… to discover your own native energies and desires, and then to find your own way of acting on them.
text_raw: To be authentic is literally to be your own author… to discover your own native energies and desires, and then to find your own way of acting on them.
author: Warren G. Bennis

provenance.earliest_print_source: On Becoming a Leader, Warren Bennis, 1989
provenance.notes: I recall this passage distinctly as Bennis, including the parenthetical etymological aside about 'authentic' and 'author' that usually accompanies it, and I place it in On Becoming a Leader (1989), his central statement on self-invention as the ground of leadership. I have not pinned the chapter and cannot rule out one of his later books or an essay reprint, so confidence sits below the verified band.

text: An inexhaustible good nature is one of the most precious gifts of heaven, spreading itself like oil over the troubled sea of thought, and keeping the mind smooth and equable in the roughest weather.
text_raw: An inexhaustible good nature is one of the most precious gifts of heaven, spreading itself like oil over the troubled sea of thought, and keeping the mind smooth and equable in the roughest weather.
author: Washington Irving

provenance.notes: The diction — 'spreading itself like oil over the troubled sea of thought' — is unmistakably early-19th-century and entirely characteristic of Irving's sketch essays, and the attribution is consistent wherever the line appears. But I cannot pin which collection it comes from (The Sketch Book, Bracebridge Hall, and Wolfert's Roost are all plausible), so I leave the print source null rather than guess a title.

text: Do not abandon trust when your ego thinks things should be different than they are.
text_raw: Do not abandon trust when your ego thinks things should be different than they are.
author: Wayne Dyer

provenance.notes: Idiomatically Dyer — the ego-versus-acceptance framing is his standard vocabulary across decades of books and talks — but I cannot locate the sentence in a specific book, and much of what circulates under his name comes from unrecorded lectures or from paraphrase. Plausible author, no source.

text: Have in your mind that which would constitute a miracle for you. Get the vision. Suspend disbelief and skepticism. Allow yourself to take the journey toward real magic.
text_raw: Have in your mind that which would constitute a miracle for you. Get the vision. Suspend disbelief and skepticism. Allow yourself to take the journey toward real magic.
author: Wayne Dyer

provenance.notes: The closing phrase 'the journey toward real magic' points strongly to Dyer's Real Magic: Creating Miracles in Everyday Life (1992), and the passage's sequence — hold the miracle in mind, get the vision, suspend disbelief — matches that book's method. That is inference from the title phrase rather than recall of the specific page, so I leave the print source null and hold confidence below the promotion bar.

text: Motivation is what happens when you take hold of an idea. Inspiration is what happens when an idea takes hold of you.
text_raw: Motivation is what happens when you take hold of an idea. Inspiration is what happens when an idea takes hold of you.
author: Wayne Dyer

provenance.notes: This motivation/inspiration contrast is a signature Wayne Dyer formulation and matches the central argument of his book Inspiration: Your Ultimate Calling (2006), where he distinguishes 'in-spirit' inspiration from grasping an idea by will. I am confident the idea and phrasing are his, but I cannot confirm the exact wording against a page in that book from memory, so I have not filled in a print source. Wording circulates in several near-variants ('...carries you where you are intended to go').

text: You miss 100% of the shots you don't take.
text_raw: You miss 100% of the shots you don't take.
author: Wayne Gretsky

provenance.notes: Genuinely Gretzky's; he used the line in press interviews in the early 1980s and it spread from there. I do not have a reliable memory of the exact first newspaper column and date, so I have left the print source blank rather than guess. NOTE: the author field is misspelled 'Wayne Gretsky' — it should be 'Wayne Gretzky'. | Suggested reattribution: Wayne Gretzky (spelling correction only)

text: I skate to where the puck is going to be, not where it has been.
text_raw: I skate to where the puck is going to be, not where it has been.
author: Wayne Gretzky

provenance.notes: Widely and consistently attributed to Gretzky from the 1980s onward, and he did say it. Important caveat: Gretzky himself repeatedly credited the advice to his father, Walter Gretzky, who coached it into him as a boy ('go to where the puck is going, not where it's been'). So Wayne is the popularizer and speaker; Walter is arguably the originator. Exact wording varies between retellings.

text: It's never too late to have a happy childhood.
text_raw: It's never too late to have a happy childhood.
author: Wayne W. Dyer

provenance.notes: I recall this line as Tom Robbins's, appearing in his novel Still Life with Woodpecker (1980), and it also circulates as a recovery-movement slogan from roughly the same era. The Wayne Dyer attribution appears to be a later quote-site accretion — Dyer used the sentiment in talks, but he is not the source. I am confident enough about the Robbins origin to flag the Dyer attribution as doubtful, but not confident enough to call the reattribution settled. | Suggested reattribution: Tom Robbins (probable; Still Life with Woodpecker, 1980 — unconfirmed)

text: Liberation is liberation from the idea of liberation.
text_raw: Liberation is liberation from the idea of liberation.
author: Wei Wu Wei

provenance.notes: Wei Wu Wei (pen name of Terence Gray) wrote exactly this kind of self-cancelling Advaita aphorism across Ask the Awakened, All Else Is Bondage, Open Secret, and Posthumous Pieces, so the attribution is stylistically very plausible. But I cannot place this sentence in a specific book or page, and Wei Wu Wei's phrasings are often paraphrased and compressed when quoted online. Honest verdict: plausible, unverified.

text: There must be new contact between men and the earth; the earth must be newly seen and heard and felt and smelled and tasted; there must be a renewal of the wisdom that comes with knowing clearly the pain and the pleasure and the risk and the responsibility of being alive in this world.
text_raw: There must be new contact between men and the earth; the earth must be newly seen and heard and felt and smelled and tasted; there must be a renewal of the wisdom that comes with knowing clearly the pain and the pleasure and the risk and the responsibility of being alive in this world.
author: Wendell Berry

provenance.notes: The diction, cadence, and argument are unmistakably Wendell Berry's, and the passage reads as authentic to his late-1960s/1970s essay work (the sensibility of The Long-Legged House, 1969, and The Unsettling of America, 1977). I cannot confirm which essay it comes from with the confidence needed to print a citation, so the source field is left null rather than guessed.

text: Live as if your life depends on it.
text_raw: Live as if your life depends on it.
author: Werner Erhard

provenance.notes: Circulates in est/Landmark-adjacent material and quote compilations credited to Werner Erhard, and the imperative framing fits his idiom. I have no primary source — no transcript, book, or dated talk — and Erhard's aphorisms are heavily paraphrased in secondhand collections. Also note the corpus category is 'humor', which looks like a mis-tag; the line is not comic.

text: Never let yesterday use up too much of today.
text_raw: Never let yesterday use up too much of today.
author: Will Rogers

provenance.notes: Very widely printed as Will Rogers, but Rogers is a documented misattribution magnet: his enormous body of dated newspaper columns means genuine lines are usually traceable, and this one is not, in my knowledge. No column, broadcast, or contemporaneous printing I can point to. Plausible but unsupported.

text: Why not go out on a limb? That's where the fruit is.
text_raw: Why not go out on a limb? That's where the fruit is.
author: Will Rogers

provenance.notes: This saying floats between several claimants — Will Rogers, Mark Twain, Frank Scully, and later Shirley MacLaine — which is the classic signature of an orphan aphorism that gets adopted by famous names. The Twain version is certainly spurious. I know of no Rogers source, and the multiplicity of claimants argues against him specifically.

text: Live in such a way that you would not be ashamed to sell your parrot to the town gossip.
text_raw: Live in such a way that you would not be ashamed to sell your parrot to the town gossip.
author: Will Rogers

provenance.notes: Among the more consistently Rogers-attributed lines in this cluster — the small-town parrot-and-gossip image fits his voice and era, and it appears across Rogers collections without competing claimants. Still, I cannot name a column or dated source, so it stays below the verification bar.

text: If you find yourself in a hole, the first thing to do is stop digging.
text_raw: If you find yourself in a hole, the first thing to do is stop digging.
author: Will Rogers

provenance.notes: This is the proverbial 'first law of holes', which was in circulation as an anonymous saying well before it began being credited to Will Rogers, and it was later popularized in British politics by Denis Healey. Rogers attributions to it appear to be retrofitted. Probable true origin is anonymous proverb rather than a named author, so I have left suggested_reattribution null.

text: God gave you a gift of 86,400 seconds today. Have you used one to say thank you?
text_raw: "God gave you a gift of 86,400 seconds today. Have you used one to say thank you?"
author: William A. Ward

provenance.notes: William Arthur Ward (1921-1994) was a prolific devotional aphorist — Fountains of Faith and widely syndicated maxims — and the 86,400-seconds gratitude line is attributed to him with unusual consistency across sources. But Ward's aphorisms circulate mostly through greeting-card and compilation channels without page citations, and I cannot place this one in a specific published collection. Note the author field gives 'William A. Ward'; the standard form is 'William Arthur Ward'.

text: There are two great days in a person's life; the day we are born and the day we discover why.
text_raw: There are two great days in a person's life; the day we are born and the day we discover why.
author: William Barclay

provenance.notes: Barclay, the Scottish theologian and commentator, is the most plausible claimant and this fits his homiletic register. Important context: the better-known variant ('The two most important days in your life are the day you are born and the day you find out why') is routinely credited to Mark Twain, and that Twain attribution is unsupported — no Twain source exists. So the Barclay line is the sounder of the two, but I still cannot point to a commentary or book where he wrote it.

text: The greatness of a man's power is the measure of his surrender.
text_raw: The greatness of a man's power is the measure of his surrender.
author: William Booth

provenance.notes: Consistently credited to William Booth, founder of the Salvation Army, in Christian devotional compilations, and the paradox of power-through-surrender is squarely his theology. I have no primary source — no sermon, War Cry issue, or biography page — and Booth quotations in circulation are frequently secondhand recollections rather than documented text.

text: Success seems to be largely a matter of hanging on after others have let go.
text_raw: Success seems to be largely a matter of hanging on after others have let go.
author: William Feather

provenance.notes: William Feather (1889-1981) was a Cleveland publisher who wrote aphorisms for his own periodical, The William Feather Magazine, and later collections — so unlike orphan proverbs, Feather attributions usually do trace back to a real author who published his own maxims. This line is attributed to him without competing claimants. I cannot cite the specific issue or collection, which keeps it under the bar.

text: He who would acquire fame must not show himself afraid of censure. The dread of censure is the death of genius.
text_raw: He who would acquire fame must not show himself afraid of censure. The dread of censure is the death of genius.
author: William Gilmore Simms

provenance.notes: Attributed to the antebellum Southern novelist and critic William Gilmore Simms in nineteenth-century quotation dictionaries and later compilations, and the sentiment and diction are period-appropriate for his critical prose. I cannot name the essay or volume it comes from, so no print source is given.

text: There is a peaceful quality to an authentic experience of love that penetrates to our core, touching a part of ourselves that has always been there. True love activates this inner being, filling us with warmth and light. An authentic experience of love does not ask us to look a certain way, drive a certain car, or have a certain job. It takes us as we are, no changes required. When people truly love us, their love for us awakens our love for ourselves. They remind us that what we seek outside of ourselves is a mirror image of the lover within. In this way, true love never makes us feel needy or lacking or anxious. Instead, true love empowers us with its implicit message that we are, always have been, and always will be, made of love.
text_raw: There is a peaceful quality to an authentic experience of love that penetrates to our core, touching a part of ourselves that has always been there. True love activates this inner being, filling us with warmth and light. An authentic experience of love does not ask us to look a certain way, drive a certain car, or have a certain job. It takes us as we are, no changes required. When people truly love us, their love for us awakens our love for ourselves. They remind us that what we seek outside of ourselves is a mirror image of the lover within. In this way, true love never makes us feel needy or lacking or anxious. Instead, true love empowers us with its implicit message that we are, always have been, and always will be, made of love.
author: William Gilmore Simms

provenance.notes: Almost certainly not William Gilmore Simms, who died in 1870. This passage is unmistakably modern therapeutic self-help prose — 'authentic experience of love', 'activates this inner being', 'the lover within', plus the anachronistic 'drive a certain car'. An automobile reference alone rules out a nineteenth-century author. The style closely matches contemporary daily-inspiration writing of the DailyOM sort, but I will not name an author I cannot confirm. Recommend rejecting the Simms attribution outright; this looks like a quote-site database collision, possibly compounded by the adjacent genuine Simms entry (q_1451).

text: History records the successes of people with objectives and a sense of direction. Oblivion is the position of small people overwhelmed by obstacles.
text_raw: History records the successes of people with objectives and a sense of direction. Oblivion is the position of small people overwhelmed by obstacles.
author: William H. Danforth

provenance.notes: William H. Danforth, founder of Ralston Purina, wrote the motivational classic I Dare You! (1931), and this line's goal-setting rhetoric fits that book's idiom, so it is a plausible source. I cannot confirm the sentence appears there, and business-motivation quotes of this vintage are frequently paraphrased or reassigned between authors in compilations.

text: To live content with small means; to see elegance rather than luxury, and refinement rather than fashion; to be worthy, not respectable, and wealthy, not rich; to listen to stars and birds, babes and sages with open heart; to study hard; to think quietly, act frankly, talk gently, await occasions, hurry never; in a word, to let the spiritual unbidden and unconscious, grow up through the common - this is my symphony.
text_raw: To live content with small means; to see elegance rather than luxury, and refinement rather than fashion; to be worthy, not respectable, and wealthy, not rich; to listen to stars and birds, babes and sages with open heart; to study hard; to think quietly, act frankly, talk gently, await occasions, hurry never; in a word, to let the spiritual unbidden and unconscious, grow up through the common - this is my symphony.
author: William Henry Channing

provenance.notes: This is the well-known prose poem 'My Symphony', attributed to the Unitarian minister William Henry Channing (1810-1884) in anthologies since the late nineteenth century — a long-standing and dominant attribution. Two cautions: it is regularly confused with his more famous uncle, William Ellery Channing, and some reference works treat the authorship as traditional rather than documented.
