The corpus text also reads 'to listen to stars and birds'; the familiar wording is 'to listen to stars and birds, to babes and sages, with open heart'.

text: The best use of life is investing it in something which will outlast life.
text_raw: The best use of life is investing it in something which will outlast life.
author: William James

provenance.notes: Widely credited to William James and popularized further by its use in modern devotional writing. It circulates in several wordings ('The greatest use of a life is to spend it for something that will outlast it'), which is a warning sign, and I cannot locate it in James's published works, essays, or letters from memory. Plausible but unverified; the variant-wording spread suggests secondhand transmission rather than a quoted text.

text: The greatest weapon against stress is our ability to choose one thought over another.
text_raw: The greatest weapon against stress is our ability to choose one thought over another.
author: William James

provenance.notes: Strongly doubtful as William James. 'Stress' in the psychological sense used here is a mid-twentieth-century coinage — Hans Selye's work from the 1930s onward — and would have been anachronistic for James, who died in 1910; he wrote about strain, worry, and habit, not 'stress'. The sentence also has the compressed, modern self-help cadence of a wellness-poster line rather than James's prose. I know of no source in his writings. Recommend dropping the James attribution; true origin unknown.

text: Nothing is so fatiguing as the eternal hanging on of an uncompleted task.
text_raw: Nothing is so fatiguing as the eternal hanging on of an uncompleted task.
author: William James

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to James across quote dictionaries for many decades, and the register matches his prose on fatigue and effort (cf. 'The Energies of Men'). I cannot place it in a specific James text from memory, so no print citation is offered. Attribution plausible and stable, but unverified — deliberately below the promotion bar.

text: Most people never run far enough on their first wind to find out if they've got a second. Give your dreams all you've got and you'll be amazed at the energy that comes out of you.
text_raw: Most people never run far enough on their first wind to find out if they've got a second. Give your dreams all you've got and you'll be amazed at the energy that comes out of you.
author: William James

provenance.notes: James genuinely wrote about the 'second wind' and habitual fatigue barriers in 'The Energies of Men' (1907), which is almost certainly the seed. But the second sentence — 'Give your dreams all you've got and you'll be amazed at the energy that comes out of you' — is mid-20th-century American motivational register, not James's 1907 prose. This reads as a self-help paraphrase grown onto a real James theme. Treat as unsourced.

text: Destiny is not a matter of chance, it is a matter of choice; it is not a thing to be waited for, it is a thing to be achieved.
text_raw: Destiny is not a matter of chance, it is a matter of choice; it is not a thing to be waited for, it is a thing to be achieved.
author: William Jennings Bryan

provenance.notes: Long-standing and consistent attribution to Bryan in quote collections, and the cadence matches his oratory. I have a weak recollection that it comes from a turn-of-the-century Bryan address, but I cannot name the speech with confidence, so no citation is given. Frequently reproduced without source, which is the usual warning sign; still, no competing claimant is known to me.

text: Right is right, even if everyone is against it; and wrong is wrong, even if everyone is for it.
text_raw: Right is right, even if everyone is against it; and wrong is wrong, even if everyone is for it.
author: William Penn

provenance.notes: Attributed to Penn very widely, but I cannot place it in Some Fruits of Solitude or any other Penn text I know. The same line circulates under Augustine and under Charles Spurgeon, which is the classic signature of a floating aphorism that later acquired a famous name. Uncertain enough that I will not name a true author.

text: We cannot conceive of matter being formed of nothing, since things require a seed to start from... Therefore there is not anything which returns to nothing, but all things return dissolved into their elements.
text_raw: We cannot conceive of matter being formed of nothing, since things require a seed to start from... Therefore there is not anything which returns to nothing, but all things return dissolved into their elements.
author: William Shakespeare

provenance.notes: Not Shakespeare — nothing in this diction, doctrine, or vocabulary belongs to him. This is classical Epicurean physics: nothing comes from nothing, things arise from 'seeds', and nothing perishes into nothing but dissolves back into its elements. That is the argument of Lucretius, De Rerum Natura, Book I, and 'seed' renders the Lucretian semina. Pliny the Elder states a close version in the Natural History, so I cannot be certain which classical author this English translation comes from, and I do not know the translator. Confident it is not Shakespeare; only probable that it is Lucretius. | Suggested reattribution: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura (probable; classical Epicurean source — not Shakespeare)

text: Humility does not mean thinking less of yourself than other people, nor does it mean having a low opinion of your gifts. It means freedom from thinking about yourself at all.
text_raw: Humility does not mean thinking less of yourself than other people, nor does it mean having a low opinion of your gifts. It means freedom from thinking about yourself at all.
author: William Temple

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to William Temple, Archbishop of Canterbury, and consistent with his devotional writing of the 1930s (Christian Faith and Life, 1931, is the citation usually given, though I cannot confirm the page or that it is correct). Worth noting the neighbouring case: the popular 'Humility is not thinking less of yourself, but thinking of yourself less' is routinely misattributed to C. S. Lewis, who did not write it; this Temple passage is the older and better-grounded member of the family.

text: Success is not final. Failure is not fatal. It is the courage to continue that counts.
text_raw: Success is not final. Failure is not fatal. It is the courage to continue that counts.
author: Winston Churchill

provenance.notes: A well-known Churchill fake. It does not appear in the Churchill canon, and the International Churchill Society lists it among quotations he never said. Quote Investigator traced early forms to 1930s American motivational and advertising copy ('Success is never final and failure never fatal; it's courage that counts'), well before it was pinned to Churchill. I recall that provenance but will not present it as a citation. No true author identifiable.

text: The pessimist sees difficulty in every opportunity. The optimist sees the opportunity in every difficulty.
text_raw: The pessimist sees difficulty in every opportunity. The optimist sees the opportunity in every difficulty.
author: Winston Churchill

provenance.notes: Ubiquitously attributed to Churchill but never sourced. Langworth's Churchill by Himself does not locate it in any speech, letter, or book, and similar optimist/pessimist antitheses circulated before Churchill was attached to them. Plausible he said something like it in conversation; no evidence he did. Note this is a near-duplicate of q_1471 — the corpus should keep one.

text: A pessimist sees the difficulty in every opportunity; an optimist sees the opportunity in every difficulty.
text_raw: A pessimist sees the difficulty in every opportunity; an optimist sees the opportunity in every difficulty.
author: Winston Churchill

provenance.notes: Same unsourced Churchill attribution as q_1469, in the more idiomatic wording. No primary source exists in the Churchill canon. Duplicate of q_1469 — deduplicate before promotion.

text: At some time in everyone's life they will stumble across opportunity. Sadly, most people will pick themselves up and walk away as though nothing had ever happened.
text_raw: At some time in everyone's life they will stumble across opportunity. Sadly, most people will pick themselves up and walk away as though nothing had ever happened.
author: Winston Churchill

provenance.notes: A corrupted derivative. The line attributed to Churchill is about truth, not opportunity: 'Men occasionally stumble over the truth, but most of them pick themselves up and hurry off as if nothing ever happened.' Even that version is attributed rather than sourced to a document. This 'opportunity' rewrite has no standing at all; it is a motivational-poster mutation of the truth version.

text: It's not enough that we do our best; sometimes we have to do what's required.
text_raw: It's not enough that we do our best; sometimes we have to do what's required.
author: Winston Churchill

provenance.notes: A smoothed paraphrase. Churchill's documented sentiment is blunter: 'It is no use saying, "We are doing our best." You have got to succeed in doing what is necessary' — from his wartime remarks of the early 1940s. The polished 'It's not enough that we do our best; sometimes we have to do what's required' circulates without a source and appears to be a later rewrite. The idea is Churchill's; this wording is not established as his.

text: We make a living by what we get, but we make a life by what we give.
text_raw: "We make a living by what we get, but we make a life by what we give."
author: Winston Churchill

provenance.notes: Not Churchill. Absent from the Churchill canon and listed by the International Churchill Society among quotations wrongly credited to him. The saying circulated in the early twentieth century before being attached to his name; it is also attributed to Norman MacEwan, though I cannot confirm that claim, so I am not naming a replacement author.

text: If you're going through hell, keep going.
text_raw: If you're going through hell, keep going.
author: Winston Churchill

provenance.notes: One of the most confidently repeated Churchill quotations he demonstrably never said. It appears in no speech, book, letter, or contemporary record; the International Churchill Society lists it as misattributed, and researchers have found no instance before the late twentieth century, decades after his death. Origin unknown.

text: I not only use all the brains that I have, but all that I can borrow.
text_raw: I not only use all the brains that I have, but all that I can borrow.
author: Woodrow Wilson

provenance.notes: Long attributed to Wilson and included in mainstream quotation dictionaries under his name, which is decent secondary evidence. I cannot name the speech or letter it comes from, so no citation is given. No competing claimant known to me.

text: Since it is all too clear, it takes time to grasp it. When you understand that it's foolish to look for fire with fire, the meal is already cooked.
text_raw: Since it is all too clear, it takes time to grasp it. When you understand that it's foolish to look for fire with fire, the meal is already cooked.
author: Wu-men Huikai

provenance.notes: Attributed to Wumen and almost certainly one of his capping verses in the Wumenguan — the image is the standard one rendered elsewhere as 'It is too clear and so it is hard to see; a dunce once searched for fire with a lighted lantern — had he known what fire was, he could have cooked his rice sooner.' I cannot reliably name the case number, and the English is a modern paraphrase, so I am not supplying a citation. Attribution to Wumen is consistent across renderings; the specific source line is not established here.

text: The fundamental delusion of humanity is to suppose that I am here and you are out there.
text_raw: The fundamental delusion of humanity is to suppose that I am here and you are out there.
author: Yasutani Roshi

provenance.notes: Consistently attributed to Hakuun Yasutani (Yasutani Roshi) in Zen literature in English, where it circulates as a remark from his teaching rather than from a book he wrote — plausible, since his teaching reached print mainly through students. I associate it with the Kapleau/Three Pillars of Zen lineage of texts and with its use as an epigraph in later nature and Zen writing, but I cannot pin a first printing, so no citation is given. Attribution stable; sourcing unresolved.

text: To assume is to be deceived.
text_raw: To assume is to be deceived.
author: Yiddish proverb

provenance.notes: Circulates in English-language collections of Yiddish proverbs, but I cannot place it in any specific anthology (Ayalti, Kumove, Rosten, etc.) from my training knowledge. Generic proverb attributions of this kind rarely have a traceable first appearance. No evidence it is NOT a Yiddish proverb either — just no confirmation.

text: When an individual has achieved complete understanding of her true self, she will no longer be disturbed by the distracting influences within and around her.
text_raw: When an individual has achieved complete understanding of her true self, she will no longer be disturbed by the distracting influences within and around her.
author: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali

provenance.notes: Not a recognized translation of any sutra I can pin down. The sense plausibly corresponds to Yoga Sutra I.16 (para-vairagya: dispassion arising from discernment of purusha, the true self, leaving one untroubled by the gunas), but the English is a loose modern paraphrase rather than a standard rendering. The feminine pronouns suggest a deliberately gender-inclusive modern translation or a paraphrase collection; I cannot identify which, and will not guess. Attribution to the Yoga Sutras is plausible but the specific wording is unverified.

text: Any change into a new state of being is the result of the fullness of nature unfolding inherent potential.
text_raw: Any change into a new state of being is the result of the fullness of nature unfolding inherent potential.
author: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali

provenance.notes: This maps closely and specifically to Yoga Sutra IV.2 — 'jatyantara-parinamah prakrty-apurat' — the transformation into another state of being comes about through the filling-in/overflowing of prakriti (nature). 'Change into a new state of being' = jatyantara-parinama; 'fullness of nature' = prakrty-apura. The underlying source text is therefore identifiable with reasonable confidence, but the English is an unidentified modern translation and I will not name a translator or edition I cannot confirm. Held below 0.8 for that reason.

text: Do everything with so much love you would never want to do it another way.
text_raw: "Do everything with so much love you would never want to do it another way."
author: Yogi Amrit Desai

provenance.notes: Yogi Amrit Desai (founder of Kripalu Center) is a real teacher and this is consistent with his idiom, but I cannot place the line in any of his books, talks, or in a Kripalu publication from training knowledge. It circulates mainly on quote sites and yoga-studio ephemera, which is weak evidence. Plausible but unconfirmed.

text: The future isn’t what it used to be.
text_raw: The future isn’t what it used to be.
author: Yogi Berra

provenance.notes: Berra used the line and claimed it in 'The Yogi Book: I Really Didn't Say Everything I Said!' (1998), so the attribution is not baseless — but the saying substantially predates him. It is commonly traced to Paul Valery, who wrote in the 1930s that the future 'is no longer what it used to be' (Regards sur le monde actuel), and English instances appear well before Berra's career-quote fame. Berra is the popularizer, not the originator. Confidence here reflects confidence in the attribution AS GIVEN, which is weak; my confidence in the earlier-origin finding is considerably higher. I have not confirmed a page/edition for the Valery line and so leave the print source null. | Suggested reattribution: Paul Valery (earlier form, 1930s); popularized in English by Yogi Berra

text: If your mind isn’t clouded by unnecessary things, this is the best season of your life.
text_raw: If your mind isn’t clouded by unnecessary things, this is the best season of your life.
author: Yunmen Wenyan

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Gateless Gate (Wumenguan / Mumonkan), Wumen Huikai, 1228 — case 19, closing verse
provenance.notes: This is the second half of Wumen Huikai's verse to Case 19 of the Wumenguan ('Ordinary Mind is the Way'): 'Hundreds of flowers in spring, the moon in autumn, a cool breeze in summer, snow in winter. If your mind isn't clouded by unnecessary things, this is the best season of your life.' (若無閑事挂心頭，便是人間好時節). Not Yunmen Wenyan — the confusion likely arises because Yunmen is the source of the similar-sounding 'Every day is a good day' (Blue Cliff Record, case 6). I am confident in this reattribution. | Suggested reattribution: Wumen Huikai (Mumon Ekai), The Gateless Gate, case 19 verse

text: Seek not to follow in the footsteps of the ancient masters. Seek what they sought.
text_raw: Seek not to follow in the footsteps of the ancient masters. Seek what they sought.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.notes: Not an anonymous proverb — this is Matsuo Basho, from the short prose piece commonly translated as 'Words by a Brushwood Gate' (Saimon no ji): 'Do not seek to follow in the footsteps of the men of old; seek what they sought.' The rendering in wide English circulation comes largely through Robert Aitken's 'A Zen Wave: Basho's Haiku and Zen' (1978); I recall the attribution firmly but not the exact page, so I leave the print source field null rather than guess an edition. | Suggested reattribution: Matsuo Basho (1644-1694)

text: Do not seek the truth, only cease to cherish your opinions.
text_raw: Do not seek the truth, only cease to cherish your opinions.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.notes: This is a line from the Xinxin Ming (Hsin Hsin Ming, 'Verses on the Faith Mind') traditionally attributed to Jianzhi Sengcan, the Third Chan Patriarch (d. 606): 不用求真，唯須息見 — 'Do not seek the truth; only cease to cherish opinions.' Genuinely Zen, so the category label is not wrong, but a specific text and author are identifiable and should replace 'Zen proverb'. Traditional authorship of the Xinxin Ming is itself disputed by scholars (the text is likely later than Sengcan), which is why I do not go higher. | Suggested reattribution: Jianzhi Sengcan (traditional), Xinxin Ming

text: If you understand, things are just as they are; if you do not understand, things are just as they are.
text_raw: If you understand, things are just as they are; if you do not understand, things are just as they are.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.notes: A widely circulated Zen saying whose textual origin I cannot establish. It is often reproduced in English-language Zen anthologies and in Alan Watts-influenced literature, and it may derive from a Zenrin Kushu couplet, but I cannot confirm a Chinese or Japanese original or a first English printing. Honest unknown.

text: When you seek it, you cannot find it.
text_raw: When you seek it, you cannot find it.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.notes: A fragment of a longer saying that circulates in several forms ('When you seek it, you cannot find it... when you no longer seek it, it is always with you'). I cannot place it in any Chan or Zen text I know, and the short form given here has no traceable source. Treat as unsourced.

text: The ten thousand questions are one question. If you cut through the one question, then the ten thousand questions disappear.
text_raw: The ten thousand questions are one question. If you cut through the one question, then the ten thousand questions disappear.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.notes: The diction ('ten thousand questions... cut through the one question') strongly resembles the teaching idiom of Korean Son master Seung Sahn, whose talks and letters ('Dropping Ashes on the Buddha', 'The Compass of Zen') repeatedly reduce all questions to one 'don't know' question. I am not confident enough to name him as the source, so I leave the reattribution null per the rules. Not an anonymous traditional proverb, in any case — it reads as a 20th-century teacher's phrasing.

text: Though the bamboo forest is dense, water flows through it freely.
text_raw: Though the bamboo forest is dense, water flows through it freely.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.notes: Genuinely traditional: half of the well-known Chan couplet 竹密不妨流水過，山高豈礙白雲飛 — 'However dense the bamboo, it does not stop the water flowing through; however high the mountain, it does not hinder the white clouds from drifting past.' The couplet is collected in the Zenrin Kushu (the Japanese anthology of Chan sayings) and appears in Chan recorded-sayings literature. 'Zen proverb' is an accurate attribution. I do not cite a specific edition/date for the Zenrin Kushu because I am not sure enough of its compilation and printing dates to state them.

text: To follow the path, look to the master, follow the master, walk with the master, see through the master, become the master.
text_raw: To follow the path, look to the master, follow the master, walk with the master, see through the master, become the master.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.notes: No basis in any Chan or Zen text I know. The five-step 'look to / follow / walk with / see through / become the master' progression is a modern Western self-development formulation of the kind that gets a 'Zen proverb' label attached to it on quote sites. Zen literature tends in the opposite direction on this theme (see Basho's 'seek what they sought', or Linji's 'if you meet the Buddha, kill him'). Recommend treating as unsourced modern coinage.

text: All of the significant battles are waged within the self.
text_raw: All of the significant battles are waged within the self.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.earliest_print_source: If You Meet the Buddha on the Road, Kill Him!, Sheldon B. Kopp, 1972
provenance.notes: This is an item from Sheldon Kopp's 'An Eschatological Laundry List: A Partial Register of the 927 (or was it 928?) Eternal Truths', the closing list of his 1972 book. The book's Zen-flavored title (from the Linji koan) is very likely why items from that list drifted into circulation as 'Zen proverbs'. I recall this specific item with reasonable confidence; I do not recall a page number and so do not give one. | Suggested reattribution: Sheldon B. Kopp

text: Life is the only thing worth living for.
text_raw: Life is the only thing worth living for.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.notes: Not traceable to any Zen text I know. It has the aphoristic register of Sheldon Kopp's 'Eschatological Laundry List' (1972), which is the demonstrable source of at least one neighboring 'Zen proverb' in this batch, but I cannot confirm this line is on that list and will not assert it. Unsourced.

text: There is nothing infinite apart from finite things.
text_raw: There is nothing infinite apart from finite things.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.notes: I cannot place this in Chan or Zen literature. The formulation reads more like Western philosophical idealism (the Hegelian claim that the infinite is not something set apart from the finite) than a translated Buddhist source, though the sentiment is compatible with Mahayana non-duality. Origin unknown; the 'Zen proverb' label is unsupported.

text: Where there is great doubt, there will be great awakening; small doubt, small awakening, no doubt, no awakening.
text_raw: Where there is great doubt, there will be great awakening; small doubt, small awakening, no doubt, no awakening.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.notes: A genuine traditional Chan/Zen maxim: 大疑大悟，小疑小悟，不疑不悟. It is strongly associated with Hakuin Ekaku (1686-1769), who quoted and expanded on it constantly ('beneath great doubt lies great awakening'), but it predates him in Chinese Chan — versions are attributed to Song-era masters such as Mengshan Deyi and appear in Boshan's exhortations on rousing doubt. So 'Zen proverb' is defensible as an attribution; if a person is wanted, Hakuin is the popularizer rather than the originator. Held below 0.8 because I cannot cite a specific text and edition.

text: Sitting peacefully doing nothing, spring comes and the grass grows all by itself.
text_raw: Sitting peacefully doing nothing, spring comes and the grass grows all by itself.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.earliest_print_source: The Way of Zen, Alan W. Watts, 1957
provenance.notes: A real Zenrin Kushu couplet — 兀然無事坐，春來草自青 — made famous in English by Alan Watts, who renders it in 'The Way of Zen' (1957) as 'Sitting quietly, doing nothing, / Spring comes, and the grass grows by itself.' The stored text ('Sitting peacefully') is a variant of Watts' wording; consider normalizing to the standard rendering. 'Zen proverb' is an accurate attribution for the underlying couplet; Watts is the English source.

text: Even a good thing isn't as good as nothing.
text_raw: Even a good thing isn't as good as nothing.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.notes: Corresponds to the common Chan phrase 好事不如無 — literally 'a good thing is not as good as nothing', i.e. better no affairs at all. It is a stock phrase in Chan recorded sayings and koan-collection commentary and appears in Zen phrase anthologies, so the 'Zen proverb' label is accurate in substance. I cannot identify the earliest text, so I stay well below the promotion bar.

text: The one has many manifestations, and the many have one essence.
text_raw: The one has many manifestations, and the many have one essence.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.notes: The idea is authentically Huayan/Chan (一即一切，一切即一 — 'one is all, all is one', which appears in the Xinxin Ming and pervades Huayan thought), but this specific English sentence is not a recognized translation of any line I can identify. Likely a modern paraphrase of that doctrine rather than a quotation. Attribution to a Zen text is unverified.

text: You must become somebody before you can become nobody.
text_raw: You must become somebody before you can become nobody.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.earliest_print_source: Transformations of Consciousness, Ken Wilber, Jack Engler & Daniel P. Brown, 1986
provenance.notes: This is Jack Engler's well-known formulation from his work on the interface of psychoanalytic developmental theory and Buddhist meditation: 'You have to be somebody before you can be nobody.' It first appeared in his 1984 Journal of Transpersonal Psychology essay on therapeutic aims in psychotherapy and meditation, reprinted in 'Transformations of Consciousness' (1986). Its Buddhist subject matter is why it gets relabeled a Zen proverb; it is a 20th-century academic coinage, not a traditional saying. I am confident about Engler and the essay, less so about exact bibliographic details. | Suggested reattribution: Jack Engler

text: Man stands in his own shadow and wonders why it is dark.
text_raw: Man stands in his own shadow and wonders why it is dark.
author: Zen proverb

provenance.notes: Widely reproduced as a 'Zen proverb' on quote sites, and occasionally attached to Emerson or to unnamed 'Chinese proverb' labels, which is itself a sign of a floating attribution. I cannot place it in any Zen text or trace a first printing. The aphorism's shape (a neat English epigram with a single ironic turn) suggests a Western origin. Unsourced.

text: If your heart is pure, then all things in this world are pure.
text_raw: If your heart is pure, then all things in this world are pure.
author: Zen saying

provenance.notes: The doctrine is authentic — the Vimalakirti Sutra's 心淨則佛土淨 ('when the mind is pure, the buddha-land is pure') is the classic statement, echoed in the Platform Sutra — but this English sentence is not a translation of any passage I can identify, and 'heart' for mind/citta suggests a loose modern rendering. Genuinely Buddhist in sense, unverified as a quotation.

text: Things are not as they seem, nor are they otherwise.
text_raw: Things are not as they seem, nor are they otherwise.
author: Zen saying

provenance.notes: This line circulates very widely and is most often credited to the Lankavatara Sutra; it is also quoted freely in Zen contexts and in Western Buddhist writing. I recall the Lankavatara association clearly but cannot confirm the passage or a translation (Suzuki's 1932 English version is the usual candidate), so I do not assert the reattribution. The tetralemma structure ('not as they seem, nor otherwise') is characteristic of Madhyamaka/Yogacara phrasing, which makes a sutra origin plausible rather than certain.

text: Not always so.
text_raw: Not always so.
author: Zen saying

provenance.notes: As a generic 'Zen saying' this is untraceable — it is a three-word English phrase, not a rendering of a known koan, sutra line, or classical Chan formula I can place. The reason it circulates in English is Shunryu Suzuki: 'Not always so' is remembered by his San Francisco Zen Center students as one of his habitual correctives, and it supplies the title of the posthumous collection 'Not Always So: Practicing the True Spirit of Zen' (Suzuki, edited by Edward Espe Brown, HarperCollins, 2002), drawn from lectures given in the late 1960s and early 1970s. I am confident that book and title exist; I cannot pin the phrase to a specific dated lecture or to any pre-Suzuki print occurrence, so I am not recording an earliest print source. Suggesting Suzuki as the proximate English source rather than an anonymous tradition, but flagging that he was himself gesturing at a general Zen attitude, so 'Zen saying' is loose rather than flatly wrong. | Suggested reattribution: Shunryu Suzuki

text: To know and not do is not yet to know.
text_raw: To know and not do is not yet to know.
author: Zen saying

provenance.notes: Not Zen. This is the signature doctrine of the Ming neo-Confucian Wang Yangming (1472-1529), the unity of knowing and acting (zhi xing he yi), stated in the Chuanxi lu / 'Instructions for Practical Living' roughly as: there have never been people who know and do not act; those who know but do not act simply do not yet know. The English wording here matches the paraphrase popularized in Western business and self-help writing — Stephen Covey used a near-identical line ('To know and not to do is really not to know') in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), which is likely how it entered circulation with a vague Eastern-wisdom label that later hardened into 'Zen saying'. I am confident about the Wang Yangming doctrine and reasonably confident about the Covey transmission path; I am not confident enough about which translation produced this exact English sentence to name an earliest print source, so I am leaving that null rather than guessing at a Wing-tsit Chan page. | Suggested reattribution: Wang Yangming (paraphrase; popularized in English via Stephen Covey)
